One key element is understanding that since Election Day, influencers and prosumers in all those different niches started adopting some version of the conspiracy theory that claims that this election was stolen. This particular type of coalition is grounded in a network of social media sites and of course in the digital campaign of Trump itself (Maly, 2020d). These groups were born within mainstream platforms like Twitter, Reddit, YouTube and Facebook before some had to move to more fringe platforms like Gab, Parler and thedonald.32win after being deplatformed. In the months before the riot, all those niched groups used digital media to construct their own normalities, their partisan views of the world. In that world, the election was stolen by the left, the liberals or the deep state. The enemy was accused of manipulating the voting machines, stealing or throwing away ballots, or organizing fraud with mail-in and absentee ballots. The seeds for this myth were planted by Trump even before his election in 2016 – but of course, they resonated with discourses on the deep state that were already popular in many of those niches – and were carefully constructed by many of his performances during and after the elections. These conspiracy theories on the deep state are not new at all; they have a long history in the United States and were always connected to a far-right agenda that framed the ‘left’, and especially ‘the liberals’, as the key figures of that deep state (Lowndes, 2008). Trump’s electoral loss was read as the deep state taking over population control again. It created a sense of urgency and opposition to the democratic institutions of the United States.

Such conspiracy theories function as contemporary Sorelian myths. The Frenchman George Sorel was a prominent and influential anti-elitist and anti-democratic philosopher within revolutionary syndicalism that had a prominent impact on fascism as an ideology (Sorel, 2014). Sternhell saw in him a key figure in the birth of fascism (Sternhell, Sznajder, & Asheri, 1994). Myth was central to Sorel’s thinking about revolution and the overthrow of the bourgeois order. He saw myths as ‘groups of ideas’ or knowledge-constructs that can direct reality, people and movements. Those ideas didn’t need to be rational or true. What was important according to Sorel was that they had affective power. For him, myths had a social function. He saw them as a means to mobilize people.

If we look at the role of conspiracy theories from the perspective of this Sorelian concept of myth, we see how they function as a site of ideology:

  1. They contribute to the creation of a feeling of togetherness, a coalition that finds itself in opposition to the order in society.
  2. As such, these myths have an agentive function in society.
  3. Those myths create a common enemy but also a specific partisan perspective on society and on themselves.

Conspiracy theories like White Genocide, the Great Replacement or Stop the Steal affect the audiences and mould them into one group that opposes the same enemy. All those political conspiracy theories create a world in which the liberal elites are destroying traditional societies, and enable multiculturalism, feminism, and the destruction of Western culture. That is why debunking the myths doesn’t work. It didn’t matter that Pizzagate was debunked; the general idea – that the liberals are morally rotten – was still seen as true. And it should thus not come as a surprise that this same narrative plays a 33crucial role in QAnon theories. Important to note again is that those myths are not only cognitive-ideational phenomena; they are grounded in a material reality – digital media that are being used to (re)produce those myths – which is as important as the affective qualities of those myths in the mobilization of people. And just like digital media allow users to easily transgress borders, so too do conspiracy theories and new right theories. The effect is that digitalization allows for the birth of a transnational contemporary new right.

If we understand ideologies as ideas that penetrate the whole fabric of communities and result in normalized, naturalized patterns of thought and behaviour, then we should realize how important the role of digital media and their algorithms are in the construction of that normality (Blommaert, 2005: 159). The flow of ideas is at least partially organized by those algorithms. Also, the reach of these groups cannot be solely explained by the discourse they produce; all of those influencers and groups deploy ‘algorithmic knowledge’ to spread their discourse and construct a community around their profiles. Even more, their discourse on ‘censorship’ from the mass media and mainstream digital media platforms helps them to spread digital knowledge. Far-right influencers constantly stress the importance of getting the news out by sharing and liking. This produces fertile ground to grow a supportive culture. The other side of the coin is that the interaction with the personalization algorithms contributes to the construction of the niched groups circling around specific influencers and pages, whereas the recommendation algorithms help to build a transnational, layered and polycentric network of different micro-populations.

If we want to analyse ‘political ideologies’ and metapolitics in particular, we must not only focus on the content or the large ‘isms’, but also on the form, the communication economy, and the uptake. We need to understand how activists adapt to this new communicative economy and understand how they use it in their political struggle. This commercial algorithmically programmed attention economy creates a very specific environment in which activists develop new social relationships, new activist practices and new discourses. These new metapolitical practices are the result of their interaction with the algorithms and values of that platform. Metapolitics 2.0 is grounded in digital media and digital culture and has, in the end, an algorithmic logic. People will try to optimize their content, link to each other, have a network of fans which they ask to share content, or even have bots to push certain content. The algorithmic logic of this attention-based media environment forces us to understand the importance of algorithmic knowledge in the dissemination of far-right ideologies on the rise. Not only the management of visibility but also avoiding non-visibility, as Bucher (2018) stresses, is a constant worry for all actors in this media system, and is thus of crucial importance for all ideological projects. In line with Thompson, Blommaert argued that ideologies need to ‘be understood as processes that require material reality 34and institutional structures and practices of power and authority’ (Blommaert, 2005: 163). Hence, they cannot be understood without looking at how people spread those ideas, who they address, which media they use, and how those media format the discourses. Studying ideologies in the contemporary era means not only looking at the input but also at the uptake. Uptake here refers to

  1. the fact that within the digital ecology, users are not only consumers but also (re)producers of discourse, so-called prosumers; and
  2. that algorithms and the interfaces of digital media play an important role in the dissemination and reproduction of ideas.

Uptake realizes visibility. Human and non-human actors (from bots to the algorithms organizing the communication on a platform) are a crucial part of any ideological and political battle.

Globalization as context

If we accept the idea that digital infrastructures have become part of ‘social structure’, and thus function as one of the deep invisible drivers behind actual conduct, we subsequently have to see globalization as context. Taking context seriously in times of digitalization means considering the meaning-making effects of the scales on which those infrastructures operate. Facebook, Twitter, Reddit, Instagram, YouTube and even Gab, Parler and DLive are infrastructures of cultural globalization. They take a central place in contemporary culture and thus in meaning-making processes. This does not result in a homogenous culture. Not only the Capitol riots showed the temporal merging of niched groups; we saw the same thing in the 2016 support of Trump and on a global scale: the growth of the contemporary new right. Digital media facilitate local cultural production as well as more globalized cultural niches and complex threads between all those centres of normativity. The national imagined community is replaced by many different imagined communities and imagined worlds operating on different scales and orienting themselves towards different centres of normativity that function as orders of indexicality (see Blommaert, 2005 and 2010 for an in-depth discussion).

Even if certain practices, norms and discourses enjoy global uptake through one of those media, we should always remember that these pieces of culture always are deglobalized: they again become part of the local as people interact with them, adjust them and appropriate them to function in their own lives and concrete contexts. The contemporary far-right is a good example of globalization as ‘a complex of processes, evolving and developing at different scale-levels, with differences in scope, speed and intensity’ (Blommaert, 2020a: 17). The success of the alt-right in amplifying its message and grabbing 35attention of American media first, and later media in the rest of the world, gave far-right actors around the world confidence. Even more, the alt-right became an important normative centre in a global network of far-right movements, individuals and actors. They introduced new metapolitical practices, new norms and discourses that were englobalized and deglobalized again by local actors. The popularization of the (meta)-political meme by the alt-right is a simple but effective example of such cultural processes. Far-right activists were not just using those alt-right memes but were adapting them to fit local situations.

A ‘simple’ example of these complex processes of globalization can be seen in the meme below (Figure 1.1). The Smug Pepe meme in support of Trump’s Border Wall plans to keep Mexican migrants outside of the United States widely circulated during the 2016 campaign of Donald Trump. The meme pictures Trump as a Smug Pepe and was first posted on July 22nd, 2015 by 36Malaysian artist Maldraw on 4chan’s /pol/ board.

This ‘simple’ example is in reality a highly complex multimodal communicative device reflecting deep social, cultural and communicative traditions that have their origins in very different normative centres of cultural production. The first poster was Malysian. Smug Pepe goes back to the Boy’s Club web strip where Pepe first appeared, long before it became a meme first on 4chan and later all over the internet. The format in which Smug Pepe was accompanied by the Feel Guy was now re-entextualized in a clearly political setting. The history of use of the meme sticks to the new political version of the meme and presents Trump as smug and edgy. Not long after that meme was posted, we saw that Pepe came to be appropriated not only in favour of Trump but also as a vehicle to open the Overton window for more far-right ideologies. Pepe, far-right trolls on 4chan claimed, was stolen by normies, and they wanted him back. This narrative around the meme becomes a very important vehicle, not only to draw attention from mainstream media, but also to build an edgy and vibrant far-right culture online (Nagle, 2017; Maly, 2018a).

The metapolitical effect of that culture was amplified by Trump retweeting himself as Pepe and Clinton (Reilly, 2016) holding a press conference on that tweet claiming that it was proof of Trump being far-right and racist. This, of course, just fed the trolls who were very fast to exploit the strategic ambivalence of ironic Pepe memes, pointing out that Pepe was just the ‘feel good’ frog from the Boy’s Club strip. The speech also grabbed the attention of eyeballs around the world and can be seen as the start of polycentric processes of englobalization and deglobalization.

In Figure 1.2 we see how the Smug Trump meme got globalized and deglobalized again. This deglobalization becomes visible in the semiotic rearrangement that makes those memes usable on a local scale. The First thing that we notice is that, in a European context, the Mexican migrants have been replaced by Feels Guys in stereotypical Islamic clothing. Note that the woman is not just wearing a headscarf but a Burka and thus functions as an emblem of extremism. This is reminiscent of the far-right discourse on Muslims and Islam as inherently radical and clashing with ‘our European values’ (Maly, 2007). The memes are not only adjusted to the European context but also to the different national contexts. In the case of Le Pen in France and Wilders in the Netherlands, Smug Pepe could be turned in to the local politicians by replacing one emblematic haircut by another. Whereas in Great Britain and Poland, Pepe was dressed in the colours and patterns of the national flag, and 37in Germany, Pepe received the official blue of the far-right political party of the AFD. Globalization is clearly not a homogenizing cultural process. And more importantly, Pepe is not ‘decontextualized’, nor is ‘the iconic image (…) ideologically empty, emerging instead as a symbol of generalized resistance’ (Miller-Idriss, 2017: 136). Pepe the Frog is constantly deglobalizated and thus re-contextualized to make it work in this new context. Important to realise, though, is that its original meaning still sticks to the meme. It is the history of Pepe, and its connection to the alt-right and the Webstrip, that makes it not only an ‘edgy’ and cool meme, but also one in which strategic ambivalence (Maly, 2018a) or ‘humorous ambiguity’ (Bogerts & Fielitz, 2019) and mischievous ambivalence (Phillips & Milner, 2017) can be exploited. Being mobilized in a new context for new goals means that the memes acquire additional layers of meanings.

If we follow Shifman’s definition of a meme ‘as a group of digital items sharing common characteristics of content, form and/or stance that were created with awareness of each other and created and shared via the internet by many users’, we see how this Smug Trump Pepe becomes an index of a contemporary transnational new right (Shifman, 2014: 7–8). From a metapolitical perspective, all those memes communicate a similar message: they promote an ethnoplural world order made up by homogenous societies. The fence and the different cultural indexes in the form of traditional clothing articulate the neo-racist message. Even more, as we can see in Figure 1.3, 38the same form and stance can be easily adapted to other far-right metapolitical messages. Together those memes preconfigure a new ethno-differentialist world order grounded in ethnically and cultural homogenous societies that target the cause of decadence and decline: the left. Important to notice is that the activists always do this from a local position. The Nordic Resistance Movement in Sweden can for instance use Skurt – a frog-like hand puppet from a children’s Swedish TV show – for metapolitical goals (Askanius & Keller, 2021). Even though Pepe is not mentioned or used here, being a frog, Skurt imports the edgy meaning of Pepe in Sweden. Activists thus use and abuse the resources circulating in niches and different scales and adapt them for local metapolitical use.

Contexts: methodological lessons

What to take away from this? The first point to take home is that we have to abandon methodological nationalism in the study of the contemporary new right. If one would only look and analyse those memes from a methodological nationalistic perspective, one would miss the layered meaning of those memes. The memes, even though local, orient themselves to different centres operating on different scales and their meaning cannot be reduced from the meaning they are attributed in a local context. Pepe in itself has become emblematic of the contemporary metapolitical strategies. Cultural practices of new right actors cannot be seen as just local activism, they are like most contemporary cultural practices polycentric, orienting towards multiple evaluative centres on different scales. The memes as metapolitical devices not only 39index a transnational far-right meme culture or meme culture in general, they exist in the combination of many different normative centres – from the alt-right, La Nouvelle Droite, Chan-culture and centres operating on the local scales. As Blommaert and De Fina (2017) argue, those polycentric cultural practices orient towards multiple evaluative centres and are being enabled and sanctioned by ever-changing timespace or chronotopic configurations. Chronotope, as a ‘new’ word for context, invites us, argued Blommaert (2020b) ‘to critically check the ways in which we use the term “context” in a wide range of disciplines within the study of language in society’. The word is of course from Bakhtin, who introduced it to refer to ‘the intrinsic connectedness of temporal and spatial relationships’ (Bakhtin, 1981: 84). Bakhtin’s notion of chronotope has been picked up in quite some sociolinguistic research (see Kroon & Swanenberg, 2020 for an overview) as an invitation ‘to extract and connect multiple social meanings and agencies represented in a story, but also more generally, as cultural chronotopes, i.e “depiction(s) of place-time-and-personhood to which social interactants orient when they engage each other through discursive signs of any kind”’ (Agha, 2007: 320) (Kroon & Swanenberg, 2020: 3). Chronotopes is in this sense an invitation to see the context in a very specific way. Blommaert (2020b) highlights four characteristics of this chronotopic interpretation of context:

  • - A view of context as a specific set of features both affecting and producing specific modes of social action;
  • - In which such features have very clear and empirically demonstrable timespace characteristics – the actual timespace constellation is the determining feature for understanding the actual text-context patterns we observe;
  • - In which some of these features can be carried over, so to speak, into different timespace constellations while others are non-exportable;
  • - And in which a precise understanding of timespace configurations is essential to account for a great deal of the sociocultural work performed in interaction.

Chronotopes invoke a sociolinguistic and ethnographic understanding of context. ‘The notion of chronotope invites us’, says Blommaert (2020b),

To treat aspects of context often dismissed or summarily taken into account in branches of scholarship, and to treat them with utmost precision as non-random elements of social situations that may account for much of how people make sense of social structure in actual moments of social action.

Context cannot and should not be narrowed down to the immediate setting of the communicative act; it should also take into account the larger ‘social 40situation’, as Goffman called it. The latter cannot be invoked as a ‘passe partoe’, a ready-made a priori context, but should be analysed in the actual communicative act. Context is thus not just something that influences communication, communication also creates context by using certain resources in specific ways. Discourse analysis should thus not stick to analysing discourses as examples of certain larger evolutions: they should analyse them as making structure, making context.

Human creativity and meaning-making doesn’t happen in a vacuum, in the abstract or in local situations only. The social situation provides scripts to make sense in a specific situation; at the same time – by choosing certain scripts above others, humans construct that social situation. As we have seen above with the small example of the meme, it is important to realize that the social situation cannot be understood as something local or stable: our object of research is language-in-motion (Kroon & Swanenberg, 2020: 2). If we try to understand how people create meaning in relation to social structure, or in other words how they contextualize their meaning-making, we should not a priori exclude the notion that this context is at least in potential global. The meme in many cases only ‘works’ on a local scale because it has historicities in other parts of the world, in other niches. Activists knowingly play, use and abuse those meanings to generate local and translocal effects. The main argument, of course, is that globalization is relevant in our understanding of local politics and political activism and thus should be part of our analysis. Post-digital societies create new possibilities and constraints for the production and circulation of discourse. New producers and new relationships have been established between the different actors in this media system and they have had fundamental effects on the construction and circulation of (meta)political messages and meanings. The new communicative economy creates a polycentric and translocal world of communication (Blommaert, 2010). Such a world is far more complex than a world dominated by the so-called ‘national mass media’. Analysing discourse in such a context cannot be limited to the ‘content’, but should also take the systems of communication, the layered transnational context, the different actors and the historicities and trajectories of cultural material into account. This post-digital world creates enormous challenges for scholars of ideology, politics and the far-right in particular; it forces us to update our toolkit. Not only does the world force us to take a more interdisciplinary approach to our research. Engaging with contextualization processes is a conditio sine qua none. The good news is that it may help us to develop more fine-grained analysis that considers the full context, including the socio-technical context. In summary, the new post-digital society forces us to take a more ethnographic stance as the foundation of more interdisciplinary approaches (Arnaut et al., 2016).

41

Digital ethnographic discourse analysis

The different case studies that I present in this book are part of a long-term digital ethnographic discourse analytical research project dedicated to the study of the new right movements and politicians and their use of digital media (see Maly, 2017, 2018a, 2018b, 2018c, 2019, 2020, 2021). I entered this field as an outsider and gradually learned the language, the memes, the cultural practices, the theoretical founding works and the different hubs that rose to power and influenced the whole network. I also entered that field as a cultural scientist with a very specific set of lenses and methodologies to analyse those groups, their discourses and ideologies. This approach is grounded in a long history of ethnographic focus on discourse (Hymes, 1996; Scollon & Scollon, 2003) and more recent digital ethnographic work (See Varis, 2016; Varis & Hou, 2019; Blommaert & Dong, 2020; Maly, 2022). I adapted this digital ethnographic approach to analyse far-right activism in a digital context. In the next sections of this chapter, I want to introduce this digital ethnographic approach to discourse analysis. I will start abstractly and work towards more concrete methods and situating the data ethnographically.

An ethnographic approach to discourse and discourse analysis

Discourse analysis has always been a very broad field of research where many different approaches are used to study ‘discourse’. And even discourse itself means several different things to different scholars working in different disciplines. In general, introductory books to discourse make a distinction between discourse as language above the sentence, discourse as language in use and discourse as a form of social practice (see Schiffrin, 1994; Cameron, 2001; Cameron & Panovic, 2014). The more linguistic approaches to discourse have through time been expanded to include a more activity-related understanding of discourse (see Blommaert, 2005 for a useful oversight). I firmly position myself in this latest tradition. And I especially side with those who see the need to also expand that focus on discourse to include non-linguistic conceptions of discourse (Jaworski & Coupland, 1999). Discourse to me is inherently multimodal. Meaning, especially in a digital environment, is usually realized through more than one semiotic mode (Kress & van Leeuwen, 1996: 183). This multimodal approach to discourse, especially in post-digital societies, where ‘not only boundaries between more speech-like and more writing-like forms of the language are undergoing rapid unravelling (and) other forms of communication are making increasing and massive inroads into the domain of communication’ (Kress, 1997: 2), is crucial to make sense of meaning-making in digital and globalized contexts.

Memes, but also YouTube videos, may be the best arguments for such a multimodal approach to discourse. We can only uncover the full meaning of memes, but also of digital influencer practices and algorithmic activism, in 42relation to the different modes of communication, and of course also in relation to the uptake of content. An approach to discourse that only looks at linguistic modes of communication, that doesn’t take actions in focus (sharing for instance) and doesn’t take context, including technologies or globalization as context, seriously, will always be narrowing the scope and lose sight of important evolutions that change the meaning. In line with Jan Blommaert (2005), I see discourse as ‘all forms of meaningful semiotic human activity seen in connection with social, cultural and historical patterns and developments of use’. Such an ethnographic perspective on discourse sees discourse as intrinsically tied to context and human behaviour. But I think we need to even expand this definition (see Maly, 2022 for a more in-depth argument): in post-digital societies; we also need to include ‘non-human’ activity. As a lot of our communication is now mediated in one way or another, it is important to take on board the role of non-human activity in meaning-making processes. Features of digital media and the algorithms of digital media are, as we have seen in this chapter, an essential part of many mediatized interactions and are thus also intrinsically part of the meaning-making processes. To be able to say something about the political impact of memes, we have to realize that this meaning is at least partially connected to the spread of memes in the digital economy and the hybrid media system in general. Pepe acquired its full political potential because it was spread not only by trolls and anons on 4Chan, but also by the presidential candidates and by mass media. Meaning-making in a digital context is inherently connected to the popularity principle (van Dijck, 2013) that is engrained in the algorithms of the platforms (Maly, 2021) and in the attention economy in general (Venturini, 2019).

A digital ethnographic approach to discourse analysis allows researchers to include all those aspects of meaning-making. This approach is first and foremost grounded in ethnography and thus has its roots in anthropology (Blommaert & Dong, 2020). Ethnography is ‘continuous with ordinary life’, said Hymes (1996: 13). By this he meant that ethnographers seek to find out knowledge that others already have. ‘Ethnography typically looks for the meaning and rationality in practices that seem strange from afar or at first’ (Rampton, Maybin & Celia Roberts, 2014). Ethnographers are thus looking to learn the meanings, norms and patterns of a way of life. This book is an example of that approach, in which I used ethnography to understand the language and knowledge that new right groups share. I entered that field in 2015 when I prepared for my Digital Media and Politics classes. In search for a topic that a very international student population had at least some information about, I started looking at the US elections, and eventually the Trump campaign in particular. The United States was my first focus, and the killing spree of Dylann Roof made me aware of far-right sites like Council of Conservative Citizens, American Renaissance, InfoWars and the Alternative Right. The first steps in that field in 2015 were overwhelming. Most sites like 43the Right Stuff or the Daily Stormer and their memes were incomprehensible when I first started to follow them. They were written in English, but in an English that rarely made sense to me at that time. I had to learn what red pilling, black pilling, cucks and normies actually were. But also what a word like identity or community actually means in their discourses. At the time, there were no dictionaries to do that, I had to learn it the hard way, by observing how people used the words in context. This is where my ethnographic background and my previous work on Flemish nationalism paid off. Even though I at first did not understand certain particular words, my work on the anti-Enlightenment tradition allowed me to historicize these particular narratives. Learning the language is a condition sine qua non in ethnographic research. The sites where my fieldwork took place may not resemble the fields where Malinowski and Boas were active, the general principle of ethnography as deep immersion in the cultural life of specific groups is the same. Ethnography allows researchers to come to ‘grips with local meanings and emergent configurations’ (Hymes, 1996: XI). To a certain extent this approach is similar to Griffin’s empathetic approach to study fascism. In this approach, he attempts ‘to understand the movement on its own terms’, ‘to grasp how people saw’ the world and address ‘[their] perceptions of life and their hopes for the future’ (Griffin, 2001). In an ethnographic approach, this would mean that the ethnographer tries to uncover the knowledge that members of a group seem to ‘expect’, find ‘natural’ or ‘normal’. Each of us, said Hymes (1996: XI), ‘speaks (and writes) in a context of understandings and taken-for-granted conventions, a network of implication and form. And it matters to do these right, observation, asking, comparison, are needed, in short ethnography’. From such an ethnographic perspective, understanding life on their own terms would not necessarily mean ‘asking for knowledge’. On the contrary, the type of knowledge ethnographers are interested in doesn’t situate itself on the explicit level. Social structure and culture function mostly as implicit knowledge. It is to be found in the presuppositions that members of a group seem to share. Understanding and being able to theoretically describe the logic of those groups in relation to the context is probably the most central ethnographic quest.

Observation and participation together with interviews and fieldwork have traditionally been associated with ‘doing ethnography’, but those methods alone don’t make research ethnographic. In an ethnographic approach, interviews do not necessarily result in knowledge, but in data that needs to be analysed. The reasons for this are multiple. First, one cannot expect that people are conscience about everything that drives them in life and organizes their behaviour and discourse. ‘People are not cultural or linguistic catalogues, and most of what we see as their cultural and social behaviour is performed without reflecting on it and without an active awareness that this is actually something they do’ (Blommaert & Dong, 2020: 3). The interview 44from an ethnographic perspective is not a reflection of what is out there, but can only be studied as ‘an interpretation which is jointly produced by interviewer and respondent’ (Briggs, 1986: 3). Second, especially in the context of politics, we should understand that interviews for politicians or activists are the essence of their political or metapolitical battle. We cannot expect them to allow us in their kitchen and read the recipes. We can only analyse what has been put out there, and even when politicians or activists explicitly talk about their goals, plans and recipes, we should not treat that as knowledge but as data that needs to be analysed.

Ethnographic knowledge is thus always inter-subjective knowledge. It is the result of a process and is co-constructed by all participants in that process. The ethnographer is an essential part of the knowledge production. The biases and preferences but also knowledge of the ethnographer all affect the research he or she is doing. From the focus to the data collection, the coding and the highlighting are all testimonies of the presence of the ethnographer in the construction of knowledge. It is the ethnographer as a person who goes in the field and is thus part of the interview, part of the observation and thus also very much an inherent part of the process of knowledge making. Self-reflection and awareness of one’s own biases is of the utmost importance, as is being meticulous in analysing one’s role in the knowledge making process. The struggle to understand words, the first shock when registering certain outrageous talk, is all part of the ‘learning process’. It is as a human that one becomes acquainted with new normativities. Ethnography is

Open-ended, subject to self-correction during the process of inquiry itself. All this is not to say that ethnography is open- minded to the extent of being empty-minded, that ignorance and naivete are wanted. The more the ethnographer knows on entering the field, the better the result is likely to be.

(Hymes, 1996: 7)

Two lessons follow from this:

  1. First, ethnography starts long before entering the field with the gathering of knowledge but also with the socialization of the researcher. In this pre-fieldwork phase, the researcher gathers as much information as possible on the field and the larger context. The better one is prepared, the better the end result will be.
  2. Second, researchers should be prepared to reconsider their initial framework. Ethnographic research is dialectical, based on a feedback loop or an interactive-adaptive method usually referred to as ethnographic monitoring (Van der Aa & Blommaert, 2015). Self-reflection is a key ingredient of good ethnographic work (Pink et al., 2016).

45Ethnography in this anthropological tradition is clearly more than fieldwork or a complex of fieldwork techniques: it is part of a total programme of scientific description and interpretation, comprising not only technical and methodical aspects but also a specific epistemology and ontology (Hymes, 1996; Varis 2016; Blommaert & Dong, 2020). Central is humanism. Ethnography starts from a perspective on man as a social being, a being that uses and invests in language. Even more, it is through language that people make culture, communities and societies, and are at the same time made by those communities and cultures. This anthropological view on humankind almost necessarily captures language in a functionalist epistemology: language is the thing that people use to become social beings (Blommaert & Dong, 2020: 7). This functionalist background has fundamental ontological consequences on how ethnographers see language. Language is first and foremost understood in terms of ‘communication’, the language that people use makes them into social beings. Language is understood as one of the main tools by which people make sense of the world around them and construct that world around them. Language is the architecture of society. If an ethnographic approach is grounded in accurate knowledge of the meanings of behaviours, discourses and institutions to those who participate in the groups that are studied, it means almost necessarily that language-use-in-society is at heart of the matter. Language, and more specifically discourse as I described it above, is the way in for ethnographers. It is in and through language that normality and thus also culture and society is constructed on a daily basis. As I highlighted above, digitalization has allowed users to use resources from different corners of the world, to make sense locally and maybe also translocally. That is why the idea of studying ‘language in society’ is so complex in a post-digital society; it forces us to take globalization as context. Adopting a chronotopic perspective on context also means that the emphasis in this approach is on the relation between language and culture, and this starts with data: the things actually people do in society, how they use language to make sense and use language and knowledge of norms to keep themselves afloat in that society.

Context revisited, once more

Language in the abstract is not important in this ethnographic approach, but language as it is used by people (and machines). Language is a tool by which people can stay integrated or create a group. This ontology sees language use, or in Hymes’ words, communicative competence, as socially consequential for humans (Blommaert, 2018a: 4). If one does not know how to communicate in a certain situation, one has a high chance of not being accepted in that group, of becoming or being seen and treated as an outsider (Becker, 1963). Knowledge of norms, including norms about language use in the broadest sense of the word (such as posting the right memes, websites, 46and using the right words), is thus always connected to power, and breaking rules has powerful effects. Language in this sense is the glue of social groups. A good example would be the function of neo-racism in the construction of communities of new racists.

This sociocultural view also means that language, from an ethnographic perspective, can never be ‘context-less.’ As we have seen when we discussed chronotopes, context is not something ‘outside’ language; it is an inherent part of language and meaning-making (Gumperz, 1982). Context is not the stable a priori world that we can use as a pre-defined décor in which we place our object of analysis. On the contrary, context is dynamic, unstable and constantly made and remade in and through language (see Blommaert, 2018a for more information). Context is intrinsically connected and interwoven in our data. Ethnography belongs to the paradigm of ‘conjectural’ sciences, in which small indices of phenomena are seen and analysed as instances of their structural characteristics (Diggit, 2020).

Contextualization has always been a central aspect of ethnographic research, but in the context of contemporary societies, ethnographers are confronted by ‘new types of issues related to contextualisation’ (Varis, 2016). The technological properties of the online world (persistence, searchability, replicability, scalability, algorithmically constructed reality) shape online interactions (boyd, 2014) and are part of contemporary meaning-making processes. Digital media are, as I have argued above, not just intermediaries, but mediators. They (partially) shape or direct the performance of social acts (van Dijck, 2013: 29) as people adapt their behaviour and communication to keep integrated into this new context. Digital media not only affords discourse production, but it also directs discursive behaviour: certain digital affordances request, encourage and push users towards ‘particular communicative and interactive practices by means of quantified processes’ (Georgakopoulou, Iversen & Stage, 2020: 24). Digital media and especially the algorithms, or at least our imagination of what algorithms do, is an inherent part of ‘meaning making’. Liking, retweeting, sharing, and editing are now not only enabling but also shaping (new forms of political) communication (Maly, 2018a, 2018d, 2018e), offline social action (Blommaert & Maly, 2019), political organizing (Gerbaudo, 2014), and affective attachment (Papacharissi, 2015). Digital media force everyone who studies (meta)political discourse (online) ‘to rethink our very definitions of terms such as text, context, interaction and power’ (Jones et al., 2015: 5) and their methodological approaches (Crosset, Tanner, & Campana, 2019; Maly, 2022a).

If we include digital media as actors and context, then we also understand that communicative competence is not only about linguistic or even semiotic practices, it also includes algorithmic imagination (Bucher, 2018) or algorithmic knowledge (Maly, 2018, 2019) and stylization of the post in relation to algorithmic circulation (Glotfelter, 2019), and thus algorithmic audiences 47(Gallagher, 2017). Brenton Tarrant not only used different linguistic and semiotic means and modes to communicate his message to politicians, mass media and online anons, but he also imagined different roles of those audiences to give meaning to his act. Even more, he also was very much conscious about the role of media themselves. The fact that he uploaded his manifesto on different servers shows that he didn’t conceive digital media as neutral intermediaries. He considered the possible algorithmic or human interventions that could have halted the uptake of his message. The same digital literacy speaks from his call to the anons to repackage his message in memes. Contemporary digital political activism is thus also about ‘digital literacies and strategies to determine how algorithms work in different environments (...) and making pragmatic inferences regarding their workings’ (Varis & Hou, 2019). Consequently, digital activist practices should be studied as socio-technical assemblages (Chadwick, 2017: 110–111) or assemblages of actions, discourse, and tools ‘associated with digital technologies, which have come to be recognized by specific groups of people as ways of attaining particular (. . .) goals’ (Jones et al., 2015: 3).

Once we take on board the ethnographic notion of contextualization and accept the idea that discourse is contextualized language, ‘we shall’, as Blommaert argued decades ago, ‘be forced to deploy concepts of considerable elasticity, adaptable to new data and new forms of analysis which will be forced upon us’ (Blommaert, 2005: 235). Contextualization in a post-digital society proves Blommaert’s point. Context today refers not only to ‘specific historical contexts and processes within which, and by means of which they (symbolic forms) are produced, transmitted and received’ (Thompson, 1990: 145), but also to the technologies in themselves (Varis & Hou, 2019). In light of the affordances of social media, user-generated platforms and web 2.0 in general, the focus on reception, reproduction and on the affordances of digital media is more important than ever. Digital affordances not only refer to the technical capabilities of a platform but also to the action-taking possibilities and meaning-making opportunities (Vatrapu, 2009; boyd, 2014) that they enable. If we take the digital context into account, we realize that contemporary digital activism is not only about producing discourse in the (passive) hope that it will circulate and get picked up. It is also very much about actively organizing uptake within the digital environments. Activists and politicians have always invested in ‘uptake’, but that has been limited to the stylization of their message in the hope mass media would reproduce it (see, for instance, Silverstein’s 2003 discussion of the Gettysburg Address and the communication of George Bush, Jr.). Today, political communication is as much about talking to humans as it is about talking to, understanding, and using algorithms of particular interfaces to construct messages. It is about preparing discourse in relation to ‘algorithmic circulation’ (Glotfelter, 2019) and ‘algorithmic audiences’ (Gallagher, 2017) in order to reach their communication goals.

48Context and contextualization, in post-digital societies, benefit from a focus on participants, actions and the situated and evolving effects of those interactions (Blommaert, Smits, & Yacoubi 2020). Context is created in those interactions between people and machines. It is again important to stress here that in those small interactions, we can see the big structural changes in society. As we have seen in the example of the meme (and will see throughout the different cases in this book): the global is very much present in the local. In the hope of overcoming some of these challenges, and contributing to the development of new ethnographic methods and practices, I combine two research approaches here: long-term digital ethnography and ethnographic case studies.

Digital ethnography

This project is first and foremost a long-term digital ethnographic project; the foundation is made up of the daily observation of many different online new right media across different platforms over the last seven years. This book and the many articles that were published in this project were based on very concrete cases (think of the killing spree of Dylann Roof and Brenton Tarrant or the Gravensteen protest of Schild & Vrienden), but those cases were accompanied or are embedded in that long-term digital ethnographic project.

Long-term digital ethnography

For over seven years, I observed the global new right as if I was a far-right militant myself. I followed key far-right figures, movements, politicians and intellectuals on a very broad range of media, such as Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, YouTube, Telegram, Gab and Parler. I subscribed to newsletters, checked the websites of those organizations and read the books of their intellectuals. When some of them shared a post from another profile or organization, I started following and read up on that profile too. This type of passive participant observation is of course different from more traditional fieldwork.

  1. First of all, contrary to traditional ethnography, in this digital project participation is ‘passive’ and digital. Concretely, it means that my participation was mostly not visible to the other members. Only admins of pages could see my subscription.
  2. Second, as a researcher of the far-right, it is important not to contribute to racism, incitements to violence and contribution to the project. Therefore I choose to never be active in chat groups. I didn’t post on their walls, nor did I ever share messages of those actors or pages. I tried, at all costs, to keep my interaction to an absolute minimum in order not to enhance their reach. The participation was at best limited to ‘algorithmic defined reach’ of posts.
  3. 49Third, and contrary to other scholars of the far-right (see for instance Tebaldi, 2022a), I did subscribe to channels and newsletters, and bought books. Ethically, this was a difficult decision as subscriptions contribute to the spread and monetization that allows for this metapolitical activist success. This was a catch-22 situation, but considering my focus on contemporary metapolitical projects as socio-technical assemblages, I was forced to understand the impact of their interactions with digital media and thus be confronted with how my subscription reshaped the digital ecology in which I was doing research.
  4. Fourth, and contrary to classic ethnographic participant observation, I never aspired nor considered acting as a normal member of the group. This has the effect that I only analysed public data that was produced for uptake and circulation. Especially from the perspective of my focus on metapolitics, this didn’t cause any problems. My interest was first and foremost on the circulation and effects of that ideological battle and I didn’t focus on the intentions. The only exceptions to that rule were when mass media asked me to analyse data that they collected. This data was used in most part for triangulation.

The immersion in the transnational new right network let me understand it as a consumer of metapolitical messages. This meant that I had to understand it as a global network: the memes that I saw being used in the United States very soon arrived in Flanders where they were adapted for local use. I also saw that Flemish activists liked activists in Sweden and the United States and vice versa. As a result of such network effects, I also learned to know new influencers and sites that I then also started to follow. This digital snowball method allowed me and forced me to abandon any methodological nationalism. Restricting myself to a local, national context would have meant that I would deliberately change the layered and transnational meaning of actions and discourses and actively disregard the global dimension, and thus their history of use and abuse. It was this participant observation that also allowed me to understand the differences and similarities between the alt-right and alt-light, the American and the European new right, but also why neo-Nazi is maybe not the most precise term to describe the metapolitization of the far-right.

During this daily long-term observation, I thus behaved as a regular user grounded in Flanders, Belgium. It is from this very specific place in the world that I observed this global network of far-right movements, intellectuals, websites, publishers and think tanks taking shape. In practice, this means that I tried to keep updated on the actions and posts of local movements like Schild and Vrienden, and follow more globally relevant influencers and movements. In the United States, I started following alt-light media like Breitbart and Milo, but from June 2015 onwards I emerged myself in different alt-right 50groups and pages. Day by day, I followed more and more figures on social media, reading the materials of key organizations like Counter-Currents, american Renaissance, the National Policy Institute, The Daily Stormer and the Right Stuff. As a result of rapid changes in this field, following those big actors meant multiple journeys across different media through time. To give some examples: whereas in 2017 altright.com was a vibrant and constantly updated platform, it is now a deserted site only interesting as a look into the history of the alt-right. At one time, the Instagram account of Schild & Vrienden had a huge following of around 50,000 followers, but after the movement was deleted, the backup account only managed to gather around 3,500 followers and is mostly inactive. The Telegram page of the group is now the heart of the activity and of course the YouTube channel Kies Dries. At the same time, we see that certain platforms are stable producers of metapolitical content. Think about Counter-Currents, American Renaissance and Brittany Pettibone on YouTube. Others, like the Golden One, are constantly and cleverly navigating between different platforms, adjusting content in order to stay integrated into the digital ecology of mainstream platforms.

Historicities: intertextuality and entextualization

Analysing discourse cannot be limited to a focus on the actions or the relation to the platforms they use: in the fields of politics, actions can only be understood in their historic context. Understanding relations between groups, intellectuals and activists through time is of great importance. It allows us to be far more precise in assessing the positions and meanings of discourse, and it also allows us to uncover more hidden layers of meaning. Memes or vlogs may be new formats, and new contexts all play a role in meaning-making, but at the same time, intertextuality gives depth to our analysis. Intertextuality refers to the fact that all communication has a history and this history sticks to the utterance (Blommaert, 2005). It is the concept of intertextuality that allows us to interpret contemporary discourse in a long tradition of speaking. In research on metapolitics, and politics and ideology in general, a focus on intertextuality is of crucial importance. In contemporary discourse, we can see not only the local and the global but also different historicities: the longue durée, or the structural time, the conjunctural time and the short or eventual time (Braudel, 1980) are fused in one. Contemporary new right discourses are not entirely new, they are synchronizations of different historicities in one. It thus is important to analyse how contemporary discourse exists in the synchronization of different voices from different historicities.

When we discuss metapolitics, we cannot discuss the structural time of what Sternhell (2010) calls the anti-Enlightenment tradition: the two-century long intellectual, cultural and political movement starting with Vico 51Giambattista, Edmund Burke and Johann Gottfried Herder fighting for a second modernity and against the legacy of the French Enlightenment, rationalism, democracy, individualism and universal rights. This anti-Enlightenment tradition became the ‘dominant ideology’ – in the form of the so-called conservative revolution – during the Weimar Republic (Sternhell, 2010: 316). La Nouvelle Droite is not only influenced by the intellectual tradition of the conservative revolution and traditionalists like Julius Evola, and especially Guillaume Faye, for instance, takes on board key ideas of the technology embracing intellectuals within the conservative revolution, labelled by Jeffrey Herf as reactionary modernism (Herf, 1984). La Nouvelle Droite, Faye and De Benoist in particular have had a huge impact on contemporary far-right political discourse (Griffin, 2008; Bar-On, 2013). La Nouvelle Droite became a pan-European phenomenon with local and more transnationally operating intellectuals like Robert Steuckers, Pierre Krebs, Marco Tarchi, and Tomislav Sunic, who influenced local activists, intellectuals and politicians. La Nouvelle Droite was ‘at the very least a European school of thought’ and ‘its influence in Germany and Italy is at least equal to that which it has had in France’ (Camus & Lebourg, 2017: 125). This European new right manifested itself in journals, magazines and websites directed at many different national audiences (Tekos in Belgium, Tragressioni & Futuro Presente in Italy, Junge Freiheit in Germany, Zur Zeit in Austria, Disenso in Argentina, Maiastra in Romania, Hersperides in Spain). All these centres of metapolitical production were influenced not only by the local context but also have had translocal impact. This metapolitical impact was not limited to the contemporary time, it has created a lasting network of actors, centres of metapolitical production and of course also a long-term impact. This is the conjunctural time that speaks through contemporary metapolitics.

Intertextuality in the contemporary time allows me to focus on the explicit and implicit intertextuality between Herder, Burke, Spengler, Evola, Schmitt, Alain de Benoist, and Guillaume Faye’s work and the discourse of contemporary alt-right and identitarian activists, and different influencers, activists and terrorists around the world. It is in this intertextuality that we see not only the global new right emerging as a polycentric, transnational niche but also see how the global new right manifests itself locally. Taking intertextuality and thus the histories of texts seriously is the best remedy against methodological nationalism. A focus on intertextuality forces researchers to take context seriously and thus to see how context functions as a resource to be deployed in metapolitical battles. This brings me to the importance of entextualization. With entextualization, following Blommaert (2005) and Silverstein and Urban (1996), I refer to the processes of decontextualization and recontextualization of discourses. Following Jones, social media platforms are ‘technologies of entextualisation’ (Jones, 2015: 35). I understand technologies of entextualization as technologies that facilitate the process of turning 52actions into ‘text’ and at the same time also facilitate the recontextualizing of those actions. Interestingly, the algorithmic nature of social media platforms means that not only humans entextualize but also algorithms. Through datafication and algorithms, the platforms themselves turn activities into ‘text’ that is presented to users of the platform (Maly, 2022a). Re-entextualization and technologies of re-entextualization are crucial to understanding, for instance, the uptake of Faye’s work, the meme culture of the Alt-right and the highly mediatized actions of the French Identitarians. Uptake through digital media generates (new) meanings in new contexts. The importance of a focus on re-entextualization is for instance illustrated in the uptake of Faye’s conceptualization of metapolitics in the United States, where the activists seem to read over his anti-Americanism. But even more, the re-entextualization of his ideas happened within a digital culture, that is a socio-technical culture, where the technical affordances ask for audience labour (in terms of influencer culture and share, likes and comments) to let ideas circulate. It is at this point that an action-centred case study method comes in handy.

The case method and live digital ethnography

In an ethnographic approach, a case method is understood as ‘a methodology in which one uses case analyses to demonstrate theory’ (Blommaert & Dong, 2020). A case study is thus not just a description of an event or an incident, it is used to make one or more theoretical claims. The case is theorized into ‘a case of something’. An ethnographic case is used because it is theoretically ‘telling’ (Rampton, Maybin & Roberts, 2014). Rather than presenting typical cases, ethnographers use ‘the particular circumstances surrounding a case… to make previously obscure theoretical relationships suddenly apparent’ (Mitchell 1984: 239 quoted in Rampton, Maybin & Roberts, 2014). The case allows ethnographers to not only go into the details but also to show how the local and the big are connected, how structures influence meaning and how the case deepens theoretical understanding.

In a case study approach, researchers can focus on the details of the actions and their effects in their social, economic, political and technological context. ‘It allows us to look not only how discursive events are staged and recorded IRL with the deliberate purpose of online dissemination’ (Önnerfors, 2021: 179), but also at the uptake and interactions it generates online and offline. Thompson (2020) directs our attention to the fact that communication and thus interaction within the hybrid media system ‘is dialogical in character; and unlike mediated interaction (e.g. telephone conversations), it is oriented towards a multiplicity of other recipients – it is many-to-many rather than one-to-one.’ While in theory, it is correct that the affordances of social media platforms like Facebook, Twitter, YouTube and TikTok allow for interaction with a multiplicity of other recipients, in practice this is far from evident. Reaching a multiplicity of users requires careful algorithmic 53work (Maly, 2018a, 2018b, 2019, 2020, 2021). As I argued in previous work (see Maly, 2022a for an in-depth methodological discussion), on the public pages (even those with strict privacy settings) there is no linear communication between sender and receivers, only indirect communication in an algorithmic and datafied environment. All online interaction on the walls and newsfeeds of social media platforms is turned into online quantified data, and on the basis of the current and previous interactions, algorithms will decide what becomes visible to whom, when, where, how and for how long or how many times. Some media will even make strong suggestions on what to post or write. Take the example of Facebook suggesting commemorative posts to users, or actively adding emoticons to certain words like ‘congrats’ in comments. These are all indexes of the agency of algorithms and of the fact that each public social media post first interacts with the algorithms and databases of the platform, and thus with non-human receivers, before ‘humans’ can interact with them (see Figure 1.4). It is those algorithms – on the basis of different goals, norms, and ideologies that are programmed in them – and the database those algorithms use, that decide what is worthy to be visible in 54the timelines of others. It is thus only after the algorithmic intervention that other humans will be able to see and interact with the post. Algorithms and databases are an essential part of mediated online interaction.

Interactions matter. They are not only part of the context, but they also contribute to the uptake of messages. These interactions are mediated and datafied in relation to algorithms. Interactions in terms of upvoting, liking, sharing and commenting thus not only directly contribute to meaning production, but they also do it indirectly by triggering algorithms who help push it throughout the media system where it reaches new audiences stretched over time and space (Maly, 2018, 2022a, Maly & Beekmans, 2018; Blommaert, 2020a;). These interactions create visibility and attribute meaning as dominant through media ideologies that tend to equate popularity with important, relevant signs of the people. Detailed and fine-grained attention to these processes allows us to avoid the fallacy of internalism. This fallacy is quite common in far-right online research that seems to suggest that uptake is an effect of the input text (Önnerfors, 2021).

In this book, I use two types of case studies in the hope of contributing to the existing methodologies and focus on the role of this socio-technical assemblage in meaning-making. The first type focusses on digital practices and cultures of one actor or a group of actors. The focus is on how far-right influencers try to integrate themselves and stay integrated in digital environments. The second type of case study focusses on events in real-time. These last case studies zoom in on how activists and movements use different media and their speed of interaction to steer the information flows.

The long-term case studies – like the analysis of Brittany Pettibone, The Golden One and Generation Identity – allow me to show how such metapolitical influencers use digital platforms for metapolitical battles. The cases that I analyse in this book are chosen from a theoretical perspective. They allow me to highlight not only the intertextual tradition in which their discourses fit but also the practices and cultures they adopt in service of their metapolitical battle. These types of case studies were long-term data-driven ethnographic studies. The focus was limited to the influencers and their media use from a perspective that saw their activities as socio-technical assemblages. The limited scope of the field allowed me to go in-depth, and to collect as much information as possible. The case on Pettibone for instance is based on data collection through long-term observation between 2017 and 2020 of Pettibone’s YouTube, Twitter, and Instagram accounts and her book ‘What Makes Us Girls’. The case on The Golden One also started with an observation. Close observations started in 2018 when I saw that many of the Flemish identitarians started to follow him. These observations were accompanied by the use of the digital archives of Twitter, YouTube, and Instagram and digital tools like Social Blade, TwitterTrails, and the Wayback machine. My analysis not only focuses on the discourse but also on the interaction 55between metapolitical influencer practices, digital technologies, and digital culture in order to generate uptake.

The second type of case study can be labelled as ‘live ethnography.’ Chadwick (2017: 71) introduces this methodological approach to describe ‘close, real-time, observation and logging of a wide range of newspaper, broadcast and online material, including citizen opinion expressed and coordinated through online social network sites’. This ‘live ethnography’ builds further on the notion of ‘live research’ from Elmer (2013: 21), who stresses the need for such a ‘research paradigm’ in order to ‘take into consideration the speed of communication’. This focus on speed is connected to the affordances of digital media that allow actors to quickly intervene in the public debate and have an impact on the information cycles. These affordances, as Chadwick (2017) has argued, have created a shift in mediated temporalities and enabled a move from the news cycle paradigm to a digital media-enabled ‘political information’ cycle. The reason why I have adopted this approach is to try to understand how activists try to ‘game’ algorithms of platforms in order to gain visibility. Time is a crucial element in order to achieve visibility. The speed of interaction and the forms of interaction can thus be analysed from an algorithmic knowledge perspective.

The case of Schild & Vrienden is an example of such a live ethnography. It was based on two days (March 8 & 9, 2019) of intensive observation of activist interaction on the second post of the video of the intervention of Schild & Vrienden at the Gravensteen Castle on their Facebook page. I monitored, collected, and eventually analysed likes, interactions and shares from a perspective of (media-) ideologies and digital literacy of the activists, and thus as an inherent ingredient of their metapolitical activism. Speed is important here, as it is the speed of interacting and sharing that triggers the Facebook algorithms and helps in constructing ‘virality’ (Maly & Beekmans, 2018). My approach to digital ‘live ethnography’ differs from Chadwick (2017) and Elmer (2013) as it is grounded in a different notion of ‘context’. Elmer’s live research for instance is based first and foremost on a quantitative notion of context that equals ‘the context of a tweet’ with the time it was posted (Elmer, 2013: 23). I understand, as already indicated above, the context in a digital ethnographic tradition. As a result of this approach, I do not use digital extraction tools but engage in the centuries-old ethnographic notion of observation in combination with screenshotting and ‘following the social’ (Latour, quoted in Crosset, Tanner, & Campana, 2019: 3). The result was a substantial collection of 289 screenshots that not only carefully mapped the rise in likes, shares and comments, but also mapped the different users interacting with the post, their comments and strategies that completely decontextualize data (see Crosset, Tanner, & Campana, 2019 for such an approach).

56The analysis of the Groyper Trolls is another example of such a live ethnographic approach. This case study was the result of my long-term ethnographic engagement with different far-right groups in the United States. Nick Fuentes’s YouTube show ‘America First’ had been popping up regularly on my radar in the months before the actual show I analyse in this book. One night, as a result of following him on Twitter, I was notified on 30 October 2019 that he would be streaming his live reaction to Charlie Kirk’s tour stop-in on DLive. In particular, the reaction to the post from Digital 5.1 Groyper claiming, ‘we are coming big boy’, triggered my attention. Once logged in, I noticed the substantial uptake of Fuentes’ message, and of course, Fuentes’ excitement about what was about to happen, was the signal to drop everything and start following the stream, what happened on Twitter and on YouTube, and collect data in the form of screenshots.

This last case makes obvious that the digital ethnographer is confronted with the fact that the ethnographic field in the 21st century is a highly stretchable concept as it is in essence a polycentric, transnational, and layered field (Blommaert, 2010; Maly & Varis, 2016) spanning large distances and timezones. Following Fuentes and his Groypers from Flanders meant night work. Continuous real-time observation of local activism may, ‘as a result of the disembodied translocal nature of digital environments (…) be impossible simply for practical reasons’ (Varis & Hou, 2019: 14). Also, the field is so vast and it changes so rapidly, that it is impossible for one ethnographer to be on top of everything. And of course, we should realize that digital technologies enable multi-situated use of communicative tools that are more or less accessible to the ethnographer. What happens in the front and the back region is not necessarily all ‘observable’. It was implicitly clear that the offline interventions of the Groyper trolls were planned before the show through means not accessible to me. It is also known that Schild & Vrienden organized itself in different closed Facebook and Discord groups (Pano, 2018), and I didn’t have access to these groups. Data collection was thus partial, but as Blommaert and Dong (2020) stress, this has probably always been the case, also in the observation of offline activism.

I try to address those issues in three ways. First of all, I use the affordances of digital media (like time stamps, seeing when one has edited, analysing comments…) to partially remedy these shortcomings. Second, I only focus on publicly available data. What is analysed is the ‘front region’, or in other words, the activism that was prepared for uptake and visibility: the activism that was stylized, planned, formatted, and discursively constructed as ‘ready for impact’. In that public communication, I had detailed attention to indexes of publicly organizing of uptake. The post above from the Groyper of course indexes the organization of uptake and activism. Third, and this is where the long-term digital ethnography pays off, the digital data produced by activists of Schild & Vrienden or the Groypers, was complemented 57with the observations I made in the last years. My data, even in cases of live ethnography, is thus not only limited to the short time frame of the live ethnography, but also includes publicly accessible posts during the last years, broader cultural content, fieldnotes, interviews, and mass media attention to the movement.

It should be clear that my approach yields a different type of data than a big data approach (See for instance Rogers, 2018, 2021). Big data approaches allow us to see networks, connections between members and large-scale evolutions. An ethnographic approach focusses on the meaning and the depth of the networks by analysing how people network, and how ideas travel and morph through networks. The difference between such big data approaches and an ethnographic approach starts at the beginning of the research project. Whereas big data research, or multimethod research, usually starts by decontextualizing data through technological means, an ethnographic approach tries to capture the meaning-making process in context. Of course, screenshots also decontextualize data, but they are still a very rich way of capturing data: We can capture the interface, the order or interactions, the images, gifs and videos, the interactions themselves, the timestamps and so on. Even more, just like in traditional ethnography, screenshotting is done together with the practice of taking field notes and following the action on multiple platforms. As a result of this method, data can be analysed as ethnographic data (see Blommaert, 2018a: 113–119, for a useful discussion): as linguistic utterances in a certain social, technological, historical, and political context. This political communication is analysed on three axes: the past (or more concretely the modes of production, available resources and goals, media ideologies, and digital literacy), the now (the placement of the message in certain digital environments and how that message interacts with messages of others), and the future (how one designs the message for uptake) (Blommaert & Maly, 2016). By analysing the posts and the interactions on these axes, the ethnographer can acquire insights into their competences, resources, and (media) ideologies, how they want to be perceived, and how they envision their audiences. Analysing these data as ‘ethnographic data’ also means that I analyse one case of far-right metapolitics in its historical context, and thus vis-à-vis other producers of discourse.

The case studies can thus not be dissociated from the long-term ethnographic focus and are used as digital ‘ethnographic key incidents’ (Kroon & Sturm, 2007: 100–101). The ethnographic key incident approach involves the analysis of all kinds of qualitative data (fieldnotes, observations, and in this case also screenshots) and analysing them as texts-in-context and thus ‘linking them to other incidents, phenomena, and theoretical constructs and writing it up so that others see the generic in the particular, the universal in the concrete, the relation between the part and the whole’ (Erickson, 1977, as cited in Wilcox, 1980: 9). It is this long-term digital ethnographic research 58and its ‘trans-local’ aspect that allows me to contextualize the data in its broader historical, societal, political, and technological context and thus to provide a ‘thick description’ (Geertz, 1973), that is, to describe and analyse the activism as a political-techno-cultural and historical phenomenon.

This case study approach allows me to go deep into one case and highlight the different scales and dimensions of sociocultural processes of contemporary political local and digital activism. What is lost in ‘completeness’ of data collection is won in the contextual richness of the data. Both types of case studies complement each other and are connected to long-term digital ethnographic observations and other historical data on new right movements in Flanders and the world. I have already sketched one reason for this broad range of data above, namely the importance of understanding language in its historical, social, and technological context. Another reason is that in a hybrid media system, we should understand the dialectical relation between digital-niched media and mainstream media. Meaning is to be found in this complex discursive interdependence between different actors, media and mediators. The ethnographic notion of context that I introduced above has a profound effect on my ethnographic approach and on the data themselves. It is here that we see the importance of the ontology and epistemology of ethnography in the study of contemporary activism that ‘situates language in a web of relations of power, a dynamics of availability and accessibility, a situatedness of single acts vis-à-vis larger social and historical patterns’ (Blommaert, 2018a: 5).

65

2 The birth of metapolitics 2.0

DOI: 10.4324/9781003283379-3

This chapter has been made available under a CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 license.

Metapolitics is back. In the 21st century, the concept of metapolitics has been taken up by new right and identitarian movements and activists in the United States and Europe (Hawley, 2017; Maly, 2018a, 2019a; Zienkowski, 2019; Tebaldi, 2022a). Several key figures (Kirkpatrick 2014; Friberg, 2015, 2017; Spencer, 2017b) of the alt-right in the United States and the identitarian movements in Europe (Sellner, 2017a, 2017b, 2017c, 2017d; The Golden One, 2019) argue that metapolitics is at the heart of their battle for the construction of a future society. Their metapolitics is on the one hand inspired by La Nouvelle Droite, and on the other hand, it is clearly very different. Alain de Benoist and even Guillaume Faye would struggle grasping the metapolitical role of Pepe the Frog, Groyper riots or the performances of The Golden One. The contemporary metapolitical battle occurs in a post-digital world (Cramer, 2014), and this new world shapes contemporary metapolitics. In this chapter, I want to focus not only on the historical concept of metapolitics, but also show how a new, post-digital metapolitics has been created: a metapolitics 2.0.

I will first discuss the ideological dimensions of metapolitics. Metapolitics isn’t about a generic cultural battle of ideas, it is very much about the ideas themselves. Metapolitics cannot be discussed without highlighting the ideas that new right intellectuals and activists want to normalize. New right metapolitics is about the re-invention of an old ideological tradition. I will argue that the French new right and the contemporary re-emergence of the global new right is the post-WWII manifestation of the anti-Enlightenment tradition (Sternhell, 2010). After this historical detour, I will zoom in on how Guillaume Faye’s critique of La Nouvelle Droite has not only redefined 66metapolitics but also allowed its radical uptake by identitarians and the alt-right in the United States.

Metapolitics, the new right and the anti-Enlightenment tradition

The idea of right-wing metapolitics, as we saw in the introduction, goes back to the 20th century, to GRECE (Groupement de Recherche et d’Etudes pour la Civilisation Européenne), the ‘school of thought’ led by Alain de Benoist and better known as La Nouvelle Droite (Bar-On, 2007, 2013). In his influential and praised work, view from the right, Alain de Benoist saw metapolitics as part of a project to reinvigorate ‘the right’, the true right. Already in the introduction, de Benoist argued that

One of the tragedies of the right (…) is its inability to comprehend the necessity of the long term. (…) it has not grasped the significance of Gramsci. It has not seen how cultural power threatens the apparatus of the state.

(de Benoist, 2017: 7)

If the right, after the collapse of fascism, wants to be of significance again, it should according to him focus on ‘creating the general climate’ metapolitically (de Benoist, 2017: 7).

Metapolitics 1.0: lessons from the left?

GRECE’s first official seminar in November 1968 focused on the question, ‘What is metapolitics?’ (Bar-On, 2007: 35). Even though most seem to focus on Gramsci’s legacy in this new right metapolitics, it is interesting to note that Gramsci himself never used the term ‘metapolitics’. According to Viereck, the term was first used by Constantin Frantz, a prominent German nationalist, in a letter to Richard Wagner where he suggested to Wagner that ‘To be genuinely German, politics must soar to metapolitics.

This Wagnerian metapolitics, just like the reactionary modernists that Herf (1984) describes, is ‘Janus-Faced. Simultaneously it looks back to romanticism, and ahead to a machine age of wage slaves and unemployed’ (Viereck, 1941: 123). Viereck’s analysis of this early manifestation of metapolitics is remarkable for the parallels it shows with later work on the conservative revolution (Mohler & Weissmann, 2018; Bures, 2020), and more importantly because of the similarities with La Nouvelle Droite’s metapolitical battle. The works of conservative revolutionary and reactionary modernist writers, as well as the books on those traditions (like the works of Mohler, PhD) were widely read by members of La Nouvelle Droite, including de Benoist. It is no coincidence that La Nouvelle Droite’s metapolitics was first and foremost directed to an intellectual elite and not a broad audience, as it follows the tradition of the conservative revolutionary intellectuals. The conservative revolution, says Bures (2020: 2), has ‘suspicion not only of political, but of all conceptual language’, it favoured ‘the rebellion of blood and soul against intellect and doctrine’, but those intellectuals who favoured the rebellion of blood and soul did this paradoxically with complex, abstract writing that tried to capture the metaphysics of man. Interestingly, this complex writing – ‘fake intellectualism’, in the words of Guillaume Faye – is also characteristic of many La Nouvelle Droite writings.
