These similarities between Wagner’s metapolitics, conservative revolutionary tradition and La Nouvelle Droite are found in form, content and strategy.

It is also interesting to see that the French new right’s claim on Gramsci has far more in common with metapolitics as defined by Viereck and Constantin Frantz than with Gramsci. La Nouvelle Droite only followed Gramsci’s insights into the political importance of ideas and culture but disregarded the relation between ideas and the material conditions, between class, intellectuals and political formations. In other words, it adopted a metapolitics that focused on the production and normalization of conservative revolutionary ideas. This metapolitics was seen as necessary to reconstruct a new revolutionary right ideology in which revolutionary ideas of Julius Evola, Oswald Spengler, Carl Schmitt and many more anti-Enlightenment thinkers found a new place. La Nouvelle Droite’s metapolitics was in that sense closer to Charles Maurras’s mantra that ‘it was necessary to first “monarchize” the nation before considering the restoration of the monarch’ (Duranton-Crabol, 1988, 141 in Bar-On, 2007: 35) than that it was truly adopting Gramsci’s insights in hegemony and the role of organic intellectuals. A return of the 68right to political respectability, especially after the horror of World War II, meant ‘questioning of these traditional methods used by the revolutionary right to attain and maintain power’ (Bar-On, 2007: 30) such as intimidation, violence and the cult of the leader. La Nouvelle Droite’s metapolitical project took the form of metaphysics. Alain de Benoist’s seminal work Vue du Droite had the explicit aim to define the nature of man and especially of communities. The claim on Gramsci, in this sense, can be seen as mainly contributing to the ‘meta’ in metapolitics. It was part of this discursive battle that tried to normalize an anti-Enlightenment organicism by portraying it as ‘neither right, nor left’. This ‘Gramscianism of the right’ (Seidel, 1986: 108) was more than a mere strategy or a politically correct manifestation of the right (Bar-On, 2012: 5). Metapolitics was deeply connected to the rehabilitation and renewal of radical right-wing ideas: It served the goal not only to legitimate and repackage old ideas but also to renew the tradition of a revolutionary right by taking on board new ideas, insights, practices and discourses. Bar-On, in his seminal work ‘Where Have All the Fascists Gone’ (Bar-On, 2007) even goes so far as to argue that La Nouvelle Droite was not only new in form and practices but also in the adoption of left-wing ideas. Bar-On (2007: 56–76) sees in La Nouvelle Droite’s adoption of post-materialist values, its criticism of capitalism and the short-lived celebration of the Soviet Union’s revolutionary fervour or its praise for the radicalness and revolutionary atmosphere during May 1968, proof that La Nouvelle Droite is the result of a left-right synthesis. He in that sense gives legitimacy to de Benoist’s claim that the French new right is an heir of the New Left. ‘By the late 1980s and 1990s’, says Bar-On (2007: 76), ‘the main ENR (European new right) intellectuals had become impregnated with a decidedly New Left-like critique of liberal democracy, capitalist modernity and Western notions of “progress”’. This framing of La Nouvelle Droite contributes to its metapolitical project. It frames the effort of de Benoist and his comrades as realizing a meta-ideology bringing together left and right. What’s missing in Bar-On’s analysis is that de Benoist’s metapolitics was, as we have seen, grounded ‘in an ideological critique of the left and a methodological critique of the right’ (de Benoist, 2017: 18). It was first and foremost a way to rethink the strategies of the true right to rearticulate the conservative revolutionary right theory made for uptake in a new post-World War II context. They faced the challenge to re-introduce the archaic values, to use the discourse of Guillaume Faye, into the 20th century by adopting the methods of the left. Any metapolitical action attempts, according to de Benoist, ‘beyond political divisions and through a new synthesis, to renew a transversal mode of thought and, ultimately, to study all areas of knowledge in order to propose a coherent worldview’ (de Benoist & Champetier, 2000). The crux is that this synthesis didn’t change the core elements of what Zeev Sternhell (2010) has called the anti-Enlightenment tradition. La Nouvelle Droite’s metapolitics is still a battle against ‘Enlightenment’ 69and thus ‘civilization in the sense of the Enlightenment tradition’, and for ‘Kultur’ and ‘Folk’ in the tradition of the conservative revolution.

It is thus important to understand in detail what elements of the left are promoted and praised by La Nouvelle Droite and what elements are absent. Once we do that, it becomes clear that Marxism, and thus class analysis is still very much criticized. Even in the Manifesto for a European Renaissance from de Benoist and Champetier (2000), seen by Bar-On (2007) as the most open to left, it is clear that they see not only liberalism but also Marxism as their principal enemy. In the chapter ‘Liberalism: The Main Enemy’, Marxist socialism is framed as a branch of the same Enlightenment tree and thus as an enemy. ‘In almost all respects, liberalism has only realized more effectively certain objectives it shares with Marxism: the eradication of collective identities and traditional cultures, the disenchantment of the world, and the universalization of the system of production’ (de Benoist & Champetier, 2012, 14). The reach-out to the Soviet Union in 1980 should thus not be seen as praising or embracing the left as Bar-On (2007: 48) seems to suggest, but as a metapolitical deed. Just like they claim to be anti-racists to redefine what anti-racism is, so too can we understand their short-lived praise for the Soviet Union. They don’t praise Marxist theories, but the ‘Russian’-ness of the Soviet Union, its collectivism, unity of hopes and unity of purpose (Bar-On, 2007: 48). In other words, they neither praised nor embraced the Marxian left here but selected and framed – re-entextualized – certain practices and discourses as left, exactly those topics that were always embraced by anti-Enlightenment thinkers.

The same metapolitical move is visible in La Nouvelle Droite’s embrace of the ‘revolutionaries of May 68’. It is no coincidence that new right intellectuals praise the metapolitics of May 1968 or the ‘revolutionary’ potential of the students of the sixties. Just like Georges Sorel emptied socialism of its Marxism, its class war, and narrowed it down to ‘revolution’ (Sternhell, 1994: 47), we see that La Nouvelle Droite praises the revolutionary potential, and thus the mythical force of May 1968. Sorel’s anti-materialistic revision of socialism echoes in La Nouvelle Droite’s praise of May 1968. In the book Le Mai 68 de La Nouvelle Droite (SN, 1998), key figures of La Nouvelle Droite not only commemorate the revolts of May 68, but they also seem to praise it. According to Bar-On, this book makes clear that ‘the members or sympathizers of GRECE and La Nouvelle Droite were deeply affected by the events of May 1968 and the revolutionary, anti-capitalist, anti-materialist ideals of the New Left’ (Bar-On, 2007: 71). But again, just like Sorel’s praise of Marxist revolution replaced class with the nation, La Nouvelle Droite uses the student revolts to articulate a national perspective on the revolt. As Spektorowski (2003: 116) rightly argues, ‘against globalism, capitalism and the total free market’, de Benoist and his comrades ‘proposed a communitarian type of capitalism’. Interestingly, in the light of the contemporary legacy of 70La Nouvelle Droite, its embrace of May 68 is constantly used as a criticism of the former radical generation. The generation of 1968 is being framed as a generation of traitors, as the generation that sold out their ‘anti-materialistic values’ now responsible for neoliberalism globalization. This motive, as we shall see, is eagerly picked by movements like Generation Identitaire, the alt-right and Schild & Vrienden. Important at this point, is the explicit intertextuality with the anti-Enlightenment tradition. Anti-materialism is not a ‘left-wing’ value. On the contrary, Marxist and democratic socialists are materialistic thinkers: they focus on the distribution of wealth in society. ‘Within the anti-Enlightenment tradition “materialism” – that is, liberalism, democracy, socialism – became the code word par excellence for evil’ (Sternhell, 2010: 48). It was the dematerialization of socialism and Marxism by George Sorel and Hendrik De Mann (Sternhell, 1986) that started the move to the right, to fascism.

This praise of ‘the left’ is thus not exactly what it looks like on a superficial level. The metapoliticians of the French right-wing school of thought learned from the methods of the left, and cherry-picked and decontextualized certain issues addressed by the left and re-entextualized them in a contemporary conservative revolutionary discourse. These entextualization practices are at the heart of what metapolitics is all about. When Bar-On (2007: 58) argues that the following New Left themes ‘the critique of modernity, liberalism and global capitalism; the valorization of regionalism, federalism and local communities; the quality of life and ecological concerns; feminist themes; the critique of the liberal and socialist “New Class”; pro-Third World Solidarity; the incessant attacks on capitalist materialism, technological utopianism and bureaucratic gigantism; and the call for more humane, spiritual and free-thinking European societies that are not governed by a political correctness “thought police’’, are adopted by La Nouvelle Droite, he is missing the fact that the way those criticisms are defined is not ‘left-wing’, but reinforce the key ingredients of the anti-Enlightenment tradition. In new right discourse, capitalism is never discussed in a Marxist materialist analysis, it is criticized because it destroys organic groups and their language and culture. What is celebrated in the revolts of 1968 is not the materialistic analysis of imperialism or the fight for human socialism, but its anti-materialism and regionalism. When feminism is embraced, de Benoist and Champetier (2012: 36) rapidly distance themselves from the ‘universalist feminists’ that ‘claim that masculine and feminine genders stem from a social construct (‘One is not born a woman, one becomes a woman’). At the same time, this embrace of feminism and the claim to fight sexism bring in a traditionalist conceptualization of sexes and gender. Under the banner of differentialist feminism, the traditionalist conception of gender as rooted in biology is reintroduced. And when post-colonialism was praised, in reality, they praised the right to the differences of people. The same is true when they embrace anti-racism 71or democracy: words and topics are put in a new text, and this changes the meaning of those words. Metapolitics recontextualizes ‘progressive’ and left-wing talking heads by integrating them into an old right discourse.

The reintroduction of these old, archaic values is indeed not identical to how it would have been defined by conservative revolutionary thinkers, fascists and traditionalists in the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th century. The ideological and strategic innovation of La Nouvelle Droite was very real. This newness of course should not blind us from the fact that on a deeper level, the theoreticians of La Nouvelle Droite do reproduce several crucial assumptions of the ‘old right’. The history of fascism has taught us that a synthesis under the banner of neither right, nor left (Sternhell, 1986) label does not necessarily mean that the synthesis is less right wing or less radical (Sternhell, 1986). It does force us to understand La Nouvelle Droite’s legacy not in terms of a superficial assessment of the school but to dig deeper in search of complexity of this new ideology. And to do that, it is important to go back to its ideological roots.

The new right and the anti-Enlightenment tradition

The ideological coherence between all the Nouvelle Droite intellectuals is the result of the influence of the intellectuals of ‘the conservative revolution’ (Griffin, 2008; Mohler & Weissmann, 2018), reactionary modernists like Spengler, the traditionalism of Julius Evola and René Guénon (François, 2014: 88), and of course also the works of Nietzsche. These influences also explain the diversity in the different discourses of the different intellectuals. Some like Faye, even though also heavily influenced by the traditionalism of Evola, are leaning more on the tradition of reactionary modernism (Herf, 1984). The reactionary modernist intellectuals embraced technology and technological progress as vital for the survival and rebirth of the community. It is the modern twist of the conservative revolution – the revolutionary aspect – and reactionary modernism in particular that new right thinkers like de Benoist and Faye found so interesting. ‘The conservative revolution’, said de Benoist, ‘is basically a conservativism turned to the future, and not a restoration’ (de Benoist, 2017: XXVII). Maybe even more than de Benoist and Dugin, Faye explicitly speaks in the tradition of reactionary modernism. ‘The conservative Revolution (…) is not enough’, says Faye (2010: 14). ‘We need to become archeofuturists’ (Faye, 2010: 15). Faye, and La Nouvelle Droite in general, don’t just retake the conservative revolutionary dogmas but blend modern, conservative revolutionary, pro-technology (Spektorowski, 2003) and post-modern thought in their work (Bar-On, 2013: 73).

What La Nouvelle Droite and contemporary new right intellectuals share is their rejection of ‘progressivism’, in the sense of Enlightenment modernism. They see Enlightenment modernism as a period of decadence and decline. 72Egalitarianism, says de Benoist (2017: 9), ‘the denier and reducer of the world’s diversity’, is the principal enemy. Egalitarianism is seen by La Nouvelle Droite as what connects liberalism and communism on a deeper level. It is this egalitarianism and its materialistic values that, according to this school of thought, causes the crisis of modernity (See Sunic, 2011). ‘The cycle of egalitarian madness’, says Pierre Krebs (2012:19) ‘consequently ends exactly where it started: from the political eradication of values of the demos’. Egalitarianism is seen as an attack on the organic people, the diversity that characterizes humanity.

To counter this globalist and universalist trend, spearheaded by America and the Soviet Union, the new right urges all nations, and particularly European nations, to disengage themselves, culturally and politically, from both superpowers, and from both liberalism and Marxism, and join in the common fight for the cause of the peoples.

(Sunic, 2011: 160)

This fight against egalitarianism is a fight for a European Renaissance (de Benoist & Champetier, 2000; Faye, 2010; Krebs 2012) through metapolitics. This renaissance will start, according to Krebs (2012: 30), ‘the moment that they (Europeans) cease to perceive the egalitarian raciophobic society as an inevitable destiny, and finally begin to feel it as a necessary challenge’.

The fight against Enlightenment modernity is shared by all members of La Nouvelle Droite, and by those influenced by this school of thought like Dugin (Southern, 2018a). Important to stress is that this fight against liberalism, capitalism and all materialistic ideologies is not necessarily a fight against the use of technologies. The work of Faye is a textbook example of this post-modern bricolage. Faye’s Archeofuturism envisages the construction of ‘a future society that combines techno-scientific progress with a return to the traditional answers that stretch back into the mists of time, (Faye, 2010: 45 & 73). Archeofuturism is Faye’s attempt to actualize the ideas of the conservative revolution (Faye, 2010: 14) while the reactionary modernists of Weimar guided him. Ideological storms are needed, says Faye, to let the new be born. ‘The world needs radical and revolutionary thought to realize a rebirth’ (Faye, 2010: 53). This archeofuturistic project is directed to the future; it doesn’t want to go back to an ancient time. Archeofuturism is defined as the selecting of the old values and traditions in function of a new future. Faye therefore pleads for a ‘vitalistic constructionism’ that is actually creating a new future grounded in old values. Even a traditionalist philosopher like Dugin, following Evola, argues that going back to tradition is not going back to the past, but to eternity: tradition is past, present and future (Southern, 2018a). Dugin sees Russia as ‘the most important pole of the great awakening’ (Dugin, 2021: 39).

73Despite their claim to produce a ‘new right’, the intellectual tradition in which La Nouvelle Droite speaks, especially on a deeper level, is obvious. Alain de Benoist, Dominique Venner, Pierre Krebs and Guillaume Faye find inspiration in key thinkers of the Weimar Republic, and the conservative revolution in general, and more traditionalist-inspired thinkers. Julius Evola, Oswald Spengler, Charles Maurras, Carl Schmitt, Ernest Jünger and even Joseph De Maistre and Charles Maurras are regularly cited or echoed. From this intertextual perspective, La Nouvelle Droite is best understood as the post-World War II articulation of the anti-Enlightenment tradition, or in discourse analytical terms: a recontextualization of the anti-Enlightenment tradition to make it relevant in an entirely new context. Sternhell traces this anti-Enlightenment tradition back to Vico Giambattista, Edmund Burke and Gottfried Herder. Burke and Herder, as he compellingly argues, were not just reacting against the French Revolution, they were the start of a new political tradition. A political tradition that stood for the opposite of the Enlightenment project. A tradition that revolted against rationalism, the materialism of liberalism, and later Marxism, the autonomy of the individual, and all that unites people: their condition as rational beings with natural rights. The ideas of these anti-Enlightenment thinkers have undoubtedly influenced the metapolitical project of GRECE. With them, they share their battle against liberalism, socialism, representative democracy, the Enlightenment, Jacobinism and the idea of universal human rights (Faye, 2010, 2011; de Benoist, 2011).

La Nouvelle Droite’s project is not a counter-revolution. Just like the anti-Enlightenment tradition was an intellectual revolution for a second modernity, so is de Benoist’s project. The anti-Enlightenment tradition took the form of a two-century long revolutionary and intellectual movement built on anti-rationalism, organicism and the attack on ‘humanism, the much derided universal values and finally democracy’ (Sternhell, 2010: 16). The idea that man is free, can be emancipated and has unalienable universal rights is what anti-Enlightenment thinkers have attacked for centuries. They saw the Enlightenment tradition, just like La Nouvelle Droite, as an attack on the natural order of things. Vico Giambattista, Edmund Burke and Gottfried Herder, Hippolyte Taine, Ernest Renan, Charles Maurras, Oswald Spengler, Friedrich Meinecke, and in their footsteps also Faye, de Benoist and Krebs; the ideological consistency in their attacks has been remarkable. All see the values of the French Revolution as the start of all evil decline and decadence. Key ideas of that intellectual movement are the primacy of the group, relativism, organic nationalism, anti-materialism, anti-rationalism (for the masses), anti-utopianism, and finally the battle against equality, democracy and universal rights (Maly, 2012, 2018a). The intellectual fundament of the anti-Enlightenment tradition is its stress on the particular group and on everything that divides the human race and isolates them: race, religion and the nation 74(Sternhell, 2010: 9). They fought to uproot ‘the idea of the all-powerfulness of the individual, reconstituting organic communities and ending the farce of universal suffrage and equality’ (Sternhell, 2010: 15).

The ethno-pluralism that is usually considered as the great renewal of La Nouvelle Droite has its roots in the primacy of ‘the organic group’ so dominant in the anti-Enlightenment tradition. ‘Organicism’, says Sternhell, ‘that supreme form of subordination of the individual to the collectivity’ is ‘one of the great “leading ideas” of anti-Enlightenment thought’ (Sternhell, 2010: 202). According to anti-Enlightenment thinkers such as Herder, Taine and Spengler,

Society was an organism, a ‘living body’ formed in the course of the centuries by innumerable generations that succeeded one another. (…) Each individual in this community is like a cell in an organized body and the cell only comes into being, subsists, develops and attains its personal ends through the health of the whole body.

(Sternhell, 2010: 202)

In this vision of society, no individual was born free, and no individual had the freedom to engage in a social contract with others. There was no social contract, but a historical contract. People were subjected to a whole tradition; they were born with a debt vis à vis their ancestors.

Just as within the anti-Enlightenment tradition, the thinkers of La Nouvelle Droite imagine and actively construct a world divided into different organic people, each with their own language, culture, habits and territory. They may have traded integral nationalism with the notion of European civilization and regional communities, but the main assumptions are still the same. Pluralism is clearly not a new invention. Pluralism as a worldview was already coined by Herder – one of the foundational thinkers of the anti-Enlightenment tradition – who argued that each organic group has its own history of change ‘in accordance with the place, the time and the inner character: each bears within itself the harmony of its perfection’ (Herder in Sternhell, 2010: 200). In Herder’s view, societies are moulded by history and are characterized by internal inequality. The leaders are pictured as the head of society, the working classes are the arms and legs. Each class has its own role and function. Nations can only thrive if each member takes up its role, and helps to push the nation to glory. It is this inequality and the role of the philosopher kings and warriors that is also praised by La Nouvelle Droite as crucial to lead the group to greatness.

This pluralism of unique organic nations and their collective greatness is threatened, anti-Enlightenment thinkers argue, by the universalism of the Enlightenment. Herder (Evrigenis & Pellerin, 2004: 64) for instance sarcastically writes that ‘All the rulers of Europe are speaking French already and 75soon we will all be doing so’. The parallel between the anti-Americanism and attack on cultural globalization by Alain de Benoist and Guillaume Faye is obvious. Just like they attack Hollywoodization and McDonaldization, Herder mocks the impact of the French Revolution and criticizes the Enlightenment not only as a process of globalization and homogenization but also as a period of decline, decadence and destruction of all that is good. And just like them, Herder defends (and at the same time constructs through his writing) a pluralist world, a world divided into culturally determined and incompatible groups. Note here that Herder’s pluralism, how idealistically it may sound if one reads back his words from the humanist relativism of Boas, is in reality a full frontal but refined attack on Enlightenment thought (Maly, 2012). Not mankind, or the individual, is what matters to Herder, but the organic group. And this position clearly echoes in La Nouvelle Droite’s fight for ‘a rights of people’ to replace the damned universal rights (de Benoist & Champetier, 2000; Sunic, 2011). With this plea, they echo Edmund Burke, who already in the 19th century claimed that ‘the pretended rights of man, which have made this havoc, cannot be the rights of the people. For to be a people, and to have these rights are things incompatible, (Sternhell, 2010: 193). This idea of pluralism is fundamental to the anti-Enlightenment tradition and its attack against democracy and universal human rights. This exact conceptualization is also at the heart of new right metapolitics. ‘The plurality and variety of races, ethnic groups, languages, customs, even religions has characterized the development of humanity since the very beginning’, argue de Benoist and Champetier (2000: 28). The only difference seems to be that Herder’s nationalism has been replaced by smaller organic groups and civilizational cooperation. The net result of La Nouvelle Droite’s pluralism is the same: an attack on democracy, equality and the Enlightenment in general.

Ethno-differentialism and organic democracy as metapolitics

This new take on Herder’s organist pluralism is at the heart of the metapolitical project of La Nouvelle Droite. As we have seen in the introduction, de Benoist (2017: 2) defines the preservation of ‘the diversity of the world, and by consequence the relative inequalities that are necessarily the product of this’ as the essence of the right. The true right in his vision understands that its ‘principle enemy’ is ‘egalitarianism’ (de Benoist, 2017: 9). The French new right opposes such ‘homogenising universalism’ and advocates a system that ‘transmits at least as much diversity as it has received. The true wealth of the world is first and foremost the diversity of its cultures and peoples’ (de Benoist & Champetier, 2000: 28). Herder’s pluralism in this new right metapolitical discourse now goes under the name of ‘ethno-differentialism’, ‘ethno-pluralism’ or even ‘differential anti-racism’ (de Benoist & Champetier, 2000). Against the anti-racism of the left – labelled by de Benoit and Champetier as 76a universal anti-racism that denies cultural differences and the existence of races –, de Benoist and Champetier call themselves differential anti-racists. ‘Differentialist anti-racism, to which the new right subscribes, holds that the irreducible plurality of the human species constitutes a veritable treasure’ (de Benoist & Champetier, 2000).

It is these organic groups with their own unique culture that are put central to the anti-Enlightenment tradition, including in contemporary manifestations of that tradition. In this tradition, man only fully becomes human as part of a group. Echoing Herder, Faye argues in his metapolitical dictionary that a people is ‘an organic community embracing a transcendent body made up of ancestors, the living and their heirs. (…) belonging to a specific people (…) distinguishes a man and makes him human’. (Faye, 2011: 211). ‘Man’, argue de Benoist and Champetier (2000: 18), ‘as such does not exist, because his membership within humanity is always mediated by a particular cultural belonging’. Note that this organicism is the foundation of their fight against globalization. The greatness of the nation, the race, the organic groups or the culture is what matters, not man or mankind. Man cannot be just an individual with rights or a member of a transnational community, but he or she is always the first and the last member of a local group, and that is the reason that ‘humanity is irreducibly plural: diversity is part of its very essence’ (de Benoist & Champetier, 2000: 19). Diversity is thus always group diversity. Just like in the anti-Enlightenment tradition, men and women are only measly cells in the body of the organic community and should be treated as such. People, nations, tribes and races are described and understood in terms of organisms in their own right. Here again, we hear a classic anti-Enlightenment echo: ‘A culture is born’, argued Spengler,

In the moment when a great soul wakens out of the proto-spirituality of the ever-childish humanity, and detaches itself, a form from the formless, (…) and it dies when this soul has actualized the full sum of its possibilities in the shape of people, languages, dogmas, arts, states, sciences and reverts into the proto-soul.

(Spengler, 2006: 73)

Humanity and man are ‘childish’, the individual produces nothing. It is the organic group that gives birth to real knowledge, real values, language and art. Nations and cultures are living entities characterized by ‘a spirit’.

This organicism starts with Herder but clearly echoes throughout the centuries. When Spengler argues that ‘Every culture passes through the age-phases of the individual man. Each has its childhood, youth, manhood and old age’ (Spengler, 2006: 74), we hear an echo of Herder. Krebs reproduces this when he claims that Europe is now ‘in the midnight of its decline, when 77it fades away behind a society which submits to its history instead of letting itself be borne’ (Krebs, 2012: 31). And finally, Herder’s pluralism or de Benoist ‘ethno-differentialism’ also echo in alt-right figure Richard Spencer’s discourse on ‘ethno-states’ and his defense of Israel as a Jewish ethno-state (Haaretz, 2018). This organic ‘pluralism’ wrapped in the credo ‘right to difference’ has become the quintessential trademark of the new right. Here we see the power and relevance of new right ‘metapolitics’. It takes old ideas – Herder’s organic pluralism in this case – and repackages it to make possible a new right project that ‘rejects’ racism and replaces the nationalism of the nation-state with

A multipolar world of emerging civilizations (…) these civilizations will not supplant the ancient local, tribal, provincial or national roots, but will be constituted as the ultimate collective form with which individuals are able to identify in addition to their common humanity.

(De Benoist & Champetier, 2000: 29)

This right to difference and the idea of common humanity seemingly places the new right in the centre of the political field. It sounds acceptable, but just like in Herder’s writings, it is a key fundament in the attack on the Enlightenment tradition. ‘It was Herder’, argues Sternhell (2010: 21),

Who gave Europe a view of history consisting of cultures that, even when not cut off from each other, regarded foreign contributions as threatening their authenticity. (…) these cultures could easily become antagonistic, and this was precisely the opposite view of culture held by Voltaire, Montesquieu and Rousseau.

Spengler was not just reproducing this Herderian view of the world as a world of cultures, he radicalized it. ‘Different cultures became completely impervious to each other with Spengler. Biological determinism was only the logical next step (…), it was the last stage in the psychological preparation that permitted the disaster of the twentieth century to happen’ (Sternhell, 2010: 371). The primacy of the organic group divides the world and serves as an attack on ‘universalism’, humanism, the rights of the individual and Jacobin democracy. Even more, it literally destroys the idea of universal values. This assessment is true for Herder, Spengler, La Nouvelle Droite and the identitarians today. Of course, times have changed. Whereas Mussolini (1932) for instance could attack democracy and universal human rights fully frontal and explicitly, we see that today, identitarians and new right intellectuals do it less overtly and far subtler. This is especially the case when they have to position themselves vis à vis hegemonic concepts like democracy or human rights, anti-racism or ‘not-racism’.

78The metapolitical project of the new right is exactly about this type of exercise, and La Nouvelle Droite’s intellectuals have been a master at the game. In his book ‘The Problem with Democracy’ for instance, Alain de Benoist pleads for an ‘organic democracy’ (de Benoist, 2011: 93–99), and in that sense puts himself in line with democratic hegemony. At the same time, the whole book is an attack on liberal democracy. The embrace of democracy is best understood as a form of orthopraxy. It is not much more than performing a hegemonic act – positioning oneself as democratic – but without subscribing to the ideology that gives meaning to ‘democracy’. ‘Orthopraxy’, says Blommaert (2005: 169), ‘is maybe the beginning stage of every ideological process that uses coercion as an instrument of homogenization’. In the context of metapolitics, we can turn this around. Orthopraxy is here used to give democracy a different meaning, to question the hegemony of democracy and introduce a new ideology that gives meaning to the concept. The embrace of democracy, in this sense, is a death kiss. The target is the Enlightened representative democracy. Liberal, representative democracy is not only in crisis, according to de Benoist, but he also argues that it destroys ‘the sovereignty of the people’. A real and functioning democracy, according to de Benoist, should be based on the sovereignty of the people which ‘resides with a collective body, the nation, whose independence thus constitutes an essential condition for the proper functioning of society’ (de Benoist, 2011: 59). Using moderate Enlightenment thinkers like Rousseau and article 3 of the Declaration of 1789, he isolates the word ‘democracy’ from its radical Enlightenment history (Israel, 2010, 2011) and re-entextualizes it into an anti-Enlightenment discourse. This becomes clear in his argument that democracy should be organized on the basis of ‘a folk’ and not on the basis of ‘the alleged inalienable rights of rootless individuals’ (de Benoist, 2011: 98). Within this anti-Enlightenment discourse, the reason for this move is evident: a pluralism of values within one community is a ‘sign of the break-up of society’ (de Benoist, 2011: 70), and thus also a break up of democracy as such. According to this Schmittian logic, de Benoist argues that democracy should be based ‘on citizenship, which sanctions one’s belonging to a given folk – that is a culture, history and destiny – and to the political structure within which it has developed’ (de Benoist, 2011: 98). The idea of ‘organic pluralism’ organizes de Benoit’s critique on liberal democracy and his plea for an ‘organic democracy’.

Just like de Benoist, Guillaume Faye (2011: 111–114) criticizes ‘liberal democracy’ and advocates an organic democracy, but he does it far more explicitly. Democracy is a ‘sham democracy, for it neglects the people’s interests’ (Faye, 2011: 111). Against the liberal representative democracy, Faye pleas, just like de Benoist, to revive the ‘organic democracy deeply rooted in the European tradition (…). Such a democracy is possible only among ethnically homogenous people’ (Faye, 2011: 113). Faye’s conception of a good, 79organic democracy, just like the conceptualization of fascist democracy, is deeply anti-egalitarian and anti-liberal: ‘Organic democracy (…) embraces the principle of aristocracy. That is “the selection of the best to rule”. (Faye, 2011: 113). Ideally, it has ‘a born leader’ who is able to shape the voice of its people. Just like all anti-Enlightenment thinkers, Faye defines the people as an organism in its own right, where the leaders are ‘the head’ or ‘the brain’ of that organic nation. The democratic renewal, Faye states, is the renewal of this organism. This ‘organic democracy’ doesn’t consider ‘immediate interests alone, but the people’s historic destiny, taking account of its memory and its future generations abiding the imperatives of sovereignty and independence, along with a faith in the longevity of its collective, biological, and cultural identity’ (Faye, 2011: 114). Democracy in new right and identitarian discourse equals an ethnocracy (see also Bar-On, 2013: 145) and an attack not only on the idea of representative democracy, but also on the idea of unalienable and universal human rights. Democracy, just like liberty or identity, acquires new meanings in the metapolitical discourse of new right intellectuals and activists. These concepts re-introduce, as trojan horses, key ideas of the anti-Enlightenment tradition.

Metapolitics, the interregnum and revolutionary rebirth

The metapolitization of the far-right as Griffin (2011: 195) calls it has had a profound impact on the political landscape in general and that of the far-right in particular. The metapolitics of La Nouvelle Droite soon spread to centre-right politicians in France and extreme-right parties like Flemish Interest in Belgium and the Lega in Italy (Bar-On, 2013: 25–26). An extreme-right party like Flemish Bloc, later Flemish Interest, not only became a large electoral force, it actually succeeded in changing the discourse on democracy (Blommaert, 2007, 2017b; Maly 2012). In Flanders, democracy now equals ‘the voice of the people’, represented by the Flemish Bloc. Six decades later, the impact of the metapolitics of La Nouvelle Droite is visible in the strategies, infrastructures and discourses of contemporary right-wing movements like the alt-right and Generation Identity (Maly, 2018a, 2022b), and in debates about migration, integration and the global rise of far-right movements.

This impact of the new right project also helped shape a new intellectual extreme-right focused not only on producing ideas that attack actual existing liberal democracy, but also helped build a vision of a post-liberal, post-democratic society in the future. As Griffin (2000: 171) argues, ‘the hallmark of the new right is its belief that the present world system is not only decadent, but that it will eventually give way to a new type of civilization based on healthy mythic forces’. This new type of civilization, in the spirit of the conservative revolution and the anti-Enlightenment tradition, is not a re-establishment of an old civilization, but the active vitalic construction 80(Faye, 2011) of a new one based on old – archaic – values. Key thinkers of the new right suggest that we are now living in the ‘interregnum’, ‘a tragic historical moment when everything is in flames and everything, like a phoenix, might rise reborn from the ashes’ (Faye, 2011: 178). The interregnum is the time when ‘rebirth’ is made possible. When surrounded by the ruins of a civilization in decline, the seeds for the new culture are planted. According to La Nouvelle Droite, we now see the end of modernity (de Benoist & Champetier, 2000; Faye, 2010, 2011; Bar-On, 2012a: 9). Europe, Faye argues in classic anti-Enlightenment discourse, is in decline. It is colonized by ‘alien people’ and ‘faces death in the first twenty years of the new millennium’ (Faye, 2011: 178). Typical of the new right is the belief that the tide can be turned if Europeans unite ‘in self-defense, expel the colonisers, throw off the American yoke, and regenerate themselves biologically and morally’ (Faye, 2011: 179). This idea of rebirth is not new, especially since the idea of national rebirth has always been a central element in fascism (Griffin, 2011). Contrary to the ultra-nationalism of many fascisms, key intellectuals of the new right focus ‘rebirth’ on different scale levels. ‘We should ask ourselves’, Faye writes, ‘whether the nation state in Europe may not be as anachronistic as Maurras’ monarchists movement was in the 1920s’ (Faye, 2010: 77). Faye, Krebs and de Benoist & Champetier plea for a European Renaissance. This new civilization will not just arise organically, it needs metapolitical work. Metapolitics is thus part of the social constructivist and revolutionary part of the political project of the new right. Typical for new right metapolitics is that it takes the assumption on board that society is a social construct and that future societies and civilizations can be made through the contemporary production of ideas or metapolitics. It is in this light that Guillaume Faye pleads for the ‘vitalic construction’ of a new golden future based on the ‘re-emergence of archaic social configurations in a new context’ (Faye, 2010: 74). Along similar lines, Alain de Benoist and Charles Champetier (2000) argue that ‘In a globalized world, the future belongs to large cultures and civilizations capable of organizing themselves into autonomous entities and of acquiring enough power to resist outside interference’.

In line with pre-WWII Fascist tradition (Spektorowski, 2016) La Nouvelle Droite intellectuals embrace transnationalism. They abandon the ultra- nationalism characterizing most pre-war forms of fascism and adopt a transnational European position. ‘Europe’, says de Benoist and Champetier (2000),

Must organize itself into a federal structure, while recognizing the autonomy of all the component elements and facilitating the cooperation of the constituent regions and of individual nations. European civilization will remake itself, not by the negation, but by the recognition of historical cultures, thus permitting all inhabitants to rediscover their common origins.

81Faye also envisions a pan-European civilization and explicitly argues for an ‘organic regrouping of kindred cultures possessing a common will’ (Faye, 2011: 24). It is the European civilization that has to be constructed, saved and fought for in order to save the ‘national’ and ‘regional’ cultures. It is this ethno-differentialist and vitalic constructionist position that enables new right activists to internationalize and build a pan-European network. Generation Identity is perhaps the most obvious pre-configuration of that idea. The movement started as a polycentric movement grounded in different cities and regions in France. It rapidly Europeanized with active chapters in Austria, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Belgium, the UK and the United States. The movement is not only organized on regional and national scales, but it is also organized on a European scale where they collaborate under the banner ‘Defend Europe’.

Guillaume Faye and the birth of metapolitics 2.0

Metapolitics, in the mind of Alain de Benoist at least, was the prerogative of the ‘philosopher kings’ (Bar-On, 2007: 86). Metapolitics was only for the intellectual elite, an elite who they imagined to have a central role in shaping society. It is clear that in the 21st century, the metapolitical project is not just an intellectual affair anymore. Metapolitics is the common ground in a network of parties, movements, activists and influencers (Maly, 2018, 2020, 2022b). Whereas Alain de Benoist and Charles Champetier (2000) understand ‘metapolitics’ in relation to elite right-wing intellectuals, we see that this traditional conception of metapolitics has been stretched sometimes beyond recognition. Contemporary metapolitics is not the monopoly of intellectuals anymore. Even more, new right intellectuals and activists increasingly also imagine politicians, activists and ‘prosumers’ as carriers of a metapolitical project. This new conception of metapolitics, metapolitics 2.0 as I call it, is the consequence of (1) the renewed interest in the project of La Nouvelle Droite and in particular the rising popularity of former head of research of GRECE: Guillaume Faye, (2) the rising importance and normalization of digital media, and especially the prosumer culture promoted by web 2.0, (3) processes of re-entextualization and englobalization and (4) the role of Arktos in the distribution of his work, and work that builds further on his conceptualizations. Re-entextualization refers to the processes by which La Nouvelle Droite’s work, and especially Faye’s branch of this tradition, is successively de-contextualized and re-contextualized, and thus made into a new discourse (Blommaert, 2005: 251). It is Guillaume Faye’s revision of La Nouvelle Droite’s metapolitics that has had considerable uptake in the last decades. Guillaume Faye is one of the key mediators of the contemporary idea of metapolitics (Maly, 2022b). His work has been taken up by activists 82around the world. As a result of Faye’s re-emergence on the metapolitical scene, we can witness renewed attention to metapolitics.

Guillaume Faye, the alt-right and metapolitics re-invented

Guillaume Faye was, as head of GRECE’s Secretariat for Research and Studies, known as its ‘number two’. After a dispute about the ideological direction of the group and financial disagreements, he left GRECE in 1987 (François, 2019: 93). In the next decades he became known as the popular media figure Skyrock, and even claims to have starred in several porn movies (Faye, 2010: 104). Since his re-emergence to the metapolitical field at the end of the 20th century, he has somewhat acquired a cult status among the European-American far-right. After his death, in 2019, most of the key figures of the global new right like Richard Spencer, Greg Johnson, Martin Sellner, the Golden One and many more praised him and his intellectual work (Maly, 2022b).

Faye’s contemporary stardom within the European-American far-right is connected to his second metapolitical life (Maly, 2022b). At the end of the 1990s, La Nouvelle Droite’s l’Enfant terrible returned to the metapolitical scene with a series of influential books: L’Archéofuturisme (Faye, 1998), La colonisation de l’Europe (Faye, 2000) and Pourquoi nous combattons: Manifeste de la résistance européenne (Faye, 2001). It is especially the translation of Archeofuturism and Why We fight in English in 2010 and 2011 by publishing house Arktos

The impact of Faye can be illustrated by highlighting how his criticism of La Nouvelle Droite’s metapolitics has been taken up by alt-right activists. In Archeofuturism, Faye argued that La Nouvelle Droite ‘had simply overlooked the fact that the cultural battle Gramsci promoted was associated with the political and economic battle’ (Faye, 2010: 29). Metapolitics, wrote Faye in his metapolitical dictionary, should not only be about ‘the social diffusion of ideas and cultural values for the sake of provoking a long-term, political transformation’ (Faye, 2011: 193). Implicitly criticizing de Benoist, he claimed that ‘Metapolitics has to avoid excessive culturalism, which risks becoming an empty intellectualism, a boastful erudition, or a philosophy of amateurs’ (Faye, 2011: 194). Metapolitics should pursue ‘the political objective of positively affirming the principal lines and central concepts of its particular social/civilizational project’ (Faye, 2011: 194). Metapolitics, in Faye’s understanding, is thus not only about producing intellectual ideas, 83but is also an ‘indispensable complement to every direct form of political action, though in no case can it or should it replace such action’ (Faye, 2010: 193). To be fair, de Benoist (de Benoist, 2017) did envision that La Nouvelle Droite’s ‘cultural programme’ could in ‘the near future’ be taken to the political field, but contrary to Faye, he did not see politics as an essential part of that metapolitical battle. Even more, de Benoist explicitly didn’t want to see his metapolitical project linked to political positions (Sylvian, 2005: 9). Metapolitics was contrasted with the traditional ‘politics of the masses’ (Bar-On, 2007: 86). Faye criticized de Benoist for this and, for instance, regretted that La Nouvelle Droite never connected with Le Front National from Le Pen. Faye disagreed with de Benoist’s understanding of the intellectual as the only agent of a metapolitical battle. Metapolitics, Faye stressed, is not only a job of intellectuals but also of politicians, activists and movements. All these actors, according to him, are necessary in a metapolitical battle (Faye, 2010: 193). For Faye, politics was a crucial scene for the metapolitical battle as politicians have privileged access to the media. Note here how Faye stresses the importance of media and media attention in the context of metapolitics. In Faye’s conception, the circulation of ideas is as important as the ideas themselves, and therefore all actors that help to distribute ideas are needed.

This conception of metapolitics as necessarily connected to politics and activism was taken up by white nationalist intellectual, publisher and editor-in-chief of Counter-Currents, Greg Johnson. In his 2012 reader devoted to the establishment of the ‘North American New Right’ (Johnson, 2012), in his 2013 book ‘New Right vs Old Right’ (Johnson, 2013) and in several blogs and essays on Counter-Currents

Faye’s understanding of metapolitics (and Johnson’s re-entextualization of it) has been taken up by different sites and activists within the alt-right and the 84global new right (Maly, 2018a). We can see it in the literal reproduction of that criticism, and maybe more importantly in the practices of the so-called alt-right activists trying to construct an American new right. Metapolitics had from the start an important role within the alt-right. In the context of the liberal society, several key figures (Kirkpatrick, 2014; Friberg, 2017; Spencer, 2017a; Leonard, 2018a) argue that metapolitics is at the heart of the new right cultural construction of that future society. ‘Any political struggle must be preceded, legitimised, and supported by a metapolitical struggle’, says Friberg (Friberg, 2017). This metapolitical strategy is also visible in the classic metapolitical structures influenced by La Nouvelle Droite – think tanks like Spencer’s National Policy Institute, publishing house Counter-Currents, American Renaissance or NPI congresses, books, papers and essays – but especially in the United States, it was also embedded in vlogs, memes and offline practices influenced by digital culture and in the political activism for Trump (Maly, 2018a, 2018b). In the American uptake, not only the goal changed (a vitalistic reconstructing of American society instead of a Europa or a Eurosiberian renaissance), but also the conceptualization of metapolitics changed. This was as much a result of the nature of the alt-right as it was about the US context and the new digital reality.

The hybrid media system and metapolitics 2.0

The uptake of the idea of metapolitics by the alt-right happened not only in a different social and political context but also the technological context was different. The metapolitical battle of the alt-right took place in a post-digital context (Cramer, 2014). This new digital reality is, as I already argued, a key ingredient of the metapolitical battle of the new right in the 21st century. In this post-digital reality, Facebook, YouTube and other social media are potentially as important, or in some cases even more important, than mainstream media in realizing the goals of this metapolitical battle. This new normality in the media field has profoundly affected who can produce ideas and let them circulate. This in turn has had fundamental effects on the construction and circulation of (meta-) political messages and meanings (Blommaert, 2019b; Maly, 2022a). The ‘democratization’ of content production facilitated by digital media has clear effects on the production or ‘input-side’. Intellectuals are not the ‘only producers’ of ideas anymore. Their ideas now have to compete with other political, metapolitical and non-political ideas and content. Thompson (2020: 21) stresses that these new forms of action and interaction, categorized by him as ‘mediated online interaction’, disrupt ‘the settled roles’ of the institutional gatekeepers:

The power of the established media organizations to shape the agenda is disrupted by the emergences of a plethora of new players who are able to use communication media to interact with others while bypassing the established channels of mediated quasi interaction.

85As I stressed, digital media are not neutral, they have algorithmic agency. This agency forces activists to produce information that fits the formats and make their message ready for uptake by human and algorithmic audiences (Maly, 2022a). As a result of this new media environment, ‘information’, leaks, scandals and junk news (Venturini, 2019) are abundantly present in the current digital ecology, and they shape contemporary metapolitics. Alt-right activists, vloggers, trolls and self-declared intellectuals have adapted to this new reality and have become DIY producers and distributors of ideas.

This new post-digital reality has also been theorized by new right activists. Leonard, an editor from far-right publisher Arktos, for instance, argues that ‘one individual on an American college campus who tapes a sign reading ‘It’s OK to be “White” to a lamppost’ (Leonard, 2018a) acts metapolitically because his action seeks ‘to shift or shatter’ the political conventions. The intellectual, the politician, the activist and the prosumer are now all imagined as part of the new right metapolitical battle, all helping ‘to prepare the way for the regime which will supplant democracy’ (Leonard, 2018a). Contemporary new right metapolitics is not limited to a purely intellectual strategy but also encompasses every social, cultural, activist and political intervention towards the construction of a post-liberal society: ‘The deepest work of the metapolitician of the right is therefore necessarily anti-democratic: he seeks to produce a society in which metapolitics, save in its conservative aspect, no longer exists’ (Leonard, 2018a). It is this broad conception of metapolitics as embodied in meme warfare, offline activism and politics that was dominant in the alt-right and is dominant in the global new right today (Maly, 2018e). Even more, just because the new right denounces parliamentary democracy, politicians are only understood within the logic of metapolitics. ‘Parliamentary efforts’, says author, CEO and co-founder of Arktos Daniël Friberg,

Can never be more than complements to broader cultural and political work. The results of elections are but products of how public opinion has been formed and how, what, and in what manner information has been spread between these elections.

(Friberg, 2015: 34)

Long Live the emperor: Trump and alt-right metapolitics

In the 21st century, it is Faye’s broad conceptualization of metapolitics that was taken up and stretched to include digital activism. It is this conception of politics as part of a metapolitical battle that informed the support of the alt-right for Trump in 2016 (Espirit Vif Media, 2016). This can be illustrated by analysing Richard Spencer’s (2016) infamous speech ‘Long live the emperor!’ at the National Policy Institute’s ‘Become Who We Are 2016’ conference. In this speech, days after Trump’s victory, Spencer hails Trump’s victory as ‘a step towards’ a ‘new normal’, ‘a moral consensus’ the alt-right is fighting 86for. Spencer doesn’t praise him because he represents the full ‘cultural programme’ of the alt-right – on the contrary, he critiques Trump on many positions in that speech – but still praises him because of his metapolitical and archeofuturistic impact: his contribution to a new America based on archaic values. Spencer praises the ‘ur-myth’ that animated the Trump campaign. To say ‘Make America Great Again’ is both radically pessimistic and boyishly optimistic at the same time. This archeofuturistic quality becomes all the more obvious when Spencer frames Trump as a future nostalgic force: ‘Yet MAGA is also forward looking’. Spencer argues, ‘This idea that we can do this, that America can be what it was, that this idealized past can be restored. More than that, that it can reach new heights, be ‘greater than ever before’, as President-elect Trump put it (Spencer, 2016). In this, the palingenetic creed shouldn’t be overlooked: the past shouldn’t just be restored, it should reach new heights.

Spencer hails Trump as an archeofuturistic metapolitical instrument, that is, someone who will help to revitalize archaic ideas in service of a new vitalistic project for America. He explicitly evaluates Trump’s campaign as part of a larger metapolitical battle, waged not only by intellectuals but also by prosumers, trolls and embedded memes. The memification of Trump as ‘emperor’, and the references to Kek and meme-magic in this speech all index the broad conceptualization of the new right metapolitical battle building further and expanding the conceptualization of metapolitics by Faye. Trump and the ‘hysteria surrounding his election’ and the left’s reaction to the alt-right memes are juxtaposed and read as indexes of the ‘liberal hegemony which governs this society’ (Spencer, 2016). The praising of Trump as emperor in Spencer’s speech should thus be understood, not as proof that Trump is alt-right, but as spreading a metapolitical meme contributing to the destabilization of the liberal order.

The alt-right considered Trump, classical intellectual metapolitics and metapolitical meme warfare as useful but ‘not enough’ to succeed in reconstructing society. At best, they are useful steps in the right direction. Leonard argues that ‘from the bottom up, through grassroots initiatives or guerrilla propaganda or meme warfare or what have you – all of this is good, is important, but it is absolutely secondary’ (Leonard, 2018a). A true new right metapolitics, he argues, should preconfigure the ideal society grounded in what Faye (2011) called archaic values. In the last analysis, Leonard stresses,

An anti-democratic metapolitics cannot depend on the demos for political transformation. We, who are not egalitarians; we, who do not hold that ‘all men are created equal’; we, who believe in the naturalness and hence the desirability of hierarchy in society and in politics, must look then, not first to forming a new people, but first to forming a new elite.

(Leonard, 2018b)

87The importance of the elite is not just an ideological position, it is informed by the facts on the ground. Just like Faye stressed the importance of politicians, and the access to mainstream media in a metapolitical battle, Leonard sees in the electoral success of far-right populism proof that politics is crucial to the success of a metapolitical project: ‘This has indeed been one of the principal lessons of the recent rise of “populism on the Right”’, he says, ‘and finds its parallel also in similar political developments of the last century: “populism of the Right” in any nation requires, as its absolute prerequisite, charismatic and capable leaders’ (Leonard, 2018b). A new right metapolitical battle should thus be grounded in a broad movement led by capable leaders. Echoing Lenin, Leonard stresses the importance of leaders, albeit they be politicians, activists or intellectuals: ‘Our principle aim should not be the production of a new people, but rather the cultivation of new leaders; for from out of a mass, a people in the true sense can only form around a magnetic centre’ (Leonard, 2018b).

Metapolitics 2.0 and the identitarian movement

The broad conceptualization of metapolitics as grounded not only in intellectual activity but also in politics and (digital) activism, pushed forward by a revolutionary activist vanguard is the legacy of Faye (Maly, 2022). It echoes Faye’s conceptualization of metapolitics and of organic democracy with aristocratic leaders showing the people the way. This focus is now central in global new right theories of praxis. Friberg for instance concludes: ‘To constitute a metapolitical vanguard, and hence to become a vital part of the broader initiative to set Europe back on the right path: this is the primary mission of the European new right’ (Friberg, 2015: 49). In the United States that new vanguard was found in the alt-right (at least prior to the discrediting of the alt-right brand after the violent attack in Charlottesville during the Unite the Right manifestations). In Europe, the identitarian movement is seen as an excellent example (even though this partly changed after the New Zealand killing spree). Generation Identity claims to be ‘a nursery for future leaders of the entire identitarian movement. Young activists trained daily’ to become ‘the militant aristocracy, the vanguard of our vision of the world’ (Generation Identity, 2013: 43). Camus (2019: 74) says, I think rightly, that it is questionable to see de Benoist and Venner as the forefathers of the ‘identitarian movement in Europe’. It is probably more correct to say that next to Renaud Camus’ work on the ‘Great Replacement’ and the works of Dominique Venner, it was Faye’s controversial and mantra-like style that clearly hit a sweet spot among the identitarians (Marchi, 2016).

Faye’s book ‘Pourquoi nous combattons: Manifeste de la Résistance Européenne’ can without exaggeration be seen as an ideological bible of the French identitarians of the Bloc Identitaire (François, 2009). Faye was very 88eager to define himself as an identitarian (TV Liberté, 2019). He explicitly wrote as an identitarian, as part of that fighting network. It is important to stress that Faye was not only a provocateur, an ideologue or a national messenger of the ideas of de Benoist, but he was also above all an educator producing a theory of praxis. His books, essays and speeches were designed to contribute to the construction of a broad metapolitical vanguard. Faye ends ‘Why We Fight’ by stating that:

We have to see ourselves as the vanguard of resistance (…) Victory won’t be won through peaceful bourgeois reform (…) We have to prepare ourselves for the coming tempest, to harden ourselves – for the sake of attacking, like a cobra, quickly and decisively, once the moment of opportunity strikes. In anticipating this moment, we need now to start arming ourselves – mentally and physically – we need to recruit, to proselytize, to educate, to organize in networks of solidarity and action.

(Faye, 2011: 272)

He clearly writes to inform and form an activist’s – and not just an intellectual – movement fighting for a new time.

The metapolitical dictionary that was added to the English edition of ‘Why We Fight’ is another excellent example of his educational role. In that dictionary, Faye (together with Belgian new right intellectual Robert Steuckers who co-authored the French version of that dictionary) is literally providing new activists and wannabe intellectuals with a metapolitical language. He teaches them to claim the key concepts of the adversary – like democracy – and provides them with the new right or conservative revolutionary meanings I described above. Faye not only explicitly explains keywords like identity, democracy, interregnum, globalism, nation and nationalism, but he also introduces a framework to help new recruits to speak and think about contemporary and future societies in a metapolitical way. The explanations he provides are explicit and thus devoid of any metapolitical quality: it is a new right to speak for dummies.

Generation Identity's reconquest and generational populism

Generation Identity’s discourse, practices and goals embody Faye’s dream of reconquest. Generation Identity describes itself as ‘a fighting community’ and ‘a spearhead of resistance’ that ‘declares war’ (Generation Identity, 2013: 8–9): ‘Our ideal is Reconquest, and we will see it through to the end. Generation Identity is the barricade upon which our Youth are mounting in order to fight for our identity’ (Generation Identity, 2013: 12–13). The first texts that the movement produces and publishes echo Guillaume Faye’s ideal 89of ‘Reconquest’ and they explicitly refer to Faye in a footnote to explain what they mean by ‘reconquest’. The assumption of the need to reconquer is of course that terrain has been lost. In other words, the assumption is that there is a Great Replacement or an ongoing colonization of Europe that needs not only to be stopped but the land should also be reconquered. Faye (2011: 41) presents his readers with hope and reasons to fight by stressing the need for ‘Reconquest’. His answer to the question ‘why do we fight’ is straightforward:

We don’t fight for the ‘cause of peoples’, because the identity of every people is its own concern, not ours (…) we fight only for the cause of our own people’s destiny. Our political activities (…) are guided by the imperative of all Grand Politics: that is, by the struggle for the heritage of our ancestors and the future of our children.

(Faye, 2011: 41)

Reconquest is only possible according to Faye in the sense of a renewel of archaic values and the re-establishment of homogenous groups. The pan-European manifestation of the identitarian movement is a pre-configuration of Faye’s dream of a European revolution. The first step is metapolitical: people should see migration in terms of colonization. After the action at the Grand Mosque of Poitiers, Generation Identitaire tried to legitimize their actions by arguing:

a nation can recover from an economic crisis or a war, but not from the replacement of its population: without the French, France will no longer exist. It is a question of survival: this is why each nation has an absolute right to choose whether it wants to accept foreigners and in what proportion.

(Generation Identity, 2013: 19)

The goal of Generation Identitaire is

Not a matter of gaining an electoral majority, but of remaking a people! We are a UFO in a political landscape that is fossilised as that of France – a vanguard to awakened the people, not a bunch of little politicians hiding behind their neckties. (Generation Identity, 2013: 40). They are defenders of ‘direct democracy’, federalism and localism.

(Generation Identity, 2013: 32)

Generation Identity, just like Faye and de Benoist & Champetier, understands democracy as based on the identity of a homogenous people. Direct democracy works if it is grounded in localism. Their battle, again like Faye’s, is 90understood in biological and cultural terms, as embedded in ‘our blood, our soil and our identity’ (Generation Identity, 2013: 10). Whereas the alt-right especially highlights the racial component of democracy in Faye’s work, we see that identitarians leave this more implicit, but they all stress the necessity of homogeneity for democracy. Identitarian activist Markus Willinger (2013: 41), for instance, again just like Faye refers to Athens when he speaks about the identitarian embrace of direct democracy and its battle against representative democracy. And he also understands democracy as based on identity and a people. And just like Faye, and La Nouvelle Droite in general, identitarians envision this identity in European – not nationalist terms: ‘Europe, is a community of civilisation and culture. (…) Europeans must recognize this bond which has united us for 30,000 years now’ (Generation Identity, 2013: 37). This vitalistic constructionism of an archeofuturistic Europe, the stress on race and ethno-pluralism, the hatred towards Islam and Muslims and advocating an organic democracy expressing the will of the European people (Willinger, 2013) makes several scholars see the identitarian movement ‘as the direct-action arm of the (French) new right intended to make new right topics such as identity politics, homeland politics and anti-immigration agitation particularly attractive for youth by adapting modern communication methods to this end’ (Salzborn, 2016: 50). What is missed in this type of assessment is that GI explicitly takes Faye’s lessons on board and less those of Alain de Benoist. Generation Identitaire does not support the right of all individuals and communities, immigrant and non-immigrant alike in one nation, like de Benoist. They fight against Islam and for the homogenous Europe of European people.

Faye’s influence on Generation Identity is not only visible in the fact that he is regularly quoted in the manifesto ‘We are Generation Identity’ or in the consistent use of the concept of ‘Reconquest’ (Generation Identity, 2013: 12, 28) as their goal, it is especially visible in their strategy. Generation Identity sees itself as a fighting community, as the ‘awakeners of the people’ and ‘role models’ whose sensational activism and its re-mediatization on social media is made for uptake by mainstream media. They target the sensationalist commercial mainstream media logic (Chadwick, 2017) in

Order to sow the seeds of the Reconquest to come. We are a signal light toward which many young people will turn once the ethnic and political polarisation of French society leads to the return of social and political movement.

(Generation Identity, 2013: 34)

From the start, Generation Identity wanted to overcome the ‘Gramscian metapolitics in which cultural victory is a condition for political victory: it’s 91super-politics’ (Generation Identity, 2013: 34). It is a fighting community, not for an abstract ‘rights of peoples’, but for regional identities and the European identity. Faye’s understanding of the metapolitical as necessarily complementary to other forms of action is at the heart of the movement and their sensationalist activism. In the beginning, Generation Identity was set up as

one of three pillars of the identitarian movement founded in 2002. This movement joins together the Bloc Identitaire, a political party and networking tool, the association Les Identitaires, which organises an identitarian summer camp each year – a place for political and militant training (…) – and Generation Identity, a fighting community.

(Generation Identity, 2013: 40)

Generation Identity is not only an offline activist movement, it is (or at least was) also very much present online. The launch of Generation Identitaire didn’t go unnoticed in 2012. The spectacular ‘occupation’ of the roof of a mosque under construction in Poitiers created a buzz, not only in France but also throughout the hybrid media system in Europe. The movement was only one month old at the time, but its ‘Declaration of War’ video was seen over 93,000 times on YouTube. The reupload of that video in 2018, after the original one was deleted for copyright infringement, managed to be seen by 68,000 viewers. The original video was already ready in summer, and it was shown to the activists during their 2012 camp (Generation Identity, 2013: 15). After its launch in October 2012, many identitarian activists throughout Europe used the affordances of YouTube to add subtitles. ‘Prosumers’ translated the declaration of the movement into different languages and the English version very quickly had more views that the original French one. The same thing happened with the introduction video of Génération Identitaire, which was translated ‘in German, Spanish, English, Greek, Italian (…) In each case the translations were personal initiatives on the part of Europeans we do not know’ (Generation Identity, 2013: 16). The message of Génération Identitaire was re-entextualized and targeted new audiences in new languages.

This stress on the ‘organic uptake’ is a central argument in the discursive positioning of the moment. As co-founder of Génération Identitaire Alban Ferrari mentions in a 2012 interview, the Austrian chapter started independently as a Facebook page (Generation Identity, 2013: 16), and the Facebook pages Generation Identity: Germany and Generation Identity Italy appeared after the sensational action of Génération Identitaire at the Mosque in Poitiers. In their communication, they like to stress the ‘spontaneous’ nature of the uptake and support. When asked if they translated the video, Ferrari highlights that ‘We had intended to, but we were beaten to the punch by spontaneous, independent initiatives’ (Generation Identity, 2013:16). In this 92discourse, the translations and birth of different national identitarian chapters across Europe are framed in a populist logic as touching a nerve among a generation: ‘the video’s success proves we are on the right track and that our way of thinking is shared by most of the young people here’ (Generation Identity, 2013: 15). If we look at this populism as a chronotopic mediatized communicative relation (Maly, 2018e), we see the importance not only of the populist claim to speak in name of a generation, but also of some understanding of what ticks among some people who are willing to engage with your message. That uptake of the message can then be discursively used to claim the legitimacy of that claim. The actions of the ‘prosumers’, the likes, shares and the followers are being presented as evidence that they truly speak in the name of this generation, not only in France but also in Europe and even in the United States. ‘Since Poiters, our call to action has been heard’, said a press release of the movement. Génération Identitaire also claimed to have received 500 messages in two days, and the Bloc Identitaire, nearly 3,000 messages. When researchers, encyclopaedia (see the Wikipedia page on the Generation Identitaire) and legacy media (FranceInfo, 2021) take over this label of populism, the discursive framing is successful: an extreme-right discourse has then been rebranded in ‘articulating the voice of the people’ (Maly, 2018e).

The occupation in Poitiers functions as a format that can be applied by the different chapters in the different countries. The action at the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin, where 15 activists from the Identitäre Bewegung put up banners reading Sichere Grenzen, sichere Zukunft (Secure Borders, secure future) and Grenzen schützen! Leben Retten! (Closed Borders! Save Lives), follow the exact format as the original action at Poitiers, including the remediatization and the attention of mass media all over the world. And also in 2020, the French chapter proves the usefulness of the format to grab media attention when they dropped a banner saying ‘Justice pour les victim du racisme anti-blanc’ from a building in Paris during a Black Lives Matter protest in June 2020 in the French capital. Whereas the French slogan is made for local uptake, the hashtag #whitelivesmatter below the slogan not only directs viewers to Twitter in search, it also indexes an intended international audience and an international association, especially with the alt-right.

Defend Europe: metapolitics and digital media

The different ‘media guerrilla actions’ on a local, national and European scale have constantly enabled the movement to enlarge its audience and its reach. This media tactic clearly worked. In May 2017, when they launched their Defend Europe Mission, the National French chapter of the pan-European movement alone had over 124.000 likes on Facebook. This mission was supported by all the European chapters, but of course also by the regional branches of the movement. The French chapter alone had branches in Nice, 93Paris, Nantes, Bretagne, Dauphiné and Lille. Those branches had offline gathering locations in the form of bars and boxing clubs and had their own Facebook pages to give information, recruit members and organize events. These Facebook pages were useful in the dissemination of information from the local to the national and the European scale, and back: they created a pan-European network of influence. A network that could share and like the remediatized actions of the movement and spread it through Europe and the hybrid media system. Just like Generation Identitaire started in 2012 with their ‘Declaration of War’ video’, the Defend Europe Mission started with a video and the launch of a brand new pan-European website.

Every week, every day, every hour – ships packed with illegal Immigrants are flooding into European waters. An invasion is taking place. This massive immigration is changing the face of our continent. We are losing our safety and our way of life and there is a danger we Europeans will become a minority in our own European homelands. Our future is under attack.

(Defend Europe, 2017a)

This quote started the Mission Defend Europe video that was posted on the Facebook page of Generation Identitaire on 14 May 2017. The uptake of this video was again huge. By December 2017, the video was watched over 319,000 times on Facebook, shared 2,000 times and over 13,000 profiles reacted with a thumbs up or another emoticon. In the video, we see four young identitarian militants talking about migration as a threat to Europe. Their discourse echoes Faye’s conceptualization of migration as an invasion and a danger for Europe and its way of life. At the same time, it also echoes the discourse that many radical right and far-right politicians were articulating in the mainstream media. Politicians like Theo Francken (Maly, 2018a) from the New Flemish Alliance, Salvini in Italy and Le Pen in France were advocating the necessity of ‘pushback’ and praising the ‘Australian Model’ (Generation Identitaire, 2017) of pushing ships back. This political discourse circulated freely in mainstream media, and it had the effect of normalizing or de-radicalizing the actions of Generation Identity.

The Defend Europe Mission was supported by different websites and social media of the national and regional branches of the identitarian movement, but they also launched a European website and specific social media channels for this specific action. On the website, which was designed according to the corporate identity of the movement, one could not only read up on the mission, or find news, one could also click on the support button. At first, this button brought visitors to a PayPal account, but after June 2017 this was not possible anymore. PayPal blocked the identitarian account.

This backlash was also an opportunity to convince the followers of the movement to donate money and frame this act of PayPal as an attack from 94the globalists. The Thumbnail clearly framed the action of PayPal as an anti-patriotic action. Considering the discourse of this movement, this act of PayPal can be seen as a reinforcement of the idea that ‘the globalists are against them’. In the video, Martin Sellner argued that through this mission ‘We want to show PayPal, Twitter and all these globalists and the mainstream media, that they can censure us, that they can block us, but that they can’t stop us’ (Defend Europe, 2017b). The videos that were recorded and posted in German (10,000 views) and English (6,900 views) generated quite some uptake. Many people commented that they had or will be transferring money or even doubling their donation. Sellner also makes sure to stress that their followers shouldn’t believe ‘the shitstorm’ started by the mass media and thus should donate. Mass media and globalists want you to believe that ‘we want people to drown. That we want the rescuing missions to end. No’, Sellner says, ‘we want the human trafficking to end. We want to rescue people before the Libyan coast, but we want to bring them back from where they came’ (Defend Europe, 2017b). Note how Sellner stresses that they are on a rescue mission. Rescuing refers to pushing migrants back and even more importantly: ‘we want to start a rescuing mission to save the future of Europe’ (Defend Europe, 2017b). The dominant discourse is thus one that fits into the narrative of Faye and Camus: they are on a mission to stop the replacement. And that mission is urgent. As Sellner stresses in another video, a couple of days before the ship would be on its way to the Libyan coast:

We live in a time of decision. This time, in our day and age, it will be decided if Europe and the whole West will have a future. At the moment this future is looking dark (…) that’s why we don’t plan our vacations, we plan to defend Europe this summer.

(Defend Europe, 2017c)

By the first of August 2017, the ship was on its way with the identitarian crew to the Libyan coast. In a short vlog, Sellner stressed that this boat sailing out was the nightmare of ‘Soros’ and all the globalists (Defend Europe, 2017d).
