Underneath that video, one could read a short status update in French, Italian, English and German. It also contained a link to their WeSearchr account. WeSearcher was set up by Charles Carlisle Johnson, an American far-right activist and troll, as an alternative to Crowdfunding sites that banned far-right projects. Even though this platform was short-lived, Generation Identity managed to collect over 300,000 dollars to fund their Defend Europe Mission (234,000 to charter the ship, and another 83,000 dollars for the crew and other expenses).

The mission was a success in terms of hybrid salience. Maniou and Bantimaroudis (2018) introduced the notion of ‘hybrid salience’. ‘Hybrid forms of salience’, they say, ‘should be approached as indices of mediated significance 95derived from interdependent and asymmetrical distributions of media power, divided between mainstream media outlets as well as grassroots digital platforms including various in-between hybrid media formations’. Hybrid salience highlights the fact that salience has now been fragmented over different media, actors and niches. In the case of Defend Europe, this salience was not only the effect of their own communication, but it was also the result of the Canadian far-right YouTuber Laura Southern praising the plans of Generation Identity during a live stream on Periscope in May 2017 that was posted on Twitter. Southern was later joined by the American far-right YouTuber Brittany Pettibone. Both Southern and Pettibone would regularly tweet and post vlogs on YouTube to update their followers. These postings were also amplified on Buzzfeed (Broderick, 2017). Considering their status in the alt-right, and globally in the case of Southern at the time, it is no coincidence that lots of key figures in the United States would support the Defend Europe Mission. The ‘ironic’ neo-Nazi site The Daily Stormer advocated the action and the former grand wizard of the KKK asked his Twitter followers to support the mission. From a metapolitical perspective, the action was a great success. It was also a success in the sense of networking. After the Mission, Sellner joined Brittany Pettibone in the United States. This trip with Pettibone was mediatized on YouTube as a work trip to allow the US movement to learn about the European identitarian movements and vice versa. It was also the start of their relationship.

Social media were thus very much part of the infrastructure of this movement. This was the case locally, but also on a national and transnational level. Most of its impact, and especially the upscaling from a French to a pan-European movement, is a result of its embeddedness in social media. The pan-European movement Generation Identity is clearly a post-digital phenomenon (Fielitz & Thurston, 2019): not only is their digital presence at least as important as their offline activism, but it is also based on digitally enabled reproduction of their message. This movement from the start benefited from the network effects of digital media: they use the affordances of digital media to connect, organize and structure different chapters on a pan-European scale and remediatize their activism for upscaling the metapolitical effect. It is also clear that they do not see the political field as separate but as an essential part of their metapolitical battle. Already in 2012, they are explicit about their connections with existing movements and youth movements of political parties like the Flemish Interest (Generation Identity, 2013: 16). In 2019, we see that the different national chapters of the official and unofficial identitarian movements in Europe have very close relations to the so-called radical right ‘populist’ parties like Rassemblement National in France, Flemish Interest in Belgium, FPÖ in Austria, Forum For Democracy in The Netherlands, the AFD in Germany and UKIP in the United Kingdom (Maly, 2018e; Murdoch & Mulhall, 2019). Generation Identity was built on sensational mediatized 96actions. It was a brand that gave a very clear collective identity to its militants. The movement was grounded in a digital and offline infrastructure enabling militants to build strong ties. Throughout the last decade, they succeeded in building a clear repertoire of collective action, readymade for uptake in the hybrid media system. It was those actions and their structure that allowed them to upscale the movement to a European and even a trans-European scale. But in the end, the real fundament of Generation is found in its metapolitics. And their version of metapolitics is the legacy of Faye.

Martin Sellner, fashwave and Faye's metapolitics

Martin Sellner, the de-facto face of Generation Identity on a European scale was de-platformed in August 2018 by YouTube in the wake of his e-mail contact with the Christchurch shooter and the juridical actions against him. Since his channel was re-instated, he has been reluctant to use his English YouTube channel. Even more, he deleted several older videos and put others on private. Among those private videos is a series of five videos he posted in 2017 that were dedicated to the work of Faye, especially focusing on his work ‘Why We Fight’. In the first video of this series, Sellner says that he read ‘Why We Fight’ in 2010 – thus before the birth of the Austrian Chapter of Generation Identity – in its German translation as part of a reading group in Vienna and claims that this book, even though he doesn’t agree with Faye on all points, has changed him (Sellner, 2017a). ‘Why We Fight’, says Sellner is one of the important inspiration sources of the identitarians (Sellner, 2017b).

Before we zoom in on the actual content of the videos, it is useful to have a look at the graphics. The opening sequence echoes a vaporwave aesthetics then quite popular online. In the first shot, we see a nineties white Lamborgini Diablo driving on vaporwave techno beats and neon rasters. The Diablo was produced between 1990 and 2001. It is an object of nostalgia, referring back to the ‘near past’. The Diablo, as the successor of the Countach, is a typical poster child and thus comes with strong emotions, especially for young petrolheads. This nostalgic feeling about a past where everything is better is enhanced by the vaporwave graphic. This adoption of vaporwave aesthetics by far-right movements was common practice around 2017 and was called fashwave. This trend combines far-right discourse with the then popular hype of synthwave. The result of this assemblage is the use of nostalgic ‘futurist’ imagery reminiscent of nineties video game culture, neon colours with a preference for purple and pink and synth beats from the eighties and nineties to promote a far-right message. The style has roots among neo-Nazis and was popularized by Andrew Anglinm from The Daily Stormer in August 2016, who called synthwave ‘the Whitest music ever’ and soon after began the ‘Fashwave Friday series posting retro sci-fi images and sounds’ (Hermansson, Lawrence, Mulhall & Murdoch, 2020:110). The style was also very popular 97among Germanica Reconquista who used the fashwave style to make historical references in their memes come across as less old-fashioned and more appealing to a younger audience (Bogerts & Fielitz:146–147). The Lambo first seems to cruise along without a real goal, but in the end, accelerates towards the lambda sun. From the moment the Lambo reaches the sun, the title of the show appears: Identity quest.

This opening sequence could be read through Faye’s Archeofuturism as a blend of nostalgia and futurism. With it, Sellner taps into a dominant nostalgia among the youth. Nostalgia, as is richly documented, is a key part of capitalist consumer societies. Interestingly, since the nineties of the last century, that nostalgia is not only very much present in advertisements, but the object of nostalgia changed fundamentally. Appadurai argued that ads increasingly:

Create what might be called “imagined nostalgia,” nostalgia for things that never were. This imagined nostalgia thus inverts the temporal logic of fantasy (which tutors the subject to imagine what could or might happen) and creates much deeper wants than simple envy, imitation, or greed could by themselves invite.

(1996: 77)

Sellner is indeed tapping into such an imagined nostalgia designed for uptake among 20 to 30-year-olds who see the eighties and nineties as ‘the past’ and 98as an epitome of coolness. It is not a coincidence that a lot of clothing and also nineties TV shows are coming back just now. Also, implicitly, it harks back to a time were most television shows – think of Friends or even Miami Vice – are mostly dominated by a heteronormative and white cast. Ergo, this vaporwave aesthetic frames his series on metapolitics through the opening sequence as something relevant for the youth, and relevant to find one’s true identity. What that identity is, and how to find it or fight for it becomes clear in the videos. In the introduction video of the series, Sellner makes it explicit why the idea of metapolitics, as Faye introduces it, is important. He argues that he sees two trends among new activists that he considers very negative. The first one is:

A radicalisation spiral, of people who think the most edgiest thing, the thing that is provoking the most, that is creating the most reactions in the internet in a comment or in a post, is the most courageous, the most true, the smartest thing to do.

(Sellner, 2017a)

Sellner disagrees: ‘I don’t think that is true’. ‘The other spiral’, he identifies, ‘is an opportunistic spiral, people who just want to pander to the mainstream’ (Sellner, 2017a). Both spirals, according to Sellner, show a lack ‘of strategic understanding, of metapolitics’. That’s why he dedicates this series of vlogs to Faye’s book. If we want to help establish an ‘archeofuturistic future’, says Sellner, we need ‘to school ourselves and that is why I will present this book’ (Sellner, 2017a).

Identity is the first concept that Sellner picks out of Faye’s metapolitical dictionary as the stuff that can inform new identitarian activists. The first video is dedicated to the ‘Identity’-lemma. Sellner calls the lemma on Identity in Faye’s metapolitical dictionary ‘prophetic’ and subscribes to the idea that culture is ‘ethnic’, that it ‘can’t be detached from the people that created it’ (Sellner, 2017b). Culture and identity are imagined to be grounded in ‘biology’, and thus in race. Humanity is ‘not universal, one united forum and then there are some superficial differences. No, the differences are very deep and very essential. (…) humanity is pluralistic’ (Sellner, 2017b). Pluralism, identity, humanity and metapolitics are thus understood in a biological and racial frame and echo Herder’s pluralism. In his copy of ‘Why We Fight’, shown in the vlog, Sellner has written an exclamation mark next to two paragraphs. In those paragraphs, Faye argues that the ‘European Identity is (…) neutralised, emptied of substance’ in contrast to ‘African, West Indian, and Arab-Muslim identities’ that are being ‘encouraged’ (Faye, 2011: 172). Sellner reads those passages in full in his vlog, and of course immediately links this with Generation Identity’s battle for maintaining the European identity and against the replacement. ‘We, as identitarianists, we cherish this (identity), 99while globalists (…) want to deny this, to overcome this’ (Faye, 2011: 172). Not only does Sellner subscribe to Faye’s definition of identity, but he also defines the actual goal of Generation Identity and their strategy in line with Faye’s focus and even explicitly reproduces his actual words and writings, but he does that in a whole new context and to a whole new audience: young English speaking identitarians.

The second vlog is entirely focused on the idea of metapolitics. ‘Metapolitics’, says Sellner, ‘is a very important concept for us, as we define ourselves as a metapolitical movement’ (Sellner, 2017b). Sellner’s introduction of Faye’s lemma on ‘metapolitics’ is immediately connected to the fundamental goal of the identitarian movement: the fight for European identity. In the vlog, Sellner not only shares Faye’s understanding of metapolitics and his critique on the ‘too metapolitical strategy of GRECE’, he explicitly takes up his copy of Archeofuturism to read Faye’s (2011: 29) claim that GRECE overlooked the fact that Gramsci’s cultural battle was linked to the political and economic battle of the communist party. Just like Johnson and more in general the American alt-right, Sellner not only subscribes to Faye’s critique of La Nouvelle Droite, he stresses that his own movement – Generation Identity – has learned from those failures. In Austria, Sellner says, the intellectual right was purely metapolitical and distinct from the activist right. ‘Brain and fist’ were separated from each other. Generation Identity, he says, is the first movement to follow Faye’s advice to ‘unite brain and fist’ (Sellner, 2017c).

New identitarian activists are thus advised to move beyond ‘pure intellectual metapolitics’, to unite brain and fist to fight for identity and against ‘globalism’ (Sellner, 2017d) and ‘individualism, the poison of the West’(Sellner, 2017e). Metapolitics is – according to Sellner, key here: activism, politics and cultural activity should all be seen as ‘part of that Ancient battle for ideas’(Sellner, 2017e). A battle that Sellner, just like Faye, La Nouvelle Droite and the anti-Enlightenment tradition, in general, directs against the idea of ‘the primacy of the individual’ and society as ‘based on a social contract’ (Sellner, 2017e). ‘The essence of society’, Sellner counterargues with references to Schmitt and Spengler, ‘is the community, not the individual. It is the primacy of the community’ (Sellner, 2017e). As always, the emancipation of the individual and his rights, the primacy of this individual and materialism are understood as part of that attack on the good society. ‘Modernism and individualism are replacing organic communities and replacing them with abstract systems and an atomized version of humanity’ (Sellner, 2017e).

The ideas of the French new right, especially in Faye’s version, are re-emerging in the second decennium of the 21st century in new digital practices, new forms of activism deeply embedded in the (mainstream) digital economy (Maly, 2019a) and in complex forms of activism addressing new audiences. ‘Archeofuturism’ and ‘Why We Fight’ are not only products of their time,

Guillaume Faye and the birth of metapolitics 2.0

Guillaume Faye’s role in the popularization of metapolitics, and especially the broadening of metapolitics from a purely intellectual practice to a broad ideological battle carried by a wide range of different actors, has played a key role in the genealogy of metapolitics 2.0. The rise of new right activists, intellectuals, movements and parties in the 21st century is not only connected to the digital economy and the digital literacy of the metapolitical activists but also to Faye’s conceptualization of metapolitics and the archeofuturistic future. His celebrity intellectual status within the global new right and the global praise after his death underline this legacy (Maly, 2022). Faye is not only an agent provocateur or a radical messenger of de Benoist ideas but also an educator. His identitarianism is a new blend of anti-Enlightenment (Sternhell, 2010), reactionary modernist, conservative revolutionary and Nouvelle Droite ideas repackaged in a new discourse, advocating new strategies, imaginaries and providing a new generation with a new geopolitical horizon and practical advice.

Generation Identity, but also key figures of the alt-right like Richard Spencer, Greg Johnson and Jared Taylor, are his living legacy: they have appropriated or re-entextualized his ideas in new practices, new battles and new contexts directing them to new audiences. Spencer even explicitly labelled himself an archeofuturist (Hawely, 2017: 65). It is in this uptake that we see why analysing ideology should not be limited to classic texts of intellectuals but should take Thompson’s lessons on board and also analyse uptake, distribution and reproduction of these ideologies within a new digital ecology. This focus on the uptake and the morphing of ideological reproduction allows us to avoid the fallacy of internalism and direct attention to an empirical understanding of the impact and meaning in society. It also forces us to take the infrastructure itself into account (Maly, 2022a).

When we do that, we not only realize that metapolitics has been taken up as a key ingredient of new right groups around the world, but we can see that many of those movements and activists mobilize similar topics and discourses in order to fight that cultural battle. The idea of white genocide or the Great Replacement, the attack on our identity, culture and values, the idea that boomers have destroyed Western society or the fight against political correctness, the left, LGBTQ+ acceptance and migration, they all have become standard discourse ingredients of the far-right around the 101world. Metapolitics 2.0 is fundamentally different than La Nouvelle Droite’s conception of metapolitics. Metapolitics 2.0 is co-constructed by the affordances and interfaces of digital media: it is an effect of the uptake of a broader conception of metapolitics as advocated by Guillaume Faye and the integration in digital cultures facilitated by the digital utopianism ideologies underpinning major digital media platform. As a result, metapolitics has been ‘democratized’: not only intellectuals engage in metapolitics, but also activists, influencers, movements and politicians. The metapolitical strategies of new right actors are not only visible in the classic metapolitical structures influenced by La Nouvelle Droite, but are embedded and enabled by digital cultures. Metapolitics can now also be found in blogs and vlogs, memes, podcasts and influencer culture and in offline practices influenced by digital culture. In the next chapters, we will further unpack metapolitics 2.0 by zooming in on metapolitical activism (Chapter 3), metapolitical influencers (Chapter 4) and conspiracy theories (Chapter 5). In Chapter 6 we focus on the offline impact of this new metapolitical digital culture.

107

3 The global new right and the algorithmic activism of Schild & Vrienden

DOI: 10.4324/9781003283379-4

This chapter has been made available under a CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 license.

In the previous chapter, I showed how La Nouvelle Droite’s metapolitics as an ideological project has been taken up by activists in Europe and the United States. I first showed the historical context of metapolitics and subsequently stressed the processes of re-entextualization in which metapolitics slowly but surely was expanded to include new strategies and new actors. Metapolitics 2.0, as I call it, was profoundly mediated by Guillaume Faye. In this chapter, I will argue that contemporary new right metapolitics not only binds together different generations of actors but also different actors around the world (Johnson, 2012; Hawley, 2017; Nagle, 2017; Maly, 2018d). Several scholars have highlighted the translocal and global dimensions of contemporary far-right groups, activists and even far-right terrorism (Miller-Idriss, 2018; Maly, 2018a, 2018b; Auger, 2020; Caniglia, Winkler & Métais, 2020). This seems paradoxical, as the new and far-right is usually associated with an anti-globalist position. I will therefore start by analysing new right discourse on globalization and arguing why we should abandon methodological nationalism, and start analysing the contemporary new right from a global context. The digital media ecology, I argue, not only allowed for the globalization of metapolitical commitment, strategies and practices, but it also reshaped them, and maybe more importantly, it gave birth to a global new right culture. Metapolitics 2.0 is one of the global ingredients of the contemporary new right.

Globalization, globalism and the global new right

Already in the nineties, new right intellectuals and far-right politicians used the rupture caused by cultural or neoliberal globalization to mobilize 108people for national, regional, anti-liberal, racist and especially anti-left stances (Blommaert & Verschueren, 1998; Kriesi et al., 2008; Wodak et al., 2014). In a widely read and translated paper, Alain de Benoist tapped into the anti-globalist left of the nineties and the first decade of the 21st century and argued (de Benoist, 1996: 125) that globalization, ‘through a flood of universal images and sounds, (…) contributes to the standardization of lifestyles, to the reduction of differences and particularities, the conformity of attitudes and behaviours, the eradication of collective identities and traditional cultures’. Globalization is here understood as a process of homogenization – and not in left-wing terms as imperialistic, causing exploitation and inequality – driven by ‘egalitarianism, the reducer of the world’s diversity’. The anti-globalization discourse is in essence directed towards a specific form of globalization. It does this by adapting popular theories on globalization as a McDonaldization (see for instance the bestselling book from Barber [1996] on Jihad vs McWorld) and thus linking to mainstream popular knowledge about globalization. This so-called anti-globalism discourse is a dominant narrative among contemporary new right activists. It is paradoxically globalized and has become one of the global characteristics of the global new right. The success of this anti-globalism discourse is not only due to the preparatory work of La Nouvelle Droite but also the result of contemporary new right actors like Lana Lokteff, Brittany Pettibone, The Golden One, Lauren Southern, Millennial Woes and many others who have global reach and are globally connected that spread it around in different niches. Of course, Donald Trump (Blommaert, 2019b) and many other figures with access to the mainstream have certainly contributed to the further popularity and mainstreaming of this discourse.

Contrary to most popular and new right literature on globalization in the nineties of the 20th century, many fine-grained ethnographic studies contradict the growth of a so-called homogenizing global monoculture, or in more popular terms, the McDonaldization of the world (see for instance Pennycook, 2012). Mature theories on cultural globalization see it as a plurality of imagined worlds (Appadurai, 1996: 5), and the imagination of the collective through every day (mediated) practices is more and more diversified, transnational or even post-national. Even more, it is not necessarily ethnic or national anymore (Maly, Blommaert, & Ben Yakoub, 2014). Culture in post-digital and globalized times is best understood as ‘a more “niched” complex of processes, developing at different scale-levels, some of them truly global, but most of them regional, national or even sub-national’. (Blommaert, 2010: 77). The truly global world of the elites, the business people and the top politicians and diplomats do impact ordinary life and usually falls beyond the reach of the common man. This scale level is highly exclusive and powerful, but globalization is more than that. Globalization also works on lower scales – the vernacular globalization that Appadurai spoke about – 109and takes the form of translocal networks of locally embedded groups that are jointly producing culture in networks (Castells, 1996). The global new right is, as we have seen, paradoxically an example of this. Digitalization has a central role in this globalization of the new right. The new generation of new right intellectuals and activists use digital media not only to engage in a metapolitical battle, or to organize offline protest, but digital media form a crucial infrastructure that allows activists to educate themselves, to network, to build culture and to shape their activism. Digital media allowed far-right activists to learn from each other, and as a result, a global new right network and culture was born.

Understanding the globalization of the new right

Global culture shouldn’t be understood as a synonym for a homogeneous culture on a global scale. Contrary to what popular parlance and new right theories on globalization want us to believe, globalization or globalism doesn’t produce a homogenization of culture, a global monoculture (See Blommaert, 2011 for a detailed discussion), but a world of countless cultural niches operating on different scales. The global new right culture is one of those cultural niches. And within that niche, we see a complex web of different centres of normativity operating on different scales. The result is a layered, transnational and polycentric culture that preconfigures the new right world order. Material and symbolic ties within that cultural niche are very real, but they are only real in unpredictable and complex ways that beg for detailed analysis. The contemporary new right is thus not a swarm of individuals, reacting autonomously but synchronized, they are structured networked publics around sites, think tanks, intellectuals, influencers, movements and activists who lead them, sometimes as reluctant leaders (Gerbaudo, 2014), sometimes taking up the role of leader. This new right global cultural niche is not unique, but a typical product of globalization processes facilitated by digital media and rising mobility.

In order to analyse and grasp the full meaning of contemporary new right metapolitics, I employ a global perspective that focusses on the mobility of resources and the layeredness of activism. In short, I argue that if we truly want to understand new right metapolitical activism in the 21st century, we need to overcome ‘methodological nationalism’. Research on politics, and in particular on nationalism and the far-right, to a large extent, still displays ‘methodological nationalism (…) the assumption that the nation/state/society is the natural social and political form of the modern world’ (Wimmer & Glick Schiller, 2002). Even though there are reasons to do that in far-right research (the regional and national claims for instance), we should realize that methodological nationalism blurs the fact that the world has always been transnational and turns a blind eye to the impact of cellular systems 110(Appadurai, 2006: 27) in the construction of the contemporary (political) world. More importantly, it blurs the fact that globalization is actually used for nationalist and regionalist goals. Miller-Idriss (2018: 132), for instance, argues that ‘many of these nationalist movements have distinctly and strikingly global aspects’ as a result of the ‘rapid transformation in communication and knowledge sharing across national boundaries’.

Methodological nationalism ignores globalization as context in meaning-making processes and thus in culture production. Contextualizing national and regional new right practices and discourses is crucial to understand the contemporary new right. Miller-Idriss describes the effect of globalization in terms of ‘deterritorialization’: far-right activists can now ‘align, cooperate, communicate, and support each other across national contexts’ (Miller-Idriss, 2018: 134). Miller-Idriss rightfully focuses on the global and mobility of meanings, but at the same time, she seems to overstate the ‘de- territorialisation’ and the ‘de-contextualization’ that globalization and digital media cause. Even though I fully support Miller-Idriss’ plea to move beyond a national or an international comparative approach and thus focus on the global and effects of mobility on meaning-making, I do think that a sociolinguistic approach to culture and globalization can deepen our understanding of far-right cultures and practices in the 21st century, and provide a more empirical and detailed account of the effects of globalization on far-right culture. The starting point in such an approach is that mobility of signs and discourses is not ‘a mobility across empty spaces, but mobility across space filled with codes, customs, rules, expectations and so forth’ (Blommaert, 2005: 73). This in practice means that signs are never fully de-contextualized or de-territorialized: they are used in those contexts and thus filled and shaped according to the norms, codes, rules and expectations of their users.

The rise of digitalization and mobility since the nineties of the 20th century has created a juncture visible in the scale, intensity and scope of globalization processes (Appadurai, 1996; Arnaut et al., 2016). Migration and digital media have not only reshaped our imagination of the world (Appadurai, 1996: 3), they also enabled the democratization of global (cultural) flows. Whereas in non-digital times, the transnational dimension of politics was to a large extent embedded in the networks of national political elites and vertebrate ‘inter-national’ organizations, this has changed in the last decades (Appadurai, 1996: 32; Maly, Blommaert & Ben Yakoub, 2014). Today, digital media function as infrastructures that enable and structure global networked activist movements (Klein 2002, 4; Wolfson, 2014; Tufekci, 2017). The rising importance of global networks, cellular systems and global cultural and political flows are emblematic of this latest phase of globalization and are largely undertheorized when it comes to new right activism. By taking on board a sociolinguistic theory of globalization (see Blommaert, 2011), I will 111analyse the Flemish identitarian movement Schild & Vrienden from a global perspective, but first I want to shed some light on digital media and the global flows in contemporary far-right culture.

Metapolitics 2.0 and the global new right

Whereas the far-right has always used digital media to propagate their ideologies (Winter 2019; Weimann & Masri, 2020), we have seen that the adoption of the metapolitical strategy has changed the form and the strategies that are being used today. Even the actors themselves have changed: metapolitics has been democratized. From highbrow far-right intellectual work, it has now morphed into a broad rhizomatic network of actors (re)producing far-right ideas in many different forms using many different channels and addressing many different (niched) audiences. These changes have had fundamental effects, not only on the metapolitical battle itself but also on the structure and scale on which far-right actors operate. The affordances of digital media have shaped and facilitated the globalization of new right actors. Some of those actors work on a local scale, others on a national or European scale, and some of them operate on a truly global scale. Martin Sellner for instance is not only a prominent member of the Austrian chapter of Generation Identity, but he also plays a crucial role on a European and even a global scale. A similar argument can be made about a key figure like The Golden One (see Chapter 3). This far-right bodybuilder and influencer may be located in Sweden, but his uptake is global and is explicitly designed for global uptake. Alexander Dugin is another example. The Russian new right philosopher merged GRECE and the Traditionalism of Julius Evola for the Russian market, but at the same time, he has become one of the most influential new right intellectuals on a global scale. He is invited to congresses around the world, interviewed by mass media and translated and distributed by Arktos. In the 21st century, the new right is a polycentric, layered and transnational new right network (Maly, 2018a). This network was in the last years the object of increasing academic attention and has been labelled as the international alt-right (Hermansson, Lawrence, Mulhall & Murdoch, 2020), new right 2.0 (Watson & Barnes, 2022) or the European-American radical right (François, 2019). All those labels describe the transnationalization of the contemporary far-right and the legacy of La Nouvelle Droite on that transnational scale. I choose to use the label global new right for four reasons:

  1. In my analysis, the alt-right is tied to activism that is first and foremost connected to the advancement of new right metapolitics in the United States. This movement in itself is indeed an international network (see Figure 3.1), but the focus of that network – even though it has received global uptake – is first and foremost the United States.

  2. 112The alt-right itself is more effectively and correctly described as a deglobalization of the European new right. The alt-right is (was) an important centre within the global new right, but it was certainly not the only centre, nor the only important one, nor the first one.
  3. The theories of the intellectuals of La Nouvelle Droite are – as I argued in the previous chapter – the ideological roots of contemporary movements that are described by those labels. In all actions of contemporary new right movements and actors around the world, we see the metapolitical injection of La Nouvelle Droite. This injection does not limit itself to Europe or the United States. Dugin for instance has appropriated it in Russia, dreaming of a Eurasian empire.
  4. The metapolitical strategy of La Nouvelle Droite is one of the elements that creates unity in this global movement. Metapolitics has been globalized, meaning that the new right battle for culture has taken roots in many different countries of the world. It was a global injection that was subsequently deglobalized by local actors like the alt-right in the United States, Generation Identitaire in France or Schild & Vrienden in Belgium.
  5. The different activists, sites, intellectuals and influencers form a truly global network. They read, share and support work from each other and use it to legitimize local and translocal goals. The Golden One reads La Nouvelle Droite, promotes Arktos books, is invited to congresses in the Ukraine and is viewed from all corners of the world.
  6. The ideas and the battle of the contemporary new right are explicitly global in nature. They do not just imagine a national world, they fight for a new world order. They call it a pluriversum, an ethno-plural world or and multipolar world. The crux is that they do not limit themselves to nationalism, but they think in terms of civilizations and empires. They think, but as we will see, also act, on a global scale.

The global new right is in this sense a far more precise term. The global new right refers to all those sites, publishers, conferences, activists, politicians, intellectuals, influencers and media sites operating as centres of normativity. What binds them is their resistance against the ‘modern world’, the egalitarianism that supports contemporary cultural globalization. They fight democracy, universal human rights, liberalism and socialism, and fight for a second modernity based on the rights of people, organicism and tradition. Not globalization is the main enemy, but globalism: the neoliberal form of contemporary globalization.

Arktos and the globalization of anti-globalism

Far-right publishing house Arktos is an excellent case to understand this alternative form of globalization. Arktos was founded in 2009 and launched in 1132010, and is now the ‘largest retailer of radical right literature in the world’ (Teitelbaum, 2019: 270). Arktos is the inheritor of Integral Tradition Publishing, a Danish publishing company which started in 2005, and Nordiska Föglaget, the far-right publishing house of Nordiska Fördbundete. Integral Tradition Publishing started as an online bookstore and publishing company specializing in occult books and texts on mysticism that promoted traditionalist and esoteric worldviews (Valencia-Garcia, 2020). The Nordiska Fördbundet publishing house was Daniel Friberg’s first attempt to set up a metapolitical publishing house and media empire (Teitelbaum, 2019: 265). It is thus not a coincidence that Arktos, as a fusion of those publishers, claims not to propagate

any specific ideology, a system of beliefs or viewpoint, nor do we seek consistency. Rather, we want to provide a voice for individuals and viewpoints who are often overlooked by the mainstream, but who offer original and challenging alternatives to our prevailing culture that cannot be found elsewhere.

(Website Arktos accessed in 2022)

Former editor-in-chief John Morgan also claimed that Arktos is not pushing a specific ideology, but that they do provide ‘alternatives for modernity’ (THA Talks, 2016). The claim not to ‘push an ideology’, is thus not to be mistaken for being neutral, or Arktos being open to each ideology. ‘Ideology’ is here used in the narrow sense, as clear-cut ideologies like liberalism, fascism, or Nazism. Ideologies with clear boundaries. Arktos is an ideological publisher in the sense that it advocates all books that support, feed and shape the anti-Enlightenment tradition. Morgan, for instance, clearly argues that a pro-multiculturalist viewpoint or liberal one would not be considered for publication (THA Talks, 2016). In other words, Arktos is open to several ideologies, as long as they question the current modernity. ‘Our mission is very simple’ says Friberg: ‘to spread the ideas of the most important thinkers of our times as broad as possible’ (React, 2016). The ‘luminary thinkers’ that shape the contemporary anti-Enlightenment tradition promoted by Arktos are amongst others: Alain de Benoist, Guillaume Faye, Pierre Krebs, Alexander Dugin, Julius Evola, Generation Identity, Arthur Moeller van Den Bruck, Charles Maurras, Dominique Venner, H.P. Lovecraft, Markus Willinger, Oswald Spengler, James Kirkpatrick, Daniel Friberg, Jared Taylor, John Bruce Leonard and Koenraad Van Elst. Arktos publishes key thinkers of La Nouvelle Droite, contemporary far-right activists like (Markus Willinger, Generation Identity, Jared Taylor), Traditionalists (Julius Evola, Alexander Dugin) and Conservative Revolutionaries (Oswald Spengler, Charles Maurras). The most important thinkers are explicitly anti-liberal or more in general, anti-materialistic. This explains why Arktos can on the one hand claim to be not 114ideological, and to be proud that it ‘has established itself as the principal publisher in English of the writings of the European “new right” school of political thought’ (Arktos website, last accessed May 2022).

Arktos de facto functions as a foundational new right centre of normativity operating on the highest scale of globalization. It is a metapolitical infrastructure providing ideological education to far-right activists and intellectuals around the world. It is also a truly global infrastructure. Arktos itself has set up shops in Sweden, Great Britain, Hungary and India. Its authors come from France, Italy, Belgium, the United States, the UK, Russia, Iran and many other countries. Arktos also publishes in 16 different languages. Most of these languages are European in origin: English, Dutch, Hungarian, Polish, German, Spanish, Czech, Croatian, French, Greek, Italian, Latvian, Portuguese, Serbian, Slovak & Swedish. Next to Red Ice, Arktos is one of the sponsors of the Identitarian Ideas conference and it was a founding partner of the now-defunct website Altright.com. All these initiatives attracted intellectuals, activists and visitors on a global scale. Arktos also doesn’t hide the fact that its operation is global in nature. On the contrary. Not only does Friberg eagerly explain that this international form of Arktos was deliberate (Teitelbaum, 2019: 270), ‘making anti-globalism global’ is the official motto of the publisher on their Facebook page. Even more, they also proudly retweeted a cartoon from Ben Garrison with the same slogan shown together with cartoon versions of Alain de Benoist, Guillaume Faye, Daniel Friberg and Alexander Dugin.

Many scholars see this motto as a paradox, a contradictio in terminis (Valencia-Garcia, 2020: 311). What is missed is that Arktos explicitly rejects ‘globalism’, and not necessarily globalization as such. Globalism is presented as the real enemy. Globalism here refers to a specific form of globalization, one that is associated with Enlightenment, democracy and egalitarianism, with multiculturalism and feminism, and of course with institutions like the EU, the UN and NATO. Interestingly enough, it also refers to the notion of cultural Marxism (Blommaert, 2019b). In other words, globalism indexes the egalitarianism so detested and fought against by La Nouvelle Droite, the identitarians and the alt-right. The fight of Arktos aligns with them, not in rejecting globalism in the form of technology, travelling or global connections, but in rejecting the specific form of globalization that is associated with open borders, the great replacement, the attack on tradition and local cultures. Globalism is the name of the ideology – egalitarianism in traditional Nouvelle Droite discourse – that shapes contemporary globalization. Arktos is promoting different ideologies that give an alternative to this particular modernism, a different globalization and modernity. The bio on their Facebook page is clear on this:

Increasingly, people sense that something seems terribly wrong with the modern world. Arktos has been founded to offer such individuals - however 115varied their philosophic and aesthetic inclinations - the resources necessary to discover for themselves a true alternative to the onslaught of modernity.

The alternatives promoted by their authors can range from the radical traditionalism of Julius Evola to Guillaume Faye’s archeofuturism. What connects these authors is a metaphilosophy (Lievens, 2013) that rejects Enlightenment in its contemporary form: the anti-Enlightenment tradition.

Just like the reactionary modernists (Herf, 1984) combined traditional values with the embrace of technology, Arktos, and the contemporary new right in general, embrace technologies for metapolitical goals. In that sense, they are modernists: they do not want to go back to an old pre-technological traditional society; they embrace technologies if it helps to revive traditional values, cultures and languages. It is a common misconception that the far-right’s reactionary politics would entail that they want to go back to a pre-technological era: they, on the contrary, want to fuse tradition and technology. The embrace of technology is realized by undoing the ‘spirit grounding those technologies’ (Lievens, 2013), the spirit of neoliberal globalization and fusing it in an archeofuturistic way, to use Faye’s discourse. All mainstream media are regularly criticized by the new right authors for being liberal, left-wing or cultural Marxist, but at the same time, they try to use them as much as possible. Arktos is a classic example of this fusion. The publisher uses print on-demand to make its business sustainable, it advertises and is present on all major mainstream social media and streaming services like Facebook, Instagram, YouTube and Spotify (with the exception of Twitter where it got banned). It also is present on more alternative niched platforms like Odysee, GAB, VK and Telegram. While all these social media and user-generated platforms are important for the metapolitical quest and the marketing of Arktos books, the most crucial is Arktos’ integration with Amazon. Several Arktos books are distributed by different book sites like Book Depository, Barnes & Noble, Free Speech library and Logik.se, but only Amazon sells them all. Even if you buy books on the website of Arktos, you are forwarded to Amazon. Customers cannot only buy the published books by Arktos there, several Arktos titles are freely available if you have Kindle Unlimited subscription and available as audiobooks on Amazon’s Audible platform. Amazon thus functions, not only as a platform that provides revenue for Arktos, it de facto functions as a metapolitical infrastructure.

It should be clear that Arktos knows its way around the globe. It is an example of globalization. Even though Arktos publishes in 16 different languages, English is the lingua franca of the publisher. That is no coincidence as it indexes the intended audience of the publisher and thus its goal to cater to an international far-right market. The translations of the English books index the world order they try to help construct: a multipolar world, but also a world characterized by a shared anti-Enlightenment tradition. This 116specific example of globalization may use the infrastructures of neoliberal globalization, but it does so to build a different form of globalization.

Arktos is an emblematic example of how globalization reshapes the far-right. The result of that interconnected and mediated cultural production is rarely a global monoculture, but is better understood as ‘locality transported in locality’ (Blommaert, 2010: 79) through processes of englobalization of local cultures and symbolic forms and deglobalization or re-indigenizing them in other places. This vernacular globalization as Appadurai (1996) calls it, or translocalisation, connects local groups with the cultural practices of other local groups. The globalization of far-right, new right and anti-liberal margins is such a vernacular globalization that has been enabled by digital media and is operating at one particular scale level, lower than the fully global one: ‘it is the connectedness of small pockets of people located (and “local”) in many different parts of the world’ (Blommaert, 2011: 77). Important here is that these globalized margins are:

  1. Fighting metapolitically to become global on the highest scale, to globalize their ideology in such a way that it organizes/structures the world.
  2. These groups are not necessarily as marginal on a national or regional scale. It is probably not a coincidence that in 2014, Arktos set up its headquarters in Hungary. The same country where the identitarian movement set up its bank account.
  3. The power of these groups is not necessarily stable but can fluctuate as a result of sudden or long-term changes. The alt-right is a case book example. The alt-right, as a result of the electoral victory of Donald Trump, suddenly became an important centre in that global new right network. It not only became highly visible in the global hybrid media system, but it also played – for a relatively short period – a central role in the culture production within this global niche.

The global new right: transporting locality in locality

As a result of digital media, digital culture and global actors like Arktos, we should seriously question the notion of national new right or Identitarian movements. In Chapter 2, we already stressed that globalization is the context in which cultural forms are produced and circulated. Taking globalization seriously as context means that we also have to question the idea of local movements. The idea of ‘local movements’, using local practices and local discourses to fight for local causes, seems more and more a fiction. This was clearly visible on a European scale when we analysed Generation Identity as a pan-European and even trans-Atlantic phenomenon in the previous chapter. This reality seems emblematic of many contemporary new right movements. Even though all new right actors claim to resist globalization, 117universalism and cosmopolitanism, they are touched by the cultural globalization processes. Central to this transnationalization and the construction of this network is the theoretical and methodological renewal of La Nouvelle Droite that broke down the integral nationalism of the old right and of course the impact of digitalization. It is through digital media that these new metapolitical actors contribute to the metapolitical project. Digital media not only allow them to connect on a global scale but also allow some intellectuals like Alexander Dugin to operate globally. Dugin, just like Arktos, embraces this and explicitly calls for a ‘conservative internationalism’ that comes together in a fight against ‘modernity’ (Southern, 2018a): he embraces ‘multipolarity’ and therefore pleas for an ‘international of nations vs. the international of the elites’ (Dugin, 2021: 32). It is in these global networks that they share cultural products and are involved in processes of joint cultural production.

The global new right illustrates, contrary to their own narrative on globalization, the point Appadurai already stressed in the nineties: ‘globalization is not the story of cultural homogenization’ (Appadurai, 1996: 11); it transports locality into locality. The deglobalization and indignation of the Pepe meme already made this point clear. This can be further demonstrated by zooming in on the alt-right as a movement, and more generally on the cultural impact of the alt-right within the global new right. The alt-right, as a local American centre within the global new right, was responsible for producing very specific discursive materials (memes, podcasts, vlogs) and practices (trolling, algorithmic activism) to further a new right agenda. Even though the uptake of these practices was global (Maly, 2018e), the practices and discourses were, as we have seen, not instances of a global monoculture within the far-right niche. Memes and trolling practices were not just shared or copied, they were deglobalized by local actors who re-entextualize them and use them in different forms and with different meanings in a local metapolitical battle. And the alt-right itself was also not ‘a local’ network. Let’s unpack these two arguments.

The alt-right movement itself gradually came into existence as a polycentric network. This network was embedded in all kinds of far-right media (Counter-Currents, Vdare, Taki Magazine, The Daily Stormer, TakiMagazine, Occidental Observer), think tanks (American Renaissance, National Policy Institute), publishers (Arktos, Radix), congresses (New York Forum, Amren conference), and fora (see Figure 3.1), and of course mainstream digital media like YouTube and Facebook. All these online and offline infrastructures were used as ‘metapolitical instruments’ and resemble the type of organizations new right movements have set up all over Europe in the 20th and 21st centuries (Griffin, 2000; cfe. Salzborn, 2016). At the same time, we see that new actors emerge in the metapolitical battle of the alt-right: trolls, influencers and Twitter activists using mainstream digital media to further the metapolitical battle. What has been labelled as ‘the alt-right’ was in reality different cells, 118media, boards, groups and individual actors of the alt-right into a networked movement: ‘it is a many-headed hydra made up of a collection of figures and groups, none of which fully control the loose movement’s direction’ (Hermansson, Lawrence, Mulhall & Murdoch, 2019). This movement was united in some actions under hashtags such as #altright and #cuckservative in their discursive battle to get Trump elected (Hawley, 2017; Maly, 2018). Even though these cells frame themselves as promoting an extreme-right alternative to the neoliberal and neoconservative Republican party and globalization (or globalism in their lingo; Hawley, 2017; Nagle, 2017; Maly, 2018), it is important to realize that this networked movement has global dimensions.

  1. First of all, different actors and cells in that networked movement are not based in the United States (Arktos is operating from London and Hungary, Weev from The Daily Stormer lives in Europe and Red Ice is partly based in Sweden).
  2. Second, in setting up these infrastructures and defining their metapolitical goal, several alt-right key figures like Richard Spencer, Greg Johnson or Daniel Friberg explicitly claimed to find inspiration in La Nouvelle Droite.
  3. The digital infrastructure they use in their battle is clearly global in nature. This is, as we have seen after Charlottesville, not a detail. On the contrary, the success and impact of the alt-right were clearly connected to their integration into the mainstream. It is also the digital media that allowed for the global impact of the alt-right.

119From this global perspective, alt-right figures like Greg Johnson and Richard Spencer, the radical right publishing house Arktos and identitarian activists are best understood as contemporary indiginizations, or re-territorializations, of the metapolitical and ideological agenda of La Nouvelle Droite. The alt-right for instance exists, according to John Morgan (editor of the radical right publishing house Arktos), first and fore most as ‘a culture primarily of blogs, memes, podcasts, and videos’, which he claims is the ‘natural outgrowth of the anti-intellectualism inherent in Anglo-American political and cultural discourse (…)’ (Morgan, 2017). In other words, the elitist intellectual battle of La Nouvelle Droite transformed into a digital culture battle carried by memes, soundbites, tweets and hashtags. This local alt-right culture was in turn taken up by other movements in other corners of the planet where the de-contextualization process starts again.

One of the most successful metapolitical instruments of the alt-right was the appropriation of the meme and the embeddedness of the metapolitical battle in the ongoing culture war between 4channers and the normies after Gamergate (Nagle, 2017: 24). This memification of the metapolitical battle for the ideals of the conservative revolution caused a global uptake and subsequent renewal of the metapolitical battle, first in the United States, but very soon on a global scale. This very specific repertoire of collective action – deeply embedded in the contemporary algorithmically determined public space – was very quickly adopted by new right and Identitarian cells around the world.

In 2016 and 2017, Pepe the Frog memes were, as we have seen, a successful export product. In Figure 3.2, you can see how the profile pic of the Flemish meme page ‘De Fiere Vlaamse Meme’ (The proud Flemish meme) uses Pepe in a local Flemish context (see Figure 3.2). Pepe the Frog is here positioned on a shield. On top we see Pepe wearing what resembles a war helmet from the Middle Ages and what appears to be a ‘Goedendag’, a weapon originally used by the militias of Medieval Flanders. Below Pepe, we see the Flemish region with the Flemish flag. On the border of the shield we read ‘1302 E Meme Divisie – Schild en Vriend’. The date 1302 refers to the old Flemish nationalist myth about the so-called ‘Brugse metten’ in 1302. In this myth, the social conflict dimension of this historical battle is downplayed to frame it as the first legendary Flemish nationalist battle against the French. ‘Schild & Vriend’ was used as a shibboleth to be able to identify the French enemies (Tollebeek, 1999). By choosing the baseline Schild & Vriend, the page positions itself in a very long tradition of Flemish nationalist politics. The E Meme Divisie probably refers to Electronic Meme Division and is clearly inspired by alt-right meming and trolling practices. Pepe is mobilized for the Flemish nationalist cause, without of course fully erasing his ‘edgy history’ in the United States. The sign itself has different layers of meaning that need to be peeled away. Whereas Pepe indexes contemporary internet 120culture and alt-right metapolitics, the words ‘Schild en Vriend’, the Flemish flag and 1302 refer to a very different spatio-temporal frame. We thus see the synchronization of different digital practices and different chronotopes in one movement.

These semiotic resources are not only de-territorialized as Miller-Idress argues, but they are also constantly re-territorialized and re-contextualized. In many local American and non-American activist discourses, we will see materials and strategies reflected from other activists in other places. Not as generic or de-territorialized resources but as re-entextualizations and re-territorialized materials. These resources are all indexes of the systematic global nature of this type of metapolitics, and thus also of the specific world order they try to build. Note also how this layeredness of metapolitical memes has phatic effects (Varis & Blommaert & Varis, 2018). The identarian activist group Schild & Vrienden was born out of the Flemish nationalist and new right meme page (Ceder, 2017) and connections with radical right student fraternities. It is their adoption of these far-right memes, and their 121schooling by Generation Identitaire, that allowed them to construct not only a new type of activist movement on a local scale but also connect different (individual) actors, movements and cells from different corners of the world, and thus contribute to a feeling of belonging and a shared group identity that transverses national boundaries. New right memes contribute to an imagination of a networked global new right community.

This meme page, along with many other actors operating on different scales in different countries make up the global new right. The global new right is thus not only a layered, polycentric and transnational niche in which practices and discourses are produced and distributed. It is also a very productive cultural learning environment where groups or individual activists are not only rapidly exchanging cultural products and discourses enabling learning from each other, but also helping each other in metapolitical battles. The result is that even seemingly local activism is deeply influenced by this global layered and polycentric cultural niche. I will illustrate this in more detail by analysing the above-mentioned Flemish Identitarian movement Schild & Vrienden.

The global new right and Schild & Vrienden's metapolitics

On March 3, 2018, ‘Schild & Vrienden’ organized an activist intervention to derail ludic protests by civil society organizations at the Gravensteen Castle in Ghent, Belgium. This Flemish far-right Identitarian movement was born out of the meme page – De Fiere Vlaamse Meme – where youngsters from different Flemish nationalist student unions (National Student Union [NSV] and Catholic Flemish High Student Union [KVHV]) and youth divisions of political parties (the extreme-right Flemish Interest [VB] and the radical right New Flemish Alliance [N-VA]) found each other. They stormed the castle because civil society organizations were protesting the ‘inhuman European migration policies’ (GentInsight, 2018). Schild & Vrienden showed up with 20–30 activists. They pulled down the giant European flag hanging on the wall of the castle and filmed their intervention. This video material was later edited into a 3-min clip and uploaded on the Schild & Vrienden Facebook page. The video immediately went viral. Before that uptake, the offline intervention already generated visibility in mass media (EDG, 2018; VTM Nieuws, 2018) and right-wing partisan media (Decker, 2018a; ‘Schild & Vrienden Activists Took Action’, 2018), which helped their video post go viral.

Attention even multiplied after Schild & Vrienden’s Facebook video was deleted and different right-wing media framed it as an effect of politically correct censorship (Decker, 2018b). After Facebook banned the movie (in reality because of copyright infringement), Schild & Vrienden reuploaded it with a 122different soundtrack on March 8, 2018, at which point it went viral again. One year later (7 March 2019), this second uploaded video managed to attract 185,000 views, 2,900 interactions, 1,200 shares, and 1,006 comments. These numbers, seen from a Flemish or Belgian perspective, are impressive. At face value, they suggest a huge fan-base. No wonder the post triggered massive mainstream media attention in Flanders (23 articles in the Flemish press in May 2018) and put them on the radar of (far-) right-wing outlets around the world like the Gateway Pundit and Red Ice TV. All this media coverage in turn boosted the fan and follower base of Schild & Vrienden’s Facebook page from around 4,000 to over 10,000 in a couple of days (May 2018). In 2021, they acquired more than 39,000 friends on Facebook, but were also blocked on Twitter and Instagram.

In the rest of this chapter, I will analyse how Schild & Vrienden use digital media for its metapolitical battle. I will argue that the movement successfully exploits the logic of ‘new’ media and old mass media to draw the attention of a broad audience to its message. Reach on social media is used as proof that they articulate ‘the voice of a new Flemish generation conscience about their heritage’. That massive reach is used as part of the populist communicative relation (Maly, 2018e). I will first address the historical situatedness of their activism and their metapolitical strategy. After that, I will show how that metapolitical strategy is adopted in relation to the digital environments by analysing the mediatization of their intervention at the Gravensteen castle in Ghent, Belgium. Concretely, I will use the concept of algorithmic activism (Maly, 2018a, 2018e) to stress how Schild & Vrienden not only fights a discursive battle but also uses knowledge of the digital environment to make their message go viral. I will show how the online and offline activism of Schild & Vrienden uses the media logic and affordances of digital media to stretch the so-called Overton window in mainstream media. In summary, I will make the case that their activism should be understood as a metapolitics 2.0. And connected to this, we cannot understand Schild & Vrienden as a local movement.

Schild & Vrienden and the deglobalization of the global new right

The Facebook page of Schild & Vrienden was established in March 2017. The group, from the start, was hierarchically structured with Dries Van Langenhove, a student at Ghent University, as its leader. Around him circled a core group of 30–40 activists and many less active activists/supporters. Van Langenhove was, after he became famous as the leader of Schild & Vrienden, elected as an independent on the election lists of the extreme-right party Flemish Interest.

On the one hand, Schild & Vrienden was stylized as a Flemish chapter of the pan-European movement Generation Identity (Maly, 2018d). Several 123members of Schild & Vrienden, including Dries Van Langenhove, were trained at the summer university of Generation Identitaire in France in 2015. The movement still has close ties to identitarian movements in Europe and beyond (Maly, 2019a). Van Langenhove, especially after Schild & Vrienden was exposed on television as racist, anti-Semitic and extreme-right, was very open about their support for Generation Identity. The activism-format that Schild & Vrienden uses is clearly modelled on the successfully mediatized activist interventions of Identitarian movements in France, Germany, and Austria. Short, controversial, and small-scale offline interventions are mediatized on social media to generate attention, build an audience, and intervene in the public debate.

On the other hand, Schild & Vrienden drew inspiration (see Maly, 2018d) from the meme-culture of the alt-right movement. Not only did they post memes on their Facebook page, but Schild & Vrienden was also embedded in a whole network of Facebook pages (e.g., Make Vlaenderen Great Again, De Fiere Vlaamse Memes, or Departement Der Vlaemsche Memes) dedicated to spreading ‘new right’ Flemish nationalist memes in general, and supporting Schild & Vrienden and Dries Van Langenhove in particular (Maly, 2018d).

At the heart of this type of activism is the idea of metapolitics. Van Langenhove describes his movement as follows: ‘Schild & Vrienden defends the interests of the Flemish youth. We are doing this independently from political parties. We are a metapolitical movement, online as well as offline’ (Patyn, 2018). Just like in other movements, metapolitics is used by Schild & Vrienden to refer to not only a cultural battle, but also an anti-Enlightenment battle. These ideological ingredients are fully visible in Schild & Vrienden. As we shall see, key topics that are addressed on the Facebook page are the Flemish nation and ‘the replacement of white autochthone Flemings’. Anti-left, anti-migration, anti-Islam, and anti-political correctness – discourses tackling the ‘fake news of mainstream media’, digital media ‘censorship’, ‘identity politics’, and LGBTQ+ issues are abundantly found. In this sense, Schild & Vrienden resembles the Identitarian new right movements in Europe, the United States, and the rest of the world. The stickers that they sell in their web shop are a good indication of their ideological positioning. They sell stickers with alt-right slogans (‘White Lives Matter’, It’s Okay to be White), classic Flemish nationalist (Linkse ratten, rol uw matten [leftists rats, get out], Leuven Vlaams [Leuven Flemish]), translations of French identitarian slogans (Zekere Grenzen, zekere toekomst), and an adaptation of Trump’s election slogan: ‘Make Vlaenderen Great Again’. The Identitarian and alt-right slogans are accompanied by stickers framing legacy media as fake news and other anti-left and anti-Islam discourse.

What is remarkable in the light of metapolitics is that Schild & Vrienden in the first instance tried to position the movement as ‘positive’ by avoiding 124‘far-right’ connotations. In all mass media interviews, Van Langenhove stressed that Schild & Vrienden ‘wants to tell a positive story’ (Ceder, 2017 (my translation)). Central in that ‘positive story’ is the stress on the Flemish identity and its culture: ‘We want to create a resilient Flemish youth’, said Van Langenhove,

And give them a perspective on a future. In our country, there are too much sissies walking around who are afraid of their own shadow. Be proud to be a Fleming, realize that we are only one generation in a long and rich tradition.

(Ceder, 2017 [my translation])

As always, we see that this battle for the future is grounded in nostalgia and a narrative of decline: ‘In the last decennia, Flanders lost track’, stresses Van Langenhove. The reasons why can be expected: ‘Individualism and mass immigration have alienated us from each other. In a land without religion, and a remarkable loss of norms and traditions, it is easy for the youth to lose the meaning of life’ (Ceder, 2017 [my translation]). This narrative of decline and nostalgia for a past that never was positions Schild & Vrienden as the rescuer of the Flemish identity and thus its future: ‘With Schild & Vrienden, we want to provide the youth with meaning again. Which greater good is there, than to take care for your family, and your people’ (Ceder, 2017 [my translation]).

The discourse strategy of Van Langenhove resembles the political discourse of the National-Flemish Alliance (N-VA) (see Maly, 2012, 2016, for a detailed analysis of this discourse) more than the discourse of the extreme-right Flemish nationalist party Flemish Interest (see Maly, 2020d). Just like N-VA, he articulates a ‘soft’ anti-Enlightenment ethno-cultural nationalism (Sternhell, 2010; Maly, 2018b) and avoids (a too) explicit blood-and-soil discourse. The fact that the Pano reportage of the public broadcasting company was understood as ‘unmasking Schild & Vrienden’ as extreme-right, racist, and sexist is an index of the success of that message (Cools, 2018; Lesaffer, 2018; SN, 2018). At the same time, we see that as a consequence of the strategic ambivalence that is so central in the political use of ‘ironic’ memes, whiteness was put central (see for instance the sticker ‘it’s okay to be white’ in the webshop, a reference to the alt-right meme campaign).

This played moderateness shouldn’t surprise us. Metapolitics was always more than just a long-term political-ideological strategy. Metapolitics gave La Nouvelle Droite an aura of intellectualism and moderation, despite the very radical anti-Enlightenment nature of their project (Maly, 2018d). Metapolitics was used to position this ‘school of thought’ as ‘new’, and thus 125seemingly different from the ‘old right’.1 The construction of normality was inherent to the metapolitical strategy that advocated using accepted and even scientific language as vehicles for new right ideas. Hegemonic concepts like democracy, feminism, and antiracism as we have seen were infused with very specific new right meanings (see de Benoist & Champetier, 2000). Nouvelle Droite intellectuals like Alain de Benoist, but also contemporary Flemish new right politicians like Bart De Wever (president of N-VA), openly quoted leftist sources and positioned themselves as ni droite, ni gauche (Maly, 2016). This metapolitical strategy was from the start also deployed by Schild & Vrienden, who wrapped their anti-Enlightenment discourse in ‘positive’ rhetoric.

The activism of Schild & Vrienden is an excellent case study to show how the global new right functions as a transnational learning environment. Schild & Vrienden is emblematic in this respect and allows me to highlight how contemporary new right movements use the affordances of digital media for their ‘metapolitical battle 2.0’. Their activism can best be seen as a fusion of all three forms of contemporary metapolitics. Digital media are central to this type of activism: they use these digital media to have a voice (Hymes, 1996) in a hybrid media system. Growing an audience was thus important. By the end of 2017, the group amassed 3,700 likes and more than 4,000 followers. The fact that by 2019, Schild & Vrienden had 33,000 followers on Facebook, 14,000 on Instagram and 5,687 on Twitter (1 March 2019), shows that they at least succeed in reaching an audience and mobilizing it for metapolitical goals, and thus can be understood as knowledgeable concerning the logics and affordances of new and old media.

An important dimension of this type of activism is the digital literacy of these activists. To engage in metapolitics 2.0, one has to have a very broad range of digital skills and insights. As a collective, they should not only be able to film, edit and design their content, make memes or post statuses, but they also need to have insights into the nature of the digital ecology. Discursive and mobilization power in this hybrid media system is about controlling the information flows in the whole media system (Chadwick, 2017: 285). Setting up successful socio-technical activism means that one should understand the contemporary media ecologies. Within these ecologies, popularity is a coded and quantified concept, and as such, it is manipulable (van Dijck, 2013: 13). It is this digital notion of popularity that opens a whole new domain of digital activism. I (Maly, 2018a) called this algorithmic activism: ‘algorithmic activists use (theoretical or practical) knowledge about the relative weight certain signals have within the proceduralized choices the algorithms of the media platforms make as proxies of human judgement, in relation to the goals of the medium itself’ (Maly, 2018a). This type of activism presupposes that activists not only subscribe 126to the message they interact with but also understand the affordances and the algorithmic construction of the medium. That they understand how interaction – according to the popularity principle – generates visibility. As we shall see, the new right activists of Schild & Vrienden use this knowledge about platforms and algorithms in service of its metapolitical strategy. Metapolitics 2.0 inevitably has an important ‘algorithmic activist’ dimension.

The metapragmatics of the Gravensteen activism

Let’s return to the central case of this chapter and zoom in on how Schild & Vrienden prepared their content for uptake. First, I shall revisit the video and analyse it at the level of ‘metapragmatics’ (Jacobs, 1997). This metapragmatic approach focuses on the indicators of the producer’s reflexive awareness of its audience and the communicative context. In other words, we can look at the producer’s intended (algorithmic) audiences, the preferred uptake of this clip (Blommaert & Maly, 2016) and their knowledge of the communicative context. In Figure 3.3, we see the different members of Schild & Vrienden march in the streets of Ghent. Dries Van Langenhove, the leader of the movement, is walking upfront with a megaphone in his hand. The framing shows us a leader and his militant followers on their way to boycott the manifestation at the Gravensteen Castle.

The first important finding is the use of English. Not only is the title of the video (‘Protecting our heritage’) written in English, the whole video is subtitled in English (see Figure 3.3). This is especially relevant considering the importance of the Dutch language within the Flemish nationalist tradition. It informs us that the message itself was from the start produced with an international audience in mind and was thus not only targeted at the Flemish population. We will come back to this point later. The second element that deserves our attention is the accompanying Dutch Facebook status: ‘The Flemish Youth fights for its heritage and its future. P.S.: The leftist tears are more visible in HD!’ (my translation from Dutch). The deployed linguistic resources in this status refer to different spatio-temporal frames.

The first sentence clearly positions Schild & Vrienden as a Flemish movement fighting for a Flemish future and trying to protect its Flemish heritage. This aligns well with the use of Dutch and is designed for Flemish uptake. But there is more. They use a populist, or more concretely, a generational 128populist format: they speak in the name of the ‘Flemish Youth’. That is also the dominant communicative frame in the Facebook video: Schild & Vrienden is positioned by its leader Dries Van Langenhove as the representatives of the Flemish youth, and that Flemish youth seemingly hates ‘the leftists’ and fights to preserve the Flemish traditions and heritage.

This discursive frame indexes the influence of Generation Identitaire. From the start, the identitarians clearly positioned themselves as generational movements, fighting against the ‘babyboomer’ generation or the ‘soixante huitards’ who are accused of advocating multiculturalism and open borders (Generation Identity, 2013; Willinger, 2013). New right activists around the world have adopted this discursive frame. They all claim that they are just like the students in the sixties. And all of them, from the kekistani in the United States (Maly, 2018a), De Lavendelkinderen in the Netherlands, to the Identitarian activists of Generation Identity operating in the different European countries, frame themselves as the avant-garde of this youth counter-culture (cf. Dols de Jong, 2018; Rusman, 2018). And Dries Van Langenhove reproduces it too, not only in this video but also in numerous posts and interviews with mainstream media. In an interview with the Flemish mainstream newspaper De Morgen, he for instance says, ‘The left-wing elite of May 68 has had its say for way too long. (…) it is time for a new counter-culture. Schild & Vrienden wants to be the avant-garde of this’ (De Ceulaer, 2018a) (my translation).

In the video, following this classic new right frame, the Flemish youth are constructed as distinct from the ‘the leftists’, even though the images in the video show many young ‘leftists’. Van Langenhove claims in the video that at the Gravensteen Castle, the ‘leftists were all 40, 50 or 60 years old. People who still believe in a dream that we should become a multicultural society with completely open borders’ (Schild & Vrienden, 2018). Van Langenhove triggers this public by mobilizing all these classic discursive new right tropes and explicitly accusing ‘left wing’ babyboomers of ‘wanting to attract hundreds of millions of new illegal migrants that have no future here. This way, the leftists are endangering our future, and the future of the whole of Europe’ (Schild & Vrienden, 2018). Implicitly, we see how Schild & Vrienden reproduces the white genocide/great replacement trope.

This frame is a truly global dimension of contemporary local nationalist activism and taps into already discursively constructed ‘public formations’ or affective publics (Papacharissi, 2015: 4) by extreme-right and radical right nationalist parties, Identitarian activists, and mass media in the last decades: the so-called ‘angry white man’ (Kimmel, 2013). The status and the communicative frame of the video are designed as a politics of recognition. It connects to affective traces that bind a new right translocal networked public together in their fear and anger. As a consequence, this format will be recognized by and resonate with identitarians throughout Europe. Not surprising, thus, that it generates instant applause and interactional support that helps this type of activism (see table) go viral.
