129Uptake of the post in the form of comments – Facebook page Schild & Vrienden.

If we now zoom in on the second part of the status update, we see a reference to a very different spatio-temporal frame. The concept of ‘leftist tears’ in the status update is an index of the influence of the alt-right movement in the United States. In the United States, alt-right activists and 4channers predominantly use the concept ‘liberal tears’ to make fun of the ‘liberals’ and the ‘lefties’ who are portrayed as ‘snowflakes’ (Seargeant & Monaghan, 2018).

Countless memes are produced and distributed reproducing this idea (see Figure 3.4). Through digital media, memes travel across borders and become global phatic instruments generating feelings of the community (Varis & Blommaert, 2018; Papacharissi, 2015; Procházka, 2016). New right activists around the world encounter these memes and adapt them for local purposes: They get deglobalized or indigenized without fully erasing their global recognizability. Liberal tears, in a Flemish context, would not really work, as ‘liberals’ in Flanders are commonly understood as a (centre-) right party. This adaptation not only shows how digital media enable the mobility of resources, but it is also an index of the global dimension of local action. It shows how local activism is creatively produced in interaction with resources circulating through digital infrastructures. We will come back to this point in the following sections.

If we now first switch our attention to the form, we get an insight into the digital literacy and the media ideology of these activists. The fact that the video fared quite well on Facebook, and that this is not a lucky shot, shows us that the activists are knowledgeable about the digital environment of Facebook and which content the medium will push under which conditions. 130When we zoom in on their digital literacy, their theoretical or practical knowledge of the algorithmic environment, and what is needed to ensure uptake, we, first of all, see that the activists use a content type that at the time was favoured by Facebook: the uploaded video. Facebook videos were a relatively new feature on Facebook, a feature Facebook launched to compete with YouTube. As a consequence, the digital platform pushes (short) videos on its platform.

The video of Schild & Vrienden is relatively short (2 min 50 s) and uses subtitles. As many people scroll through their newsfeed on their smartphone or computer in places where the sound of the video would be inappropriate, subtitles are a crucial feature to have ‘reach’ and ‘engagement’. Failing to adhere to these format guidelines means that the video will not ‘take off’ and thus fail in its metapolitical goals. Timing is also crucial. In this case, the video was published 10 min before 10 o’clock in the morning, when most people are already behind their computers ready to interact. Immediate interaction with the post in terms of likes and comments, but especially in terms of ‘shares’ (Maly & Beekmans, 2018), is crucial for uptake on Facebook. Interestingly, members of Schild & Vrienden are among the first to like, share and comment on the post. That is no coincidence and I will return to this below.

If we analyse the interaction with the video, we see that the activists of Schild & Vrienden clearly know the game. In the first 15 min (see Image 14), 131the video generated 330 views, 157 interactions, 17 comments, and 24 shares. After half an hour, it generated 880 views, 221 interactions, 27 comments, and 41 shares. The uptake of the clip was spectacular, and as a result, the Facebook algorithms further pushed the video. The uptake shows that the producers managed to tick all the boxes: not only did the clip go viral two times, it gathered a solid number of views (92,000) and likes (2,200) (May 2018). If we zoom in on these likes, we see that around 1,500 profiles ‘like’ the video, 536 ‘love’ it, and around 100 profiles are ‘sad’, ‘angry’, or ‘surprised’. This result is remarkable, especially if you realize that the video was posted on a Facebook page with only 3,000 followers. This wasn’t a lucky shot either, as Schild & Vrienden manages to acquire impressive reach on Facebook.

Virality and populism as a communicative relation

Virality, likes, shares, comments, and overall ‘Facebook reach’ are important ingredients of the populist discourse of Schild & Vrienden. In a tweet, Dries Van Langenhove, the president of Schild & Vrienden, claimed that their Facebook community has a monthly reach of 250,000, up to 500,000 people. He ends his tweet with the suggestion of non-Schild & Vrienden fans ‘that there is a world outside their bubble’. The reach of Schild & Vrienden on social media is thus used as proof that ‘the other’ – the left – is living in a bubble. It is this quantitative dimension of ‘reach,’ followers, and views that are regularly used to support the claim that Schild & Vrienden speaks ‘in name of the Flemish youth’. In his discourse, Van Langenhove frames his movement and its social media success as a generational effect, as proof that they articulate the voice of the young generation:

Especially Generation Z, let us say, everyone who today is between 15 and 25. That generation is more conservative than Generation Y, the millennials, and even that generation was already more right-wing and more conservative than the previous one. Schild & Vrienden resembles the spirit of time.

(Segers, 2018 [my translation])

Uptake online is an inherent part of the communicative relation that is necessary to make the populist claim stick (Maly, 2018e). It is here that you see how Schild & Vrienden acquires political capital by using the popularity logic of digital media to assure mass media attention and construct their message of articulating the voice of a generation. As KhosraviNik (2018) states, the essence of social media logic is constructing creditability ‘gained by visibility/popularity in a context where popularity results commercial gains regardless of their consequences’ (p. 438). Success on social media leads to visibility in mass media. And not surprisingly, one of the main motives in questions of mass media journalists when interviewing Van Langenhove and reporting on Schild & Vrienden is their ‘social media success’ (see, e.g., Segers, 2018). 132In mainstream media, a rise in likes and followers on the social media of Schild & Vrienden is frequently understood as a rise in popularity and support for the movement (see, e.g., Raeymakers, 2018). In such cases, virality is interpreted within the generational populist frame that Schild & Vrienden produces and is read as support from the Flemish youth, and thus contributes to the construction of the meaning of their activism. The populist discourse is legitimized through a discourse that focusses on vanity metrics: likes, shares and (positive) comments are framed by Van Langenhove as proof of them articulating the needs of their generation.

The facts do not support this populist reading of uptake. If we look in more detail at the profiles sharing the Facebook video from Schild & Vrienden (see Image 18), the activity that generates the largest reach on Facebook (Maly & Beekmans, 2018) – we not only get to see how ‘niched’ and ‘targeted’ but also how global their audience is. This spread was not a coincidence either, as the clip, from the very start, was not only formatted in order to generate algorithmic uptake, but it was also designed for global uptake.

On the first day, March 8, 2018, the video was shared 127 times (by 123 different profiles) (of which only one profile shared it to criticize them). This considerable number of shares could easily be mistaken for popularity among the Flemings, the Flemish youth or even among ‘concerned citizens’ approving the message and the offline intervention by Schild & Vrienden. 133The thing is that from the 123 profiles that shared the post on that first day, only 55 indicate that they are from Belgium (four profiles do not give a country of origin). Seventeen people claim to be from the United States; 13 people indicate that they live in the United Kingdom. Profiles from 24 different countries shared this post on the first day it was online.

If we look at the last 70 shares of the video (see Image 19), we see that the Belgian profiles only account for 10% of the shares. South Africa (nine shares), the United Kingdom (seven shares), and 16 sharing profiles don’t give a ‘home-base’. Especially, these last 16 profiles are truly ‘global’ new right activist profiles: They only seem to exist in order to share (new right) content from all over the world.

The claim of Schild & Vrienden and the superficial reading of some mass media journalists, in which the shares in themselves are read through a populist framework, only contribute to the metapolitical goal of these shares. It is part of the populist communicative relation (Maly, 2018a) and legitimates the populist claim of Schild & Vrienden that they speak in the name of the Flemish youth.

The data, as illustrated, clearly point in a very different direction. These shares are best understood as metapolitical activism of an affective new right public embedded within a global new right mediascape (Appadurai, 1996). The virality of the remediatization of their offline activism is to a large extent the result of this translocal network. This affective public and its 134infrastructural dimension became very visible when I revisited all the profiles sharing the Schild & Vrienden video on May 30, 2018. At that time, Tommy Robinson, the former head of the English Defence League and Pegida UK, who is well networked with Martin Sellner of the Austrian chapter of Generation Identity, was sentenced to 13 months of imprisonment for contempt for the court. Robinson was arrested on Friday, May 22, 2018, and pleaded guilty. Within five hours he was arrested, sentenced, and jailed. New right activists around the world set up petitions and posted their outrage on social media. His arrest was framed as proof of the power of the liberal elite and the fact that the truth had to be silenced. If we look at the profiles initially sharing the Schild & Vrienden post, we see that 51 of the 123 profiles also shared at least one post on Tommy Robinson between 28 and 30 May. And again, this was an example of the global dimension of this new right activist network. Activists from 12 different countries posted memes, petitions, and outrage in favour of Tommy Robinson.

Generational populism, new right metapolitics 2.0 and algorithmic activism

The shares and the superficial reading of shares as an instance of ‘networked individualism’ (Castells, 2015) are analytically insufficient. From the moment one starts to give attention to the ‘details’ and starts investigating the profiles that share the video, we see the ‘organized’ nature of this ‘popularity’. This is not a spontaneous movement that starts from a spark of outrage. These are not just ordinary citizens showing their support for this message by sharing. It is also not an act of ‘slacktivism’ or a feel-good activity as Morozov (2011) and Gladwell (2010) would call it: virality is an essential ingredient of metapolitics 2.0 in which new right activists wrap their radical ideas in normalcy by claiming to articulate the voice of the people by organizing virality.

Considering the importance or ‘reach’ and virality of the populist claim, it is important to understand how this virality is achieved. Key ingredients of virality are simple packaging, humour, augmented participation tools, prestige, positioning, and the provocation of strong emotions (Shifman, 2014: 94–96). This understanding of virality, implicitly, assumes that virality is an organic phenomenon. That virality is the result of producing a good message, a message that is ready for uptake and resonates with the people. This understanding of virality contributes to the populist claims of new right movements. Trying to explain virality by only looking at the content of the video would be committing the fallacy of internalism (Thompson, 1995). New right activists would like you to think that this uptake happens ‘organically’ and locally. It is this assumption that legitimates their populist discourse.

As I have shown, most of the classic elements of virality are in place, but there is more. The video was not only formatted and metapragmatically prepared for algorithmic and global uptake; the uptake itself was actively 135organized. The first people who were liking, sharing, and commenting on the video were largely members and dedicated followers of Schild & Vrienden. In many cases, they would react by tagging fellow activists to notify them that the video was back online, and ask them to share or tag their ‘men’ (see Image 20). The tagging led to the activation of more structured interaction with the posts from militants and local pages of the extreme-right Flemish party Flemish Interest. Very quick, one would see a rise in people sharing the video, or reacting underneath it, all in similar ways: tagging, liking, and sharing.

136Interaction is a key parameter triggering the Facebook algorithms. The supporters of Schild & Vrienden are clearly aware of this fact. Interactions were fast, and as a result, in a matter of minutes, a much broader uptake was realized. In a matter of 20 min, the video received likes, comments, and shares from new right activists from all over the world. It is this global uptake that was very important in organizing virality. Most of the local reach of the Schild & Vrienden video was not only realized by the sharing of local individuals but also through the sharing of the post by national and international pages and communities. This is remarkable because the Facebook algorithms favour ‘personal profiles’ (Arbel, 2018). Pages only generate 4% of the Newsfeed traffic. Nevertheless, we see, in the case of the first day of sharing, that 110 individual profiles sharing the video 114 times only managed to generate a measly 158 likes and 30 additional shares in total.

Thirteen (community) pages (most of them with no apparent connection to Flanders or even Belgium), on the other hand, sharing it 13 times, generated a whopping 808 likes and 195 additional shares on that first day. The page that generated the most shares (75) and likes (108) for the Schild & Vrienden video was ‘Weekblad ‘t Pallieterke.’ ‘t Pallieterke was founded in 1945 as a right-wing, Flemish nationalist weekly close to the extreme-right Flemish nationalist party Vlaams Belang. It is through their sharing that several Vlaams Belang militants started sharing the video.

And we see the same dynamic on a translocal scale where Facebook pages and communities engage local militants in sharing content. Pages like ‘Trump 2020,’ Quotidian Conservative News and the Red Symposium were all set up in 2015, using a very similar design and duplicate content from each other. They were clearly set up to support Trump. And the same is true for pages like ‘Boer: Aktueel’ (47 likes and 28 shares), the Finnish Defence League (20 likes and 5 shares), White is beautiful (219 likes and 38 shares), or the Traditional Britain Group (208 likes and 70 shares) who trigger local activists to share the video. One of the most influential communities in generating likes (169) and shares (22) for the Schild & Vrienden video is called ‘Triggering Memes for Regressive Teens II’. This Facebook community of more than 29,000 Facebook profiles is truly global, generating shares and likes for the Schild & Vrienden video by profiles from the United Kingdom, Canada, Romania, Germany, Spain, Switzerland, Australia, and the United States.

It is not hard to see that most of the pages and profiles sharing the video were deeply committed to the battle of new right voices. Some of the Facebook pages, communities, and even profiles are truly global activist pages. The profile of ‘Alan Gerard’ is interesting in this respect. The profile shared the Schild & Vrienden video a whopping 21 times. The profile does not mention a location and does not have a profile picture, but does manage to have more than 1,300 friends. On 30 May alone, this profile shared more than 60 posts, all connected to new right political movements and politicians around 137the world, ranging from pro-Tommy posts, to posts supporting Le Pen and promoting anti-migration. The pages and communities clearly function as important hubs that structure the global flows in the new right niche and organize and mobilize local cells for global activism. Many of these pages have a clear local goal and audience but nevertheless support other radical new right nationalist movements around the world by sharing their content. What probably helped realize this global uptake by new right activists and pages was paradoxical in that the first video was deleted from Facebook. This allowed us to reupload it with the famous narrative of ‘left wing’ control over social media. That narrative was redistributed by famous radical right media like Red Ice TV (‘Schild & Vrienden Activists Took Action’, 2018).

Schild & Vrienden, new right metapolitics 2.0, and algorithmic populism

Numbers and virality are social facts. The activism of Schild & Vrienden becomes visible through the mediatization on social media and in mass media. This generational populist frame resonates with the radical right, the identitarians, and alt-right activists around the world.

Communication always addresses a specific type of people and excludes others (Scollon & Scollon, 2003; Blommaert, 2013; Blommaert & Maly, 2019). In this case, it is clear that they targeted the global new right niche: the metapragmatic cues were perfectly managed. The video reproduces a discourse that is dominant within that niche. The enemy par excellence is framed as the ‘older generation’ of ‘multicultural’, ‘open border leftists’, fake news media under the control of pocos. The video was metapragmatically prepared for algorithmic and global uptake.

As we have seen, not only the format of the post was designed for algorithmic uptake, but uptake was at least partially organized by members of the movement themselves. Digital literacy is a crucial ingredient of this type of metapolitical activism. Activists use (theoretical or practical) knowledge about the relative weight certain signals have within the proceduralized choices the algorithms of the media platforms make as proxies of human judgement, in order to reach their (meta)political goal. In this sense, ‘algorithmic activism’ contributes to spreading (and thus functions as a vehicle for normalizing) their message by interacting with the post in order to trigger the algorithms of the medium, so that they boost the popularity rankings.

This virality is discursively exploited to present radical new right discourse as the ‘voice of a new Flemish generation of youngsters’ being sick of the leftists destroying the Flemish nation, its heritage, and traditions. Their success in organizing virality also succeeds in connecting the logic of social media with the logic of mass media. Since the nineties of the last century, mainstream media have been fully incorporated in a neoliberal logic of ratings and 138commercialization. Success on social media is also understood as a potential ‘successful story’. The popularity logic of digital media clearly resonates with the mainstream media logic. As a result, online success is very fastly read as the popularity of the movement in general. It is their visibility through the use of digital media that contributes to the idea that Schild & Vrienden are representing a real ‘thing’ and should thus be reported on. This ‘activist action–mediatization–organizing virality–ensuring mass media attention’-loop establishes a populist communicative relation and contributes to an expanding social media audience. The rise to 10,000 followers in the slipstream of this activist intervention at the Gravensteen Castle, the visibility of their posts in mass media, and the reporting on this social media reality in mainstream news (cf. Cools & Andries, 2018; HR, 2018) construct an image of popularity and relevance, and even more, it gives attributes credibility to their populist discourse.

From the start, the group used mainstream digital media like Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram as metapolitical tools. The activists of Schild & Vrienden use these media to (1) choreograph assembly (Gerbaudo, 2014; Maly, 2018c), (2) (re)mediatize that activism (Maly, 2018d), (3) steer the information flow and production of Message, and (4) gain followers in order to have more leverage for future activism. In doing this, they use and traverse the logics of older and newer media to advance their political-ideological battle. This complex cycle of activities on the online–offline, old media–new media nexus is the essence of this type of socio-technical activism.

The success of the intervention of Schild & Vrienden is not only due to social media. It is, as Chadwick (2017: 184) stresses, the result of complex, hybrid assemblages of older and newer media logics. The activism of Schild & Vrienden is activism on the offline, online, and television nexus. Their offline activism at the castle was first mediated by mainstream news. This immediately caused an increase in their online followers. The publication of the video on their Facebook page started a new cycle of reporting on Schild & Vrienden. These cycles have not stopped. With modest means, and the use of the platforms of mainstream digital media like Facebook, and to a lesser extent Twitter and Instagram, we see that the activists succeed in dominating the political information cycle and infusing their radical ideas into the mainstream.

The global new right

Important to stress here again is that this local Flemish activism cannot exist outside of this global new right niche. The practices, discourses and methods are the result of the socialization of the members of Schild & Vrienden within that cultural niche. And also the uptake was a transnational uptake. This global new right audience was not reached as an accident du parcours, 139it was addressed through the explicit use of English, and their knowledge about the norms and common discourses within that niche. If we scrutinize the different sharing profiles we encounter what we, with Appadurai (1996: 36), could call an ‘ideoscape’: a global cultural flow consisting of a string of images, often directly political and trying to capture (a piece of) state power. The master concepts in this chain of concepts and ideas in the ideoscape under scrutiny here are without a doubt ‘the community’, and it connects with familiar concepts such as ‘our values’, ‘heritage’, ‘norms’, ‘our culture’, ‘borders’, ‘anti-migration’, ‘anti-left’, ‘anti-liberal’, ‘anti-cultural Marxism’ and ‘anti-globalism’. It is an anti-Enlightenment narrative (Sternhell, 2010) carried forward by activists who fight for a world order based on cultural differences, on borders and homogenic nations or entities, not for democracy and not for inalienable universal human rights.

Even though this ideoscape is characterized by a remarkable ideological coherence, it should be stressed that it still is a layered and polycentric landscape. If we for instance compare the Romanian far-right profiles sharing the Schild & Vrienden video with the Belgian profiles, we see that in the Romanian profiles, there is far more stress on religion, traditional family values and homophobic content, whereas the Belgian profiles in general stress the ‘acceptance of LGBTQ’ as part of ‘our tolerant culture’. These differences in the new right or anti-Enlightenment ideoscape can be explained by looking at how they intersect with the local, national and transnational media and ethnoscapes. Or put differently, how they interact with the infrastructures and hegemonic constellations working on different scales.

When Schild & Vrienden started this action, it was foremost operating on a local, Flemish scale. As a result of mass media attention, the uptake of their mediatization on Facebook and the remediatization by right-wing outlets like the Gateway Pundit, the star of Schild & Vrienden started to shine. Van Langenhove was a guest at Red Ice, and later he was also invited to the summer university of Generation Identitaire, not as a regular guest, but as a keynote speaker. He was also asked to speak at the American Renaissance conference of Jared Taylor. All of a sudden, Van Langenhove and Schild & Vrienden were operating at a larger scale of globalization.

To summarize, the memification of the metapolitical battle for the ideals of the conservative revolution caused a global renewal of the metapolitical battle. This very specific repertoire of collective action – deeply embedded in the contemporary algorithmically determined public space – was very fast adopted by new right and Identitarian cells around the world. It was globalized. The affordances of digital media allow fast upscaling and transnational collaboration; this not only leads to ‘global cultural homogenization’, but also to complex processes of englobalization and deglobalization (Blommaert, 2011). Digital media did not only give birth to metapolitics 2.0, digital media facilitated a global new right network of organizations 140and individual actors that have created a layered and polycentric metapolitical learning environment where individuals are not just consumers, but very quickly also producers of metapolitical discourse. The result of this process is the emergence of a global new right that crystalizes around different centres of normativity. Arktos is probably the most global and stable centre of normativity in this network. Metapolitical influencers, activist groups like Schild & Vrienden, Generation Identity, activists like Richard Spencer and sites like Counter-Currents form the material infrastructures of this global new right that becomes visible in the shared practices, discourse, places and the consumption of media. Some of these structures are stable, while others eventually disappear. It is in this unstable, constantly changing network that the global new right is enacted and becomes visible.

4 Metapolitical influencers and far-right culture

DOI: 10.4324/9781003283379-5

This chapter has been made available under a CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 license.

In the previous chapters, we have seen that identitarian movements remediatize small but spectacular offline interventions by uploading videos on social media in the hope that mainstream media would report on them (Maly, 2019a). In a similar vein, one cannot have missed the fact that the alt-right and 4chan trolls have been successfully trolling mainstream media in order to amplify their message (Phillips, 2018) throughout the whole hybrid media system. Memes have become successful metapolitical vehicles (DeCook, 2018, Weatherby, 2019; Askanius & Keller, 2021; Trillo & Shifman, 2021). The contemporary new right exists as a whole ecology of digital media platforms for metapolitical goals: new right activists not only have their own websites and blogsm but also upload podcasts and vlogs on mainstream platforms like YouTube and use social media to find an audience. In this chapter, I will show how they appropriate micro-celebrity or influencer culture for metapolitical goals. Metapolitical influencers adapt to the technical requirements of mainstream digital platforms, they integrate into their cultures, and their content is made to fit the content and form requirements of these platforms. New right cultures, discourses and styles are produced in relation to these platforms and their cultures.

Analysing the digital practices of metapolitical influencers in such niches allows us to gain insight into how exactly this new right network takes shape. How they try to normalize their ideology and how it is taken up and thus influences consumers and prosumers. In the first part of this chapter, I will delve deeper into the growth of a global new right culture around those metapolitical influencers by focusing on the details of style. Style is here understood as the way an image is communicated (See Silverstein, 2003 for an elaborate discussion). Style in this analytical sense is understood as 147having degree and depth of organization; it contributes to the construction of the image of an influencer. This image in turn is intrinsically part of the message of those influencers. Style is part of contemporary metapolitics and is co-constitutive of contemporary new right culture in general. The digital practices of those influencers co-construct a new right cultural niche in which activists and sympathizers are socialized. I will make the case that we should understand the contemporary new right as a transnational, polycentric and layered micro-population constructed around such metapolitical influencers, websites, fora and social media accounts. All those metapolitical producers function as centres of normativity. In the second part of this chapter, I will therefore zoom in on two metapolitical influencers – The Golden One and Brittany Sellner – and analyse how they use style, metapolitical intimacy and staged authenticity to create a brand. This brand, with its stress on identity, is a metapolitical act that contributes to the construction of that global new right culture.

Far-right micropopulations, style and influencers

Metapolitical influencers play an important role in the emergence of a global new right culture (Mattheis, 2018; Maly, 2020c, Leidig, 2021, Tebaldi, 2022a). In the previous chapter, I showed how the new right is best understood as an instance of (vernacular) globalization. Metapolitical influencers take up a central role in the construction of that network, and more in particular, in the construction of a new right culture, including a specific style, rhetoric and feelings of belonging. To highlight the role of those metapolitical influencers, it is first necessary to introduce and further clarify the notion of ‘orders of indexicality’. Indexicality, a key term in ethnography, refers to the meaning that emerges out of text-context relations. An index – that is a verbal or non-verbal sign – points to a feature of a certain context. A concrete example is how smoke indexes fire. A more fitting example in the context of this book is Pepe. Pepe – since the rise of the alt-right – indexes far-right actors. Utterances, symbols or signs may thus indexically invoke certain political positions, roles, identities and social norms: Pepe = far-right = Bad (or good, depending on your side of the political debate).

The concept of ‘orders of indexicality’ stresses ‘the non-arbitrary, socially and culturally sensitive way in which indexicality operates in societies’ (Blommaert, 2005: 253). In other words, the indexicals are ordered in the sense that they are connected to the groups that are using them. Pepe only became an indexical of the far-right after 4chan trolls, alt-right activists and eventually, also Hillary Clinton attributed this meaning to this symbol. Blommaert introduces the concept of orders of indexicalities to stress the fact that such ordered indexicalities ‘themselves occur in the form of stratified complexes, in which some kinds of indexicalities are ranked higher than 148others’ (Blommaert, 2005: 74). In other words, Clinton’s contextualization of Pepe functioned on a higher scale of globalization and thus was a more prestigious and influential attribution of meaning than one of far-right activists operating on a lower scale of globalization. Trump’s appropriation of Pepe in a tweet, and the embrace of Clinton’s notion of Deplorables to describe Pepe sharing people, provided Pepe with a new meaning. Considering his victory, we could argue that on a national scale, Trump succeeded in teaching his followers how to understand Pepe.

The notion of ‘orders of indexicality’ facilitates to analyse metapolitics in an empirical way. Metapolitical influencers function as centres of normativity: they are the producers of norms and meanings that enable their followers to distinguish between good and bad, cool or not, and normal or abnormal. Depending on the scale they do this, they can contribute more or less to the metapolitical battle. The orientation of individuals to orders of indexicality is what creates identities, groupness and culture. Considering the fact that the global new right exists as a polycentric, transnational and layered network, we can find different centres of normativity operating at different scale levels around which we not only see individuals doing identity work, but also the shaping of groups. Orders of indexicality, together with the notion of scales, give direction to an empirical agenda in which we can study individual metapolitical influencers as nodes in a network. It allows us to analyse how individuals do identity work (the uptake of message) in relation to one or more of those centres. This is important because it is in this identity work in relation to concrete orders of indexicality where the actual process of hegemonizing anti-Enlightenment ideologies takes place. Metapolitical influencers not only mobilize discourse but also style in their metapolitical strategies. Strategic authenticity and intimacy but also Search Engine Optimization and Social Media Optimization are used to generate uptake, bind audiences and eventually normalize their ideological positions. Some of these influencers do this on a local scale, others work on a global scale. The metapolitical strategy of La Nouvelle Droite could be considered successful when it moves from vernacular globalization to operating on a truly global scale. Only then would the ethno-plural world they dream of come alive. This global dimension also explains the globalization of the new right.

From this perspective, it becomes clear why mainstream digital media – a key infrastructure of contemporary neoliberal globalization – becomes so important in contemporary metapolitics. This global network of far-right activists, websites, fora and YouTube channels succeeds in the construction of several imagined worlds operating on different scales and in different niches. These different worlds, taken together, make up a far-right culture shaped in a global network. This network can best be described as a ‘micro-population’. Varis and I (2016) introduced the term in order to make sense of identity and social groups in a world that has become more complex due to new kinds of 149migration patterns and mobilities, the influence of new communication technologies such as the internet, as well as the neoliberal logic of consumption and commodification. Culture and social groups in the post-digital world are complex translocal, transnational, polycentric, layered and stratified phenomena not only visible in style and embedded in (both local and translocal, and online and offline) infrastructures, but also constantly (re)produced through specific discourses (Maly & Varis, 2016: 14). Micropopulations group people together in such a translocal, layered and polycentric network, recognizable by their ‘style’, identity discourses, cultural practices, and by the places (online and offline) where they hang out and the places where you can’t find them. They are the material and cultural expression of temporary and emerging micro-hegemonies (Blommaert & Varis, 2011), or on a more detailed level, of countless orientations to different constellations of orders of indexicality. Micro-hegemonies refer to the multiple sets of norms that govern the details of social life: or in other words, the niches in which individuals produce culture and thus establish normativity. All these niches together, with their values, traditions, practices and discourses, form the global new right network.

If we take the ‘Identitarians’ as an example of such a micro-population, we see a stunning but layered uniformity in discourse, cultural practices and styles. The uniformity in discourse is, as I have discussed in Chapter 3, a direct legacy of La Nouvelle Droite. The theories, concepts, ideas and the intellectuals that La Nouvelle Droite promoted give some kind of coherence to the new right movements worldwide and identitarian individuals. They all stress the importance of the organic community, one’s identity and culture, and attack the baby-boomers, the left, the cultural Marxists, the liberals and migration. As we already indicated, this discourse has been taken up by many different activists in different corners of the world. Identitarians also engage in larping, meme-ing, vlogging and trolling; it has all become part of their cultural repertoire (Fielitz & Thurston, 2019; Maly, 2019a). This global uptake comes, as we have seen in the previous chapter, with de-globalizing effects: discourses and practices are adopted to fit local conditions. The anti- Americanism, so prominent among key intellectuals like de Benoist and Faye, has been made invisible in the discourse of alt-right activists like Richard Spencer or Greg Johnson. Memes have become a global language in this far-right niche, but the memes are reformatted to fit the local context serving local metapolitical goals (Maly, 2018a, 2019b). A similar analysis can be made when we highlight the global and local dimensions of far-right fashion and style.

Alpha males and the metapolitics of style

Style is not only the way the image is communicated, it is also part of the design of the message (Silverstein, 2003: 15; Lempert & Silverstein, 2012: 55), and thus deserves thorough analysis. Style and fashion are key ingredients 150of meaning-making processes and they cannot be analysed or understood without taking the different orders of indexicality into account. The Washington Post, for instance, operating on a truly global scale, made a point of Richard Spencer’s looks: ‘He dresses in three-piece Brooks Brothers suits, gold-coin cuff links and $5,000 Swiss watches, and he sports a swept-over hipster haircut known as a “fashy” (as in fascist). Spencer, who has degrees from the University of Virginia and the University of Chicago, dismisses such labels as Nazi, racist and white supremacist, preferring to describe himself as an ‘identitarian’.

Note here that Spencer’s style is not an individual style, it is emblematic of contemporary new right fashion. In Figure 4.1, we see Richard Spencer from the National Policy Institute, Gavin McInnes from the Proud Boys, Martin Sellner from the Identitaire Bewegung, and Dries Van Langenhove from Schild & Vrienden. Even though the four men are representing different fractions of the global new right movement – Gavin McInnes being a self-declared American nationalist (and alt-light), Richard Spencer only sometimes accepts the identitarian label, Sellner has become the face of the European identitarian movement on a global scale, while Dries Van Langenhove is mostly known in Flanders. They are all four operating in different parts of the world and working on different scales. Nevertheless, the similarities in style are striking.

All of the men sport a ‘stylish’/hipster-like/fashionable style. They all sport the ‘fashy’ hairstyle. This hairstyle became fashionable again in the second decade of the 21st century and was swiftly appropriated by identitarians and far-right activists. The fashy communicates ambivalent edginess and hipness at the same time and is thus an ideal metapolitical tool. Males combine this hairstyle with traditional suits or more leisure-oriented polos, shorts or T-shirts. Especially among the activists in action, polos are very much in vogue. The appropriation of mainstream brands such a Fred Perry, Lyle & Scott, Alpha Industries and Stone Island is common. The logos of these brands, just like the fashy hairstyle, all function as indexes of their metapolitical position. Many of them are reminiscent of Nazi symbols (Miller-Idriss, 2018: 66), but are also seen as ‘cool’ and normal by youth. It is this strategic 151ambivalence (Phillips, 2015) that generates the metapolitical usefulness of these style cues. In modern clothing and fashion, in particular, details are of crucial importance. It is the ‘next-to-nothing’ that carries the distinguishing role in clothing (Barthes, 2006: 66). Clothing, argued Barthes, is fundamentally an act of meaning, an act of signification, and thus a social act at the heart of the dialectic of society (Barthes, 2006: 97). Whereas in the Ancién Regime, the clothing style indicated one’s class, in modern mass-produced clothing, this social-cultural function of clothing is now in details. The function of the detail – in this case, the logos and the overall style – is to get recognition from one’s peers. The logos index the edginess of people in the know, but this edginess can easily be denied by stressing the mainstream nature of these brands. Even more, by wearing brands that are in vogue, they create a hip brand for themselves. It is in this complex dialectic between the radical margins and the mainstream that the metapolitics of style functions. The appropriation of hip brands makes sure that they appeal to youth cultures and stay integrated and mainstream, while at the same time, they communicate an edgy image.

153The suit has a similar function. It helps to distinguish them from the classic neo-Nazis with their bomber jackets, but also from the left and their own militants. A good example can be found in the clothing styles of Schild & Vrienden. When in action, the members of Schild & Vrienden wear polos or T-shirts with the logo of the movement. This clothing functions as a uniform, unifying all members of the movement. Remarkable is that the leader of Schild & Vrienden is increasingly wearing his suit, even when the others are in their ‘activist uniform’. The suit clearly functions as a distinction criterion between the leader and the regular activists. It also functions as a diacritic between the right and the left, and thus as an identity emblem. Remarkable about the post above (Figure 4.2) is that the more common members of Schild & Vrienden are now also sporting a suit. The status of the post – the Chad nationalists vs the Virgin communists – written in English, shows how the suit functions as a diacritic to distinguish themselves from ‘the left’. The suit communicates them as successful, part of the mainstream and as ‘normal’, as ideal sons-in-law. These identity effects are enlarged by contrasting them with the ‘virgin communists’ who look shabby, unsuccessful and unorganized (see Figure 4.2). The suit is framed in the status of the post as an emblem of ‘chad-ness’. Chad is a term that is highly uncommon in Flanders and only people well-integrated in the transnational far-right culture or 4chan will make the association with the Chad meme that generally contrasts the Chad – the emblematic alpha male – with the Virgin, the Incel or the left. It is the costume that indexes the ‘chadness’ here of these activists. The fact that the post is written in English thus functions as an index of the fact the makers of this meme image that can potentially generate global uptake. The global and the local are thus connected in complex ways.

All these clothing styles are in themselves examples of processes of deglobalization. Just like Generation Identity has its own clothing brand – Phalanx Europe,
