The importance of this far-right trolling and meme culture in the contemporary far-right pro-violence culture cannot be underestimated (Maly, 2018a). Tarrant himself was clearly a product of that culture and he did all he could to please them. Not only did he post the announcement with the live stream, but he also made a soundtrack from extreme-right video memes. This soundtrack was beat to his live stream of the mosque shootings – a soundtrack that was heavily discussed on 8chan during his livestream by anons who got the references.

He thus explicitly produced raw material for the production of memes in the hope that they would catch on, go viral and spread the message. Even more, 241he gave them the assignment to do so. As a member of such a community, he not only understood their role in the continuity of the distribution of his manifesto and stream, he also knew the cultural potential of that community in normalizing far-right violence. As we have seen, those memes not only contribute to the normalization of a certain logic of action, they also contribute to a specific terrorist culture. This culturalization of Tarrant is now a fact, not only in New Zealand but also around the world.

In the spring of 2021, I was asked by Telefacts, a news show on VTM, a commercial television channel in Belgium, to analyse data they had gathered on far-right radicalization. In those data, I encountered a new young Flemish identitarian group that operated on Instagram under the name Volksverbond (People’s Union). On their public page, they would post metapolitical slideshows to ‘inform’ the people about the colonization of Belgium by migrants. In their private chats, they not only celebrated Brenton Tarrant’s terrorism or shared memes about him, but they also normalized having guns and learning to use them. In a meme posted in their chatbox, the members of the group not only presented him as Jesus and thus not only as a saint but also as a saviour; they also claimed that his music was on their playlists and that watching his video is the best indoctrination video in the world. Here you see that (1) the live streaming is aimed at ‘the highest degree of publicity possible’ (Schlegel, 2021b: 7), (2) live watching generates not only live watching but also extended watching. It becomes a resource around which a culture can grow. This culture is again not a local affair, but potentially a global one. It uses the gaming format and its associated normality to normalize terrorism. In those memes, just as we have seen in the terrorist culture around Roof, we witness the reframing of the act of Tarrant. In the gaming format, Tarrant has become the hero of the narrative: he is the winner of the game, the saint. As a direct result, you see a normalization of violence and a culture of guns. Considering the Belgian context, where guns and their use are strictly regulated and where no mainstream gun culture exists, it shows how Tarrant’s terrorist attack produced a culture that was deglobalized and resulted in further radicalization. The irony of the meme facilitated a culture where far-right violence was celebrated. Gamified language, and thus also gamified far-right terrorist culture, shouldn’t be just disregarded as unimportant, a mere by-product. Language as we know is performative (Pocock, 1973): it is through language that we acquire a perspective on reality. Gaming cultural resources are potentially powerful in shifting the perspective on violent terrorism by normalizing it. It is through the logic of the action frame of the game that Terrant and Roof became seen as Saints, heroes or chads. Even if the members celebrating those perpetrators make those comments in an ironic way, they still contribute to the distribution and normalization of his violent actions and his far-right ideology. Or in other words, it contributes to the social relatedness of the group (Schlegel, 2021b: 7).

242The fact that Tarrant’s manifesto, his stream and his playlist have generated such substantial uptake means that they contributed to white terrorist culture. This not only indexes his knowledge of those niches but also how powerful they can be. Scholars refer in this context to the recruitment effect of the gamification of terrorism. The introduction and appropriation of gaming culture in far-right terrorism generates further uptake and thus visibility of the act in the hybrid attention economy. It is through his live stream that Tarrant generates massive visibility. Tarrant and the gaming culture of white terrorism have provided a format for far-right attacks. This format not only has the potential to normalize, but it is also made for uptake within the whole hybrid media system. The power effects become clear when new far-right terrorists step into his footsteps. John Timothy Earnest, who stormed a synagogue in Poway, California, and opened fire on the Jewish congregation, said he was inspired by Tarrant, and also the man who murdered 22 people in El Paso claimed to be a supporter of the Christchurch shooter (Daerden, 2019c). In Norway, a man followed Tarrant’s example. Not only did they all write manifestos and claim to be inspired by Tarrant’s manifesto, but they also posted on bulletin boards to announce their attacks (Daerden, 2019b). The usual label of copycats or lone wolfs obscures the cultural and social aspects of these logics of action.

White terrorist culture and metapolitics 2.0

Both terrorist attacks of Roof and Tarrant can, from a cultural perspective, be understood as part of a dialogue. A dialogue with very specific niched communities within the global new right. Roof’s manifesto oriented itself to American nodes in that global network, whereas Tarrant was in a clear dialogue with his ‘lads’ on 8chan. Tarrant was also with the identitarian movement in Europe whom he had financially supported by donating over 2,500 British pounds (Daerden, 2019a). Tarrant especially was very much integrated into the global new right, and white terrorist culture in particular. He knew the theories of the global new right and had, or at least claimed to have, studied the practices and manifestos of previous far-right terrorists and used ready-made formats, including the gamification of his killing spree, which was already an existing format.

Tarrant himself stresses the social dimension of his attack when he frames himself and his actions as part of a group of ‘soldiers’. The categorization of ‘lone wolf’ presupposes an old hierarchical form of organization with clear leaders. In a post-digital era, with its gamification and ‘leaderless’ resistance (Crawford & Keen, 2020: 3), this is an anachronism. Instead, the concept of leaderless far-right resistance is adopted by the American Klansman Louis Beam (Crawford & Keen, 2020). The problem with this concept is that it obfuscates more than it illuminates. The seemingly leaderless resistance is not so 243much leaderless as it is networked. Offline (and online) mobilization is more and more the result of so-called reluctant leaders or soft leaders (Gerbaudo, 2014). These leaders lead by example, by posting things online, setting up pages or administering groups. It is through the network effect and the affordances of digital media, and its facilitation of networked individualism (Miller, 2011) and digital cultures, that the coherence of the fifth wave of terrorism, in terms of discourse and logics of action, are shaped. Roof, Tarrant and the Buffalo Shooter are not just terrorists, they also act as leaders within those niches. They hoped to make people aware and to lead by example. In his manifesto, Tarrant explicitly wanted to persuade other white men to become soldiers. And of course the same is true for their own behaviour: they themselves were influenced by others who led by example. If we take on board one of the fundamental insights of symbolic interactionism, namely that ‘(...) social interaction is a process that forms human conduct instead of being merely a means or a setting for the expression or release of human conduct’ (Blumer, 1969: 8), we understand how the ‘lone wolf categorization’ doesn’t work to describe and understand the acts of Roof and Tarrant. Their behaviour is not only individual behaviour, it is also social and cultural behaviour. The fifth wave of terrorism is rooted within the global new right. It is the result of a cultural synchronization of far-right ideologies and myths like the Great Replacement theory, digital culture in general and the cultural gamification of terrorism. The result of this polycentric culture is visible in specific logics of actions: the announcement of the act, the search for media uptake through the use of mass and hybrid media logics, the appropriation of gaming culture and infrastructures for massive effect, and the publication of a manifesto for metapolitical goals. The Buffalo Shooter is an excellent example of this type of terrorism. He was adopting the logics of action of Brenton Tarrant: he used his killing spree to generate attention for his manifesto, which was also clearly inspired by Tarrant. Just like Tarrant, he metapragmatically preformulated the news by interviewing himself. The manifesto also echoes Dylann Roof’s manifesto, as he, just like Roof, describes the different races. What is more, there is again that link to a whole series of nodes within the global new right: from /pol /to The Daily Stormer and Breitbart. His discourses are mainstream within the global new right, and his killing spree is a tool to generate attention, to let people search for the Great Replacement.

If we take Tarrant as an example, we see that he is socialized, or formed as you wish, in relation to many different centres of normativity operating on different scales. Tarrant’s manifesto, in form and content, shows a remarkable resemblance to the manifest of Breivik. And Tarrant himself explicitly praised ‘knight justiciar Anders Behring Breivik’ as a model from which he took inspiration. And this normativity of Breivik becomes clear in the main motifs that echo Breivik’s manifesto. Tarrant constructs himself, just 244like Breivik, through gamified language as a knight: a crusader. Moreover, he even claims, probably falsely, to have contacted Breivik and ‘receiving a blessing for my mission after contacting his brother knights’. Brenton Tarrant thus not only looks at Breivik, he imagines himself as a member of the reborn Knights Templar, a crusader against ‘cultural genocide’ fighting for ‘Millions of European and other ethno-nationalist peoples that wish to live in peace amongst their own people, living in their own lands, practicing their own traditions and deciding the future of their own kind’. This reference to ‘millions’ supporting his cause is also a direct intertextual link connecting Tarrant’s and Breivik’s manifestos, and a constant theme in Breivikian circles.

If we further analyse the discourse in that manifesto, we see next to the link with the identitarians Camus and Faye, which I already discussed, that his discourse also orients to contemporary alt-right discourses on white nationalism and white genocide as expressed by people like Richard Spencer, YouTube channels like Red Ice, or extreme-right sites and publishers like Counter- Currents. He, for instance, frames himself as ‘an Ethno-nationalist Eco-fascist’ fighting for ‘ethnic autonomy for all peoples with a focus on the preservation of nature, and the natural order’. Such eco-fascist rhetoric was also to be found in Richard Spencer’s infamous Charlottesville Manifesto where he defined man as having ‘the potential to become nature’s steward or its destroyer’ (Spencer, 2017a). The terrorist act is legitimated in the manifesto by taking refuge in existing new right discourse. The result of his killing spree and the launched manifesto is that it creates echo-chamber uptakes, for instance in an article on Counter-Currents that ‘explains’ his killing spree from the same assumptions and discourses that Tarrant mobilizes to explain his deed (Johnson, 2019b): ‘We obviously don’t know all the facts yet, but based on the manifesto attributed to Tarrant entitled “The Great Replacement”, Tarrant believes that whites are being replaced in our homelands by fast-breeding non-whites, including Muslims. This is absolutely correct’. Johnson of course distances himself from this killing spree and claims that it is against white interests, but at the same time, he uses this act to stress this could ‘not have happened in a homogeneously white society’. Ergo, if you want to avoid racial violence, you should not stop the racists or far-right terrorists, but the mixing of races.

8chan was clearly one centre to which Tarrant oriented. The fact that he speaks the language and understood the rules of online practices show the degree to which he was a member of this group (See also Ebner, 2020). He not only knew the group culturally, but he also knew their language and ways of doing. His post on 8chan indexed to his 8chan peers that he was one of them. He treated the anons as ‘fellow crusaders’ in a battle to save the white nations of the world. He did see a clear distinction between ‘their cultural war’ and his killing spree. He saw it as their duty to start spreading memes and engage in shitposting to spread his message further. He thus did everything he could to not only please them but also to activate them. Again, we see how through his acts and discourse a lot of other people’s voices are reproduced.

245What looks like an individualist action offline has clear social-cultural and political online dimensions (Veranoudi, Lu, Molnar, & Liza Tóth-Szöllős, 2019). He not only acted offline as an individual who made the choice by himself, but also imagined himself online as a Knights Templar warrior and a member of several polycentric and transnational white nationalist networks. And importantly, he not only imagined himself as part of a group with a goal, his followers and the followers of Roof took on board the same mission. Even though Tarrant explicitly states that he is not a member of any nationalist or political group or organization, we should be careful to label Tarrant a ‘lone wolf’. Legally speaking, he probably acted alone. The Norwegian judges passing judgement on Breivik concluded that too. But if we analyse the roots and formats and discourses of those perpetrators we see that this labelling is inadequate to understand white terrorism as a contemporary phenomenon. The concept of a ‘lone wolf’ comes with associations of individuals radicalizing themselves while being isolated in society. It immediately triggers the frame of ‘the freak’ with mental issues. This individualist ‘freak’ frame has an offline bias and uses an anachronistic model of political and activist organization, which makes us blind to the social, cultural, and political dimensions of these types of radicalization. The thing is, his offline behaviour had an enormous online shadow.

Dissociating the individual act from the broader social, cultural, political and technological context in which his voice is produced causes us to miss the broader picture of white terrorism. It is a socio-cultural and technological fact. It is constructed in collaboration with other people from different corners of the world and different timeframes in niched online spaces. In digital culture studies, scholars have now been arguing for several years that digital media are spaces where new types of social groups emerge. These groups are light communities (Blommaert, 2016), micro-populations (Maly & Varis, 2016), networked (boyd, 2001) or affective publics (Papacharissi, 2015). They do not necessarily share the same location, nor do they know each other’s name, but they do function as social groups. They produce norms and normality, and engage in structured and formatted modes of practice (Blommaert, 2017b) and logics of action. Note that these social groups are in themselves also polycentric. Roof oriented himself towards largely American-based hubs in the global network, whereas Tarrant operated on a more global scale. Many more different configurations are possible. One example is the Hanau terrorist who combined Great Replacement rhetoric with even more marginal conspiracy theories (Crawford & Keen, 2020).

White terrorist culture is thus in itself a polycentric social group that occurs as a network of different nodes that come together with an individual or a series of individuals. Important is that we cannot understand white terrorism without looking at the emergence of contemporary new right metapolitics. It is this ideological dimension, embedded in YouTube channels, fora, journals, books, think tanks, Discord servers, memes and manifestos that 246explain an essential part of the rationale of the terrorist and the cultural material informing his acts. White terrorists cannot be understood if we detach their individual acts from the social and online dimensions that shaped them and generated audiences for them.

To conclude this chapter, I want to zoom out again and try to understand the effects of far-right terrorist culture within the global new right. As I see it now, far-right terrorism and violence always have four effects. First, violence always comes with a spike in attention not only to the violence, but also to the ideological project of the perpetrators. Secondly, it usually comes with a surge in the digital media the perpetrators were using to announce their act. Thirdly, we see a break-up of the groups after the attack. Some seem to laud the violent action, others clearly want to walk a more metapolitical path. Fourthly, new media are used to further the metapolitical goals, or even more, new alt-tech media is set up, or one tries to re-integrate that media in the digital mainstream. This results in many more niched groups that again can start to grow, to create their own metapolitics and logics of action. Important to realize is that fragmentation in niche groups, from a meta-perspective, doesn’t harm the metapolitics, it only redistributes the actors who can recruit in their own niches. Even more, those niches are from an ideological perspective still connected, and nothing prevents them from coming together again when certain situations call for it.
