7 The global new right Between mainstreaming and deplatformization

DOI: 10.4324/9781003283379-8

This chapter has been made available under a CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 license.

Mobility of resources, the flows of discourse and the role of algorithmic knowledge have taken up a central place in my analysis and description of the global new right. It’s now time to add a last dimension: complexity. This book has been in the making for the last seven years, and it very soon became obvious to me, and now also to the reader of this book, that it is rather impossible to describe the global new right in a traditional sense, adopting a synchronic descriptive stance. First of all, it should be obvious that a purely local or national perspective on the new right is inherently problematic. Not only do many of these actors surpass the national scale, or theorize the future in terms of empires at higher and lower scales than the national, it is also unmistakably so that even purely local action is informed by discourses, formats and practices from different corners of the world. What presents itself as local synchronic discursive action – think of the Schild & Vrienden’s mediatized activism in Ghent – is increasingly the result of stuff from different chronotopes that are blended together. It is in these discursive practices that the global new right gets its shape. Second, it is this reality characterized by a high mobility of actors, resources and practices that generates unpredictability: what is there today, is not necessary there tomorrow. The global new right is perpetually changing and in motion: it changes form, appearance, actors, infrastructures and discourses. It is a complex system.

Perpetual change: introducing complexity

Taking up this challenge of mobility and complexity is a paradigmatic challenge. In my mind, it demands a close ethnographic analysis of what activists, influencers, intellectuals and politicians actually do. It urges us to adopt a 252diachronic perspective, and thus to look at discourse as language-in-action: detailed attention to the discourses they deploy and how they mix stuff together is a prerequisite of understanding the contemporary new right. But there is more, as we have seen throughout the cases in this book: the contemporary new right is constantly emerging and changing. The analysis of Schild & Vrienden shows a movement at the start of its rise, which is visible in the sudden upscaling of its impact, not only nationally but also internationally. Four years later, the movement is hardly visible anymore. It has been banned from Twitter, Instagram and Facebook. Its reappearance on Instagram is not really successful (2,981 followers instead of the 25K before the ban). Their leader is still active and visible, but now as a politician and YouTuber. The ethnographic approach, I will argue throughout this chapter, forces us to see the global new right as a complex system that is constantly in motion. Such systems, argues Blommaert (2013: 9), are ‘open and unfinished’. They are the result of ‘several apparently unrelated forces’ that operate ‘simultaneously but without being centrally controlled or planned’ and work in and on those systems. In such a system, change is endemic and perpetual. If we understand the global new right as such a complex system, we have to focus not so much on the essence of that system, but on this perpetual process of change and describe it as such. It also means that we shouldn’t isolate the actors from their social, political, economic and technological contexts. On the contrary, it becomes crucial to understand the global new right as a socio-technical assemblage, and thus to see the interdependence between actors and platforms, actors and government, and of course also actors and users of platforms.

Anyone working on the contemporary new right will recognize the feeling that we are always working and publishing on actors, practices and power relations of the past. Most of the actors that I have described in this book until now may not have the same weight anymore, operate on lower or higher scales then I describe them in this book, have moved to different platforms or were the object of complete deplatformization (van Dijck, Winkel & Tobias Schäfer, 2021). Movements disappear but reappear under a different banner, in a different field or even morph into new forms with different actors in the front region, operating on different scales, using different discourses. What seems like ‘non-related’ or chaos is not an absence of order but is in fact a very specific form of order ‘characterized, intriguingly, by the increased interaction, interdependence and hence coherence between different parts of a system’ (Blommaert, 2013: 9). Adopting this perspective of complexity lets us see the new right actors in relation to the infrastructures they use for their metapolitical work. The order of the global new right as a system is shaped not only by the new right actors themselves, but also by the platforms they use, the states with all their powers of the countries they work in, and of course by the general political, cultural and economic context that influences all these systems.

253This complex relation between the internal dynamics of the global new right network and external pressures from platforms, activists and governments on the network is important to sketch diachronically. Considering the metapolitical goal of this global new right network, success would, at least in emic terms, be defined as hegemonizing their world view. In so far as they succeed in this, external pressures on the global right as a system would diminish: their discourses and their practices would seem normal not only in their own niche but at large. The metapolitical dynamic, when their ideas become hegemonic, would end up in uniformity. This uniformity is generally understood as ‘mainstreaming’, or in Gramscian terms, cultural hegemony. This hegemony is clearly not just a matter of ideas, but also of the infrastructures and social groups that are supporting hegemony. The trench warfare that Gramsci saw as essential to a battle for hegemony in Western Democracies (Anderson, 1977) is today very clearly also a battle to dominate, control and use the digital infrastructure to disseminate ideas. The metapolitics of the contemporary new right is thus also a battle to use (and control) the digital infrastructures in order to build hegemony. This process of uniformity or hegemonization necessarily operates in a complex, layered, polycentric and transnationally connected world. Even the global new right itself is, as we have seen, layered and transnational, and thus organized on different scale levels and in different chronotopes.

What is considered normal in one chronotope is not necessarily normal in another. Important is that those chronotopes can influence each other: the normalization of a certain metapolitical position by Trump can have a normalizing effect on other chronotopes. The opposite is also true. When the Pano documentary framed Schild & Vrienden as racist, anti-Semitic and potentially violent, it also had potential effects on Thierry Baudet and Forum for Democracy in the Netherlands. The press was aware that Van Langenhove was present at several activities of Forum for Democracy, as Baudet himself had posted a selfie with Van Langenhove on Twitter. Their connection was a public thing, and could thus render Baudet vulnerable. Baudet or his team rapidly deleted the selfie after the Pano documentary went live and sparked controversy. We can see this move as one that tries to maintain a metapolitical edge and tries to limit the effects of external pressures in order to stay integrated into the digital mainstream and avoid damage to the metapolitical project in the Netherlands. Sometimes those pressures are not controllable at all. This was the case with Generation Identitaire in France. The movement got convicted in 2021 and officially stopped existing. This of course does not mean that the activists actually disappear, and many of them were active in Generation Reconquest, the political youth movement that supported the presidential campaign of Eric Zemmour. It does change the configuration of the movement, and consequently also has effects on the global new right network: a key infrastructure in the network at risk to disappear. As a result 254of these internal dynamics and external pressures, the global new right is constantly shifting and perpetually changing, hoovering between the mainstreaming of certain new right ideas and actors, and the total deplatformization of others.

In this last chapter, I want to describe the global new right as a complex system in search of hegemony. First, I will further zoom in on the success of La Nouvelle Droite and contemporary new right metapolitics, in the sense of the uptake of key ideas by more mainstream, or at least influential, actors. I’ll argue that a lot of La Nouvelle Droite’s ideas have found legitimacy in the mainstream. At the same time, it is important to show how external pressures – in the form of juridical actions, deplatforming and even deplatformization – affect the structure of the global new right. I will first focus on how metapolitical influencers try to manage their visibility and avoid, prepare and deal with deplatforming. After that, I will elaborate on the effects of deplatformization by analysing how The Daily Stormer is still trying to influence the debate from the margins of the digital ecosystem. Lastly, I will focus on how Generation Identitaire reappeared in many different shapes and platforms after the movement was dissolved by the court. This last chapter of the book highlights the diachronic description we have seen throughout the book by focusing on the constant change and how movements, activists and influencers we have discussed in previous chapters look in 2022. I explicitly focus on this mainstream and marginal nexus, or the visibility - invisibility nexus.

The new right and the contemporary anti-Enlightenment

La Nouvelle Droite’s metapolitics may be the most successful export product of this far-right school of thought. Not only was La Nouvelle Droite responsible for the metapolitization of fascism (Griffin, 2008: 195), but it also had an enormous effect outside of the far-right niches: ‘As for the efficacy of the ND’s Gramscian strategy’, Bar-On (2012: 25) stressed that, ‘its ideas and discourse shifts soon spread to French political figures on the centre-right and the extreme-right, including former president Giscard D’Estaing, interior minister Michel Poniatowski, in the governments of Jacques Chirac and Raymond Barre’ (Bar-On, 2012: 26). According to Bar-On, the impact of La Nouvelle Droite didn’t end there ‘Through Dugin and Panarin’, he argues, they also

influenced the Russian new right. Even more importantly they impacted the discourses and topics of almost all European extreme-right-wing political groupings. La Nouvelle Droite’s metapolitics helped the rise of extreme-right parties, usually framed as populist parties in the nineties of the last century.

(Bar-On, 2012: 26)

255The rise of extreme-right parties all over Europe in the nineties, and especially their framing of migration and integration, had a substantial mainstreaming effect on the idea that homogeneity is necessary for a nation’s survival. The so-called migrant debate discussed by left and right parties was a result of the electoral power of the extreme-right, grounded on ‘the idea that the ideal society should be as uniform and homogeneous as possible’ (Blommaert & Verschueren, 1998: 117). This cultural racism, or culturism as Schinkel calls it, is at least partially informed by the differentialism introduced by de Benoist and his comrades. This ideology was further amplified as a result of 9/11. The essay and book of Samuel Huntington on the ‘Clash of civilization’ was now seen as the work of a visionary predicting the clash of cultures (Maly et al., 2007, Maly, 2009). 9/11 was commonly seen as an index of the ‘truthfulness’ of Huntington’s thesis (Said, 2001). Islam and Muslims in particular became the dangerous other instead of the exotic other (Said, 1978). Head scarfs, mosques, the ‘integration problem’, Qur’an lessons and radical jihadist terrorism were topics that were regularly discussed in mainstream media as inherently problematic and threatening the local culture. Far-right politicians like Wilders in the Netherlands, Haider in Austria, Flemish Bloc (later Flemish Interest) in Belgium, and of course Front National in France, were driving forces of this framing of Islam and Muslims as the enemy par excellence. ‘The trope of the Trojan horse’, argue Bracke and Aguillar (2020), ‘is central to the imaginary and analytic of what we conceptualize as Europe’s “Muslim Question”. Central in all the debates, but also legislation and policies, practices and discrimination and violence, argue Bracke and Aguillar, is the notion of ‘Islam’ as (1) invading the nation as an alien body that (2) needs to be regulated through integration and assimilation. This debate on Islam may be instigated by electoral success. Especially after 9/11, it was and is still further amplified by mainstream parties from the right, but also from the left.

The success of Huntington, and the rise of the Muslim Question since the nineties, has the effect of normalizing (at least to a certain extent) certain theses of Guillaume Faye. Not unsurprisingly, Faye echoed Huntington’s theory in the nineties in Pourquoi nous combattons. ‘The Twenty-first century’, Faye argues, ‘heralds a clash of civilisations – not the advent of a unified, humane civilisation, as modernists believe’. (Faye, 2011: 108). Faye followed Huntington who argued that the differences between civilizations are not only cultural but are also here to stay. Cultural Differences, said Huntington (1993: 4), ‘are far more fundamental than differences among political ideologies and political regimes’. But Faye doesn’t just adopt Huntington’s work, he deepens it and radicalizes it. Whereas Huntington argued that ‘the West is at a peak of power’ (Huntington, 1993: 7), Faye defended the complete opposite: ‘Western civilization’, he argues, ‘is not actually a civilization at all, but rather a technical mode of life, lacking depth, based exclusively on a quasi-Pavlovian domestication of material habits; and, as such, it’s ephemeral, for 256it rests on no memory, no tradition, no cultural substance, but rather on modes as fleeting as a culuminimbus cloud, on the most superficial forms of condition’ (Faye, 2011: 108). Where Huntington sees the West as superior, Faye sees a weakened and degenerated civilization in decline. The decline is, as is typical for all anti-Enlightenment thinkers, seen as the effect of materialistic ideologies. This radicalization and criticism of Huntington may have sounded out of place in the nineties of the 20th century, but it will get picked up in the second decade of the 21st century.

A second fundamental difference between Huntington’s hypothesis and the one of Faye is that Huntington first and foremost locates that clash of civilizations on a global level, and thus focuses on the ‘the interaction between the West and non-Western civilizations and among non-Western civilizations’ (Huntington, 1993: 4). Faye sees the same enemy as Huntington – namely Islam – but he locates the danger locally, within Western civilization. Islam is seen as colonizing Europe, ergo, as the Trojan horse. Islam is framed as a monolithic block that ‘denounces Western civilization, like it formerly denounced Communism, and for good reason. But what it proposes instead is something even worse: another form of totalitarianism’ (Faye, 2011: 108). Faye sees in Islam a civilizational project that is totally incompatible with European culture, and together with American Western civilization, it is seen as the principal adversary of European culture. Faye adopts ‘an ultra-version of the “clash of civilizations,” becoming the prophet of the impending unification of the white race, first in “Eurosiberia,” then on a global scale with the advent of “Septentrion” (The North)’(Camus, Lebourg & Todd, 2017: 141).

Almost three decades after Huntington’s thesis, it is not only quite normal to frame Islam as a foreign enemy and a local Trojan horse. Even more, Faye’s framing of the West as a non-civilization, and even Europe as a civilization in decline, is more widespread than most could have imagined in the nineties. Faye was convicted for spreading racism and hate after publishing the French version of the colonization of Europe and was explicitly ousted from GRECE once more in 2000 as a result of that thesis. Today, the whole notion of ‘The Great Replacement’, and thus the colonization of Europe, is far more widespread than even Faye himself could believe. This is the work of identitarian movements and far-right intellectuals such as Faye and Renaud Camus, and far-right parties like Flemish Interest (Maly, 2021) who explicitly embrace the notion.

In Flanders, we see that Flemish Interest president Tom Van Grieken explicitly refers to Camus when discussing ‘mass-immigration’: ‘Defending the Flemish identity is at the heart of my party’, he writes (2017: 80); ‘our singularity is pressurized by mass immigration, islamization, political correctness and the Belgian non-identity’ (…), and this phenomenon also occurs in other Western-European countries. The French writer Renaud Camus talks about ‘Le grand replacement’, or replacement immigration, which replaces the native 257population and replaces it by allochthones’ (Van Grieken, 2017: 80–81). Not only does Van Grieken here explicitly cite Renaud Camus, one of the key intellectuals of the identitarian movement, but he fully subscribes to the idea of ‘replacement’ and the identitarian agenda and discourse. This identitarianism also becomes visible in his plea for a new post-EU Europe as ‘an association of free, independent and sovereign states that freely cooperate on some domains (…). He, again, wants a Europa were we all can be proud of, proud of our civilization and our patchwork or marvellous people and cultures’ (Van Grieken, 2017: 334).

That an extreme-right politician is quoting Renaud Camus’s ‘Great Replacement’ theory is relevant, but maybe not all that surprising. What is more surprising is how the press discussed this book of the then new president of Flemish Interest. Van Grieken’s book got an exceptionally favourable reception in the mainstream media (Maly, 2020a). Especially his style was celebrated by the mainstream media who even labelled him ‘the ideal son in law’ (Brinckman, 2017). The most popular newspaper of Flanders, Het Laatste Nieuws, claimed that his book was full of ‘surprising ideas’. Brinckman, from the newspaper De Standaard, claimed that whereas the programme is still radical, Van Grieken ‘in his language never takes things too far’ (Brinckman, 2017). The renowned media-intellectual Jonathan Holslag not only wrote the preface but called Van Grieken ‘a talented young force who commits to politics from an honest concern about our society’ (Holslag, 2017). In the preface and later interviews, Holslag praised Van Grieken’s stress on identity, national values and certain proposals.

Holslag is not known as a radical or extreme-right intellectual in Flanders. On the contrary, he is regularly invited on news bulletins and talk shows to give his opinion about foreign affairs, China and the position of our country in the world. He functioned as ‘a special advisor to the First Vice-President of the European Commission’, led ‘research projects for the European Parliament’ and advised ‘Fortune Global 500 companies’ on their Asia Strategy (Bio Holslag on his website). This clearly isn’t the resume of a far-right activist, but one of a renowned professor. At the same time, we see that Holslag shares several assumptions with far-right thinkers like Guillaume Faye and echoes a Spenglerian perspective on world history. When Holslag for instance enrolled himself in the Belgian army as a volunteer, he justified his decision with the following discourse: ‘I think that’s a nice European ideal: a strong spirit in a strong, combative body. We live in interesting times. (…) We must all become warriors, that is the essence’ (Holslag, 2017). This commitment to becoming a warrior is contextualized in a larger narrative of sacrifice and patriotism on the one hand and in a narrative of moral and cultural decay on the other. ‘The greatest threat to the Flemish society is its own weakness. Culture and identity are not achievements. There is effort necessary and the Flemish themselves are not really inclined to make the 258effort’ (Holslag, 2017). The people should again fight for the nation’s values and culture. And Holslag sees it as a lack of will to sacrifice themselves for the community, with Flanders and Europe in decline. According to him, we are dealing with a civilizational crisis. (Holslag, 2017): we have ended up, writes Holslag, in a ‘situation that many historians have described as decadence: a lot of people just prefer not to be confronted with arguments that point to the hollowness of their prosperity’ (Holslag, 2017). According to him, today we live in ‘post-cultural’ times. Paving the way out of that decay is therefore not a matter of redistribution, more rights, or a deepening and scaling up of democracy, but should be found in strengthening the soul. If we want to grow and be strong again, argues Holslag, then we as a nation and as a European culture must: ‘One: restore our dignity. Two: sharpen our values. Three: strengthen the economy. Four: build a positive European sphere of influence through strong diplomacy. And five: have a strong military force to defend’ (De Ceulaer, 2018b).

Once again, we see the Spenglerian ideal of a culturally, economically and militarily strong nation in a strong Europe. ‘We all have to become fighters’ says Holslag, for ‘if the soul and the militancy and the citizenship of people disappear, it’s game over. That’s an important one lesson from history’ (Holslag, 2017). The nation (and by extension Europe) can only become great if her people are noble, if we are all warriors for the whole and if our elite excels. And we can only become strong warriors if we are first proud of ourselves, our identity, our culture and our truth. Only then we can be a power factor again. Because ‘no matter how individualistic one becomes, the we-feeling remains crucial and that asks for symbols, values, language, and so on. Throughout history, identity has been a source of inspiration, strength and self-confidence’ (Holslag, 2017). Holslag clearly echoes the discourse of the conservative revolutionaries. Faye would have appreciated how his discourse is injected into the mainstream without triggering labels like far-right, conservative revolutionary thought or even new right. The resemblance with the identitarian discourse cannot be denied. It is remarkable how this discourse corresponds to the discourse of radical groups such as Schild & Vrienden, Generation Identitaire or a far-right intellectual such as Guillaume Faye. All those identitarians advocate putting our traditions at the centre and plea for renewed resilience of our youth as a response to the decline of our civilization that has occurred since May 1968. The idea that our society is under threat – and that the nation’s strength is in its culture and in the will of its members to propagate that culture and amplify it – is widespread. What is even more interesting is that Holslag and Van Grieken are not the only two voices in Flanders that echo this rhetoric of decline.

Marc Elchardus, a renowned intellectual in Flanders, known for his intellectual impact on several generations of Social Democrats, joins the choir. In his most recent book – Reset: On identity, community and democracy 259(Elchardus, 2021) – he follows Sorel in his analysis that class has lost its mobilizing force: ‘As for the pursuit of “big identity”, the class project now seems dead’ (Elchardus, 2021: 16). Elchardus’ distinction between ‘small’ and ‘big’ pursuit of identity is grounded in a Durkheimian perspective that defines the ‘big identities’ – like race, class and the nation – as the foundation of ‘thick communities’. These thick communities are the necessary foundation for solidarity according to him. As Elchardus sees class warfare as something of the past, he follows Sorel in the embrace of the nation as the foundation of a social democratic project. This embrace rapidly brings him to an attack on the radical Enlightenment, Wokeness, politically correct thinking (Elchardus, 2021: 235), and the philosophy of universal human rights (Elchardus, 2021: 238). What really bothers him, just like all anti-Enlightenment thinkers, is the universal dimension of human rights. Human rights, to him, are nothing more than ‘Liberal sameness in a straitjacket’ (Elchardus, 2021: 460). Elchardus here literally echoes Alain de Benoist: liberalism is understood as the great equalizer and destroyer of democracy.

Elchardus, in his search to renew social democracy, fully and explicitly embraces the anti-Enlightenment tradition. Burke and Herder are all of a sudden fighters against racism, colonialism and imperialism because they ‘respect the diversity of cultures and civilizations’ (Elchardus, 2021: 242). Culture – in the form of the Durkheimian thick communities – is framed as the main driver of the world. Those cultures are, just like the intellectuals of La Nouvelle Droite understood them, constructed as national, religious or at least large-scale cultures grouping many people together under one identitarian banner through shared norms, values and traditions. Nationalism replaces class warfare as a mobilizing myth in his discourse. This nationalism takes such a central role that he explicitly pleads for a ‘communitarian democracy’, which he contrasts with the Jacobin democracy that is grounded in the ideal of universal human rights. The first condition to realize such a ‘communitarian democracy’ is that ‘the attractive, workable communities of nation states protect their own project’ (Elchardus, 2021: 348), not only because this gives its citizens the possibility to live according to their own insights, but also because it can serve as an example and a source of inspiration for other communities. To protect this ‘project’, communities have two instruments: ‘selection’ and ‘socialization’. This communitarian democracy is nothing more than the ‘organic democracy’ in traditional Nouvelle Droite discourse. Elchardus sketches a world dominated by a diversity of nations and communities that should try to protect their culture, traditions and identity. This is why ‘liberal democracy’ and universal human rights are defined as problematic: they do not align with the diverse needs of those cultures and traditions: they push a monocultural liberal culture. This argument of course echoes La Nouvelle Droite’s criticism of liberalism, democracy and human rights, and it is thus not a coincidence that Elchardus quotes de Benoist.

260This anti-Enlightenment ideology that prioritizes the nation or the organic community is not only popular in Flanders. All over the world, new politicians have stood up to reproduce this vision on the nation or the ‘organic community’. In the Netherlands we have Thierry Baudet and Geert Wilders, in France we have Marine Le Pen and Eric Zemmour, in Great-Brittan we have UKIP, in Austria we have FPO, in Italy, Salvini, in Brazil, Bolsonaro and, of course, in the heart of the world system we have had Trump. Trump has been the most influential ventriloquist of the anti-Enlightenment. Even though he further polarized the country and thus didn’t succeed in realizing hegemony, he has generated a global uptake of his ideas. Slogans like ‘America First’ construct a Schmittian world of competing nations and an urge to be the best nation in that world. The ‘Make America Great Again’ slogan also adds nostalgia in the mix, a nostalgia for better times, to the America of parents and grandparents. Implicitly, it thus gives people a sense of ‘ownership’: those old generations have built America and are thus entitled. This is further reinforced by Trump’s use of a specific nationalism. Whereas Obama, but also Bernie Sanders, refers to America as a ‘nation of immigrants’, Trump refers to ‘our nation’, a nation that is rooted in values and our love for our country. This nationalism has, throughout the years, become increasingly central to his discourse. His 2022 campaign to ‘Save America’ is about ‘rebuilding our nation’. This rebuilding is done by ensuring that we always keep ‘America First, in our foreign and domestic policy. We take pride in our country, we teach the truth about our history, we celebrate our rich heritage and national traditions, and of course, we respect our great American Flag’ (Trump, 2022).

In all of these discourses, we see how the notion of decline and degeneracy of the community’s culture and tradition needs to be countered. Elchardus, Van Grieken, Trump and Holslag all see the group, its culture and its traditions as crucial for any future of their society. And it is the materialistic ideologies, the left and the liberals with their universal human rights who they see as responsible for the decline, the attack on the nation and its traditions. This attack comes in the form of the expansion of universal human rights, migration and wokeness. The new right has influential people who articulated some if not all of their ideas, and they do this on the front stage, nationally and in the case of Trump also internationally. No matter how loud and how wide these key figures articulated their voices, they didn’t do this without resistance.

Deplatforming, deplatformization and hegemony

Even though several core ideas of La Nouvelle Droite and the global new right have become hegemonic, or at the very least are being articulated by people in power or powerful people, several contemporary actors struggle 261to keep themselves integrated into the digital mainstream. The most famous case is of course the deplatforming of Trump, not just by Twitter, but by all major Western digital platforms. The deplatforming of one of the most followed and powerful men in the world invites us to analyse the role of those platforms in guarding hegemony and the impact these platforms have on the circulation of new right discourses. Platforms are not just socio-technical infrastructures that enable groups to communicate, but they are as Srnicek (2017: 48) argues,

A new type of firm (…) characterized by providing the infrastructure to intermediate between different user groups, by displaying monopoly tendencies driven by network effects, by employing cross-subsidisation to draw in different groups and by having a designed core architecture that governs the interaction possibilities.

Those firms do not just host social interaction of their users, but they also organize, circulate and moderate those interactions (Gillespie, 2018). These social media platforms, considering their Western monopolies, have tremendous power in structuring the ‘public sphere’, and thus also in making metapolitics visible or invisible. They have a commercial, socio-cultural role, but they also have a crucial political role, as they organize and structure the public sphere.

Platform, deplatforming and deplatformization

Considering the commercial nature of those platforms, the commercial and political importance of network effects, and the impact of social media governance strategies of deplatforming and deplatformization it is important to understand the tension between the commercial nature of those platforms and their political role. The deplatforming and deplatformization, especially of highly popular accounts, may be deemed necessary from a democratic logic but is in potential contradiction with the commercial goals of those firms (van Dijck, Winkel & Tobias Schäfer, 2021) as platforms need successful users, generating uptake. It is those users – micro-celebrities – that generate uptake and make sure that platforms can engage many users to stay active on the platform many times. From this perspective, non-intervention seems to be in line with the neoliberal ideology of those platforms and with their libertarian commitment to non-moderation. But as Gillespie compellingly argues, no matter how much platforms boast about their commitment to absolute freedom of speech, platforms cannot not moderate. Making money – at least within the corporate ecosystem – means getting and holding as many users online for as much time as possible, interacting as much as possible. From a negative perspective, this means that they shouldn’t only make sure that 262influencers attract people, they also need to take into account the negative effects of toxic cultures on their platforms, as radical right influencers can push more users of a platform than they attract. Platforms thus have to balance between ‘too little curation, and users may leave to avoid the toxic environment that has taken hold; too much moderation, and users may still go, rejecting the platform as either too intrusive or too antiseptic’ (Gillespie, 2018: 12). Of course, all kinds of algorithmic artifices are possible in regulating the user environment without using their ultimate weapon. It is thus not coincidental that deplatforming and deplatformization are the last steps in a long process of trying to moderate the platform. The point is that all social media platforms ‘do and must, moderate the content and activity of users using some logistics of detection, review and enforcement’ (Gillespie, 2018: 21).

Platforms have internal and economic motivations to moderate their platforms. It is a result of their moderation policies that they also shed light on the values that organize that moderation. Most GAFAM platforms were first ruled by a libertarian and neoliberal moderation logic. They were children of the digital utopianism that characterized so many Silicon Valley start-ups. This utopianism was founded in the alliance between the techno-libertarians of the computer industry, the former counter-culturalists of the San Francisco Bay area, and the social conservatives of the new right (Turner, 2008: 233). This ideological merger came with a big distrust of the state, and all external or internal interventions. Technology, and especially the internet, should be completely free. In John Barlow’s speech on ‘declaration of the independence of cyber-space’ he declared that

The global social space we are building to be naturally independent of the tyrannies you seek to impose on us. You have no moral right to rule us nor do you possess any methods of enforcement we have true reason to fear.

(Barlow, 1996)

This is emblematic of this media ideology. The legitimacy of the state to intervene online was from the start seen as illegitimate within this Californian ideology (Barbrook & Cameron, 1996).

The need for moderation was forced upon platforms as a result of external forces. Especially ‘crises’ have pushed platforms to increasingly moderate online. That started already in the nineties of the last century after several cases of defamation, hate speech, doxing and porn. Political speech was rarely focused on, and the far-right successfully managed to use this commercial ecosystem for their benefit. By the end of the first decade of the 21st century, there were many different far-right sites, BBS and social media pages that were used for ideological purposes, but the real spike happened in the first year of the second decade of the 21st century (Winter, 2019) when the far-right was fully integrated into the Web 2.0 platforms. Next to traditional, 263more conservative outlets like the American Conservative, VDARE, the Occidental Quarterly, The National Policy Institute and American Renaissance, more niched far-right platforms, emerged. Between 2008 and 2013, the alt-right would produce content that is emblematic of contemporary new right movements: essays, books, blogs and vlogs.

Starting in about 2015, however, the alt-right began embracing new tactics (…) It now also has a constellation of online message boards, such as /pol/, My posting Career, and Salo Forum, where the radical right gathers anonymously and shares ideas and content.

(Hawley, 2017: 19)

It is also in this period that the Alternative Right site was launched. Together with the old school magazines and sites, this new right culture of blogs, podcasts, memes and vlogs that Morgan was referring to grew rapidly. It is during this period that the alt-right discovered memes and trolling for metapolitical goals. Slowly but surely the alt-right got its shape as a polycentric network with centres like American Renaissance, The Daily Stormer, and The Right Stuff. But their real success was the result of using trolling and memeing on newspaper sites, Twitter, Facebook and YouTube. In other words, the digital utopianism of the Californian ideology facilitated the far-right to integrate themselves into the booming social network platforms and to reach new audiences outside of their own bubble. This new edgy, ‘funny’ digital face of the movement existed next to the more traditional new right formats like blogs, think tanks, conferences and essays. The latter allowed for the theorization of the movement while the first allowed them to recruit new members and militants. And even more importantly, it got them massive amounts of attention, not only within those digital platforms, but also globally in the whole hybrid media system. It is this attention that allowed for the upscaling of the movement and its integration and influence on the global new right.

This libertarian ideology underpinning the mainstream social media platforms has been foundational to the growth and expansion of the global new right. The rise of the global new right is hard to imagine without their integration into the digital economy. In assessing the role of this media ideology, it is important to keep the lessons of the British sociologist Raymond Williams in mind. The rise is not so much the result of the technology itself, but of how that technology is used and structured in relation to the broader socio-economic and political context. The new right was profiting by responding to the commercial logic and structure of Web 2.0. The different nodes of the alt-right, including undisguised neo-Nazi sites like The Daily Stormer and The Right Stuff, were an integral part of the digital mainstream in that period. They were hosted, had web addresses, could be found on Google, had accounts on Twitter and Facebook (except for the most radical factions), and 264received financial support from companies like PayPal. Also, alt-light sites like Breitbart were very much present in the digital mainstream. Facebook still tolerates the medium, Apple still offers the Breitbart app and Taboola provides traffic and advertising revenue.

Metapolitics and the digital guardians of hegemony

The inclusion of the alt-right in the mainstream digital economy was critical to its metapolitical strategy. On the one hand, the alt-right generated visitors through Facebook, Twitter and other social media, and in this way built up a following. On the other hand, the mainstream digital platforms provided the necessary income. It’s no coincidence that Infowars launched a campaign against internet marketing company AdRoll when it refused to host any more ads. Nicas (2018) also found that the deplatforming of Infowars had serious negative effects on his uptake. Contrary to Jones’ statements, Infowars didn’t thrive after the ban. On the contrary, it lost half of its visitors. No matter the far-right discourse about the positive impact that deplatforming has on their metapolitical enterprise, the reality suggests otherwise: most of them invest a lot in visibility on the mainstream platforms. The struggle to stay integrated into the mainstream digital economy is not just a technical matter. Integration is, as we have seen throughout this book, also very much a cultural thing tied up in the ideologies that are embedded in those technologies. Those ideologies are not only those of its owners and makers but also increasingly those of the societies they function in. Public protest and political actions put pressure on the ‘everything goes’ mentality. Facebook, Twitter and Google were initially quite vocal about their position: they denounced their role as editors and the associated responsibility. Of course, they did moderate and steer the results, pages and users, but the general discourse was one of ‘non-intervention’. Twitter did let the alt-right do their thing for a very long time. Milo Yiannopoulos has grown up on Twitter, and the alt-right saw Twitter as a crucial tool spreading and reading real news (Righton.net, 2016). But after the troll campaign against actress Leslie Jones (who starred in the 2016 Ghostbusters remake in which the heroes are all women), the pressure on Twitter to do something about harassment and bullying increased considerably. As a result, Yiannopoulos was one of the first in a line of several alt-right stars to be blocked. Milo, immediately, framed this as a political move from Twitter: ‘There’s a systemic bias against conservatives and libertarians [on Twitter]’, he said. ‘The progressive press is going to take their side, dishonestly suggesting that I was making life difficult for a black woman’. He added: ‘This is a political decision. With this they are sending a message to conservatives that they’re not welcome on Twitter’ (Ng, 2016). The negative effects of that ban were immediately downplayed by him (and by Alex Jones). ‘I’m not going to pretend I’m upset’, said Milo. ‘It has served me brilliantly. And this has done me no harm – it has turned me into a free speech martyr. (…) This is the 265most gigantic possible gift!’ (NG, 2016). Milo here was referring to the free publicity, and thus the further uptake of his message. One year later, when he was disinvited from CPAC and Simon & Schuster cancelled his book after Milo supported adults having sex with him when he was 13, he still presented himself as unaffected by everything. Three years later, when Facebook banned him, one more time, he was not that vocal anymore: ‘Before I was banned everywhere, I had four million fans across various platforms’, he wrote in a post on the Milo Yiannopoulos Discussion Facebook page. ‘FOUR MILLION. No, I am glad to get 3,000 views on a meme on Telegram. That’s what they did for me. That’s what they did for us. It was a declaration of war’. (Berr, 2019). Three years later, Milo has just over 33,000 followers on Telegram and has almost been forgotten entirely in the mainstream public space.

All this aligns with research done by Rogers (2020). When analysing the impact of deplatforming strategies of the major Western tech giants, he came to the conclusion that the audiences of the new platforms have thinned substantially. This goes to show how important the major digital structures are in waging a metapolitical battle. Digital platforms are, seen from a new right Gramscian perspective, part of the complex structure of the current hegemony that makes it resistant to direct attacks (Anderson, 1977: 7). In other words, and from a new right perspective, successful metapolitics is not possible without realizing hegemony in this digital ecosystem. That is of course why the new right used them in full. ‘The internet’, argued managing editor of Altright.com Vincent Law (aka Bogdan Olegovich Polishchuk) (2017), ‘provides an infrastructure that allows the truth of the red pill to circulate, to undermine the impact of the elites and overthrow them’. According to Law, the seeds for the new world order, a world of nations, have been planted. The internet as an infrastructure was seen by alt-right activists as crucial for the global advance of the new right, as something that would inherently awaken, red pill more and more people.

In the first week after Trump’s election, Twitter banned a series of alt-right activists. Several alt-right voices framed this as proof of the liberal omnipotence and criticized what they saw as the politically correct mock trials. The Twitter Trust & Safety Council, which was founded in February 2016, was initially the main target. This advisory body was made up of more than 40 organizations specializing in bullying, internet literacy and hate speech. The alt-right presented this body as a ‘feminist, Orwellian’ cover to take out the alt-right, especially ‘white men’ (Righton, 2016). They framed Zuckerberg and Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey as puppets of the liberal establishment. They controled the public space. This pushback against the alt-right was seen as the old order, which refused to adapt to the new developments (Law, 2017). ‘Instead of accepting the fragmentation of new media by the internet and adapting to that new landscape, the governing elite have created “fake news” to bring voters back to the traditional and verifiable sources of information’, says Law (2017). This discursive action was of course trying to prevent further deplatformings of far-right actors. Any intervention from the 266government, the law or the platforms was systematically framed as part of the liberal elite oppressing the freedom of speech, the voice of the people and even the truth. Trump’s fake news rhetoric, of course, contributed to the demonization of the mainstream press as conspiring against the right. Jones rang the same bell after being de-platformed by YouTube and Facebook. He described social media platforms as a weapon system ‘now attacking the United States with traitors inside the major security agencies blocking Trump’s resistance of the program’ (Nicas, 2018). From 2016 onwards, the far-right is increasingly framing digital media as the guardians of the liberal hegemony or the deep state. Whereas at the start of these bans, new right actors still referred to the Streisand law and boosted that this wouldn’t impact their uptake, which changed rapidly in the subsequent deplatforming and deplatformization waves in the years to follow. The boasting martyrdom discourse is thus best seen as an instrument in trying to stop being deplatformed.

The impact of such deplatforming strategies shows the importance of seeing the global new right as a complex system in motion. Digital platforms were an intrinsic part of the rise of the global new right. New right actors didn’t just ‘use’ those platforms, and the platforms had, as we have seen, a huge effect on their discourse, their visibility and the upscaling of the movement. Digital uptake was used as proof of their articulation of what their generation wanted. The moment that those infrastructures, under pressure from the outside world, made adjustments to the digital utopianist principles had huge effects on the global new right. Many different actors lost their access to the mainstream and had to readjust their metapolitical strategies. Facebook and Instagram have lost much metapolitical appeal as a result of these deplatforming strategies. It meant that not only a lot of those activists, like Martin Sellner and Milo but also The Golden One, had to reassess their strategies. Some of them took refuge in Telegram (which is one of the most successful far-right media), others like The Golden One adjusted their discourse to stay integrated into YouTube and started a new account under a different name on Instagram (thegoldenjarl) while setting up accounts on GAB, Odysee and Telegram. As a result of these external pressures, the global new right is perpetually changing. To understand how exactly the global new right changes, it is important to look at the dynamics behind the different de-platforming and deplatformization waves.

Crises and deplatforming and deplatformization waves

2016 saw the first high-profile cases of deplatforming, and Milo was emblematic of this. The first big deplatforming wave happened shortly after the deadly car attack during the Unite the Right manifestation in Charlottesville in 2017. All organizers of the Unite the Right manifestation and movements and alt-right media that were present or mobilized for the rally were dumped by one or more online services in the following weeks. Eli Mosley, CEO of 267Identity Evropa, saw his Gmail deleted. Google Play shut down the alt-right social network GAB. Richard Spencer’s blog Radix and his think tank The National Policy Institute were banned from the Squarespace platform and went offline. Mailchimp refused to send future American Renaissance newsletters. The League of the South website was denied by the hosting company. WordPress threw American Vanguard off its platform. Cloudfare refused to provide services to neo-Nazis. Even Über deleted the accounts of alt-righters and Airbnb blocked them. Facebook and Twitter banned prominent and less prominent alt-right media and personalities from their platforms. On August 16, 2017, Counter-Currents’ Facebook account and that of its editor-in-chief Greg Johnson were deleted. Facebook issued a warning to American Renaissance and blocked the page for seven days. The Facebook pages of the League of the South, Vanguard America and National Policy Institute, Radix Journal, Identity Europe and VDARE were removed. Payment services such as PayPal and platforms such as GoFundMe also intervened. PayPal shut down Counter-Currents, Richard Spencer, Jihad Watch, American Renaissance (AR Staff, 2017), League of the South, VDARE (Brimeow, 2017), and many other alt-right media. Square Cash banned AltRight.com. Social media and search engines allow the alt-rights to reach an ever-widening audience, but services like PayPal, GoFundMe, and Patreon hit these organizations at the very heart of their financial enterprise. AR and Counter-Currents indicated that the PayPal ban could potentially cause them to lose a large portion of their regular monthly donations and some of their sales (Johnson, 2017).

After Charlottesville, the sites of most of these radical factions of the alt-right could still be found via Google (only The Daily Stormer had to be looked up on the dark web). But their exclusion from social media like Facebook and Twitter inevitably affected their reach and growth opportunities, and their exclusion from digital payment platforms went to the heart of the alt-right business model. In retrospect, we can see how these collective deplatforming and deplatformization strategies gave a serious blow to the alt-right network. Charlottesville introduced the first collective wave of deplatforming radical right actors. Many platforms and actors took serious digital hits after this deadly car ride in ‘meatspace’. The Daily Stormer was hit the worst: in their case, it amounted to full deplatformization. Whereas deplatforming refers to the removal of one account from a certain platform, deplatformization applies more broadly ‘to the denial of infrastructural services deeper down the stack, for example, browsers, cloud services, pay systems, app stores, advertising services, domain name systems and so on’ (van Dijck, de Winkel & Schäfer, 2021: 5). In the case of The Daily Stormer, it meant that the site was pushed to and over the edges of the digital ecosystem into the dark web.

Here we encounter what I see as the negative dialectic of metapolitics. The more a new right actor becomes visible and has an impact outside of its own network, the higher the chances that this account will be noticed by users who report it, governments who become aware of the law-breaking activity of that 268actor and platform algorithms that detect the content. The threat of invisibility, and thus the end of the metapolitical project, is always a real possibility, and that possibility has a serious impact on the content, form and practices of metapolitical actors. Especially after 2017, more and more far-right actors are not only trying to stay integrated into the digital ecosystem of GAFEM, but they also prepare for potential invisibility. See for instance the hypermedia strategy of The Golden One and how he uses, just like Brittany Pettibone, the status of his YouTube video to direct viewers to all his other channels. First, we see his own commercial sites listed, then his social media beginning with niched and less moderated platforms like Telegram and GAB. In the end, we see the sites where users can support him through bitcoins and money transfers.

Within the mainstream, commercial digital ecosystem, visibility and invisibility are very unstable and layered phenomena. One can be deplatformed by Facebook and shadowbanned on YouTube while still being very visible on Twitter. Deplatforming and deplatformization are only the most extreme gradations of the management of the visibility of users by the platform. Platforms can shadowban, ban hashtags, downrank content, temporarily ban users, label misinformation or ban a specific post. On top of all that, we should keep in mind that the algorithmic architecture of news feeds and trending topics are not automatically imposing visibility on all subjects; on the contrary, it is always a scarce good that needs to be carefully managed (Bucher, 2018: 85). The more radical and explicit actors become, and the better they manage their visibility in this ecosystem, the more chance that something triggers external human and non-human actors to undermine their visibility.

Deplatforming of individuals or individual accounts happens increasingly and is a regular practice on most of the mainstream digital platforms. Banning users first ‘rose in popularity when social media platforms struggled to come up with solutions to fighting the Islamic State’ (Rauchfleisch & Kaiser, 2021). Today we associate this governance policy first and foremost with the banning of far-right actors. The deplatforming of many users or the full deplatformization of many far-right actors at once happens in waves, usually connected to larger socio-technical crises, scandals or eruptions of violence. As we have seen, there was a deadly attack needed in the ‘meatspace’ of Charleston before digital platforms started to act against new right metapoliticians. Facebook decided to ban Generation Identity from its platform in 2018, one month after several members of the Austrian chapter were arrested, but the real blow to the European identitarian movements came after the Christchurch attack. The Capitol Riots were the reason to finally deplatform former President Trump from Facebook and Twitter. And in his slipstream, on 12 January 2021, Facebook announced a huge crackdown on QAnon accounts, and Twitter decided to suspend those accounts. The Capital Riots were also the reason to put Parler offline and several individual far-right influencers and activists were also deplatformed. Nick Fuentes, for instance, who at the 269time was already banned from most mainstream platforms, was now also banned from DLive. In many cases, the platforms or users who are the subject of deplatforming or deplatformization already encountered several less far-reaching interventions that already negatively affected their visibility in the mainstream digital ecology. Trump’s tweets were already accompanied by a warning, Dries Van Langenhove was temporarily banned several times and Nick Fuentes was already pushed outside of the digital mainstream.

Such waves of deplatforming or deplatformization are connected to specific online and offline practices. Physical violence in ‘meatspace’ is maybe the most obvious one. The Capital Riots, the Charlottesville terrorist attack, and the attack in New Zealand all had huge online backlashes from the far-right online. Symbolic violence in the form of trolling, doxing and explicit threats with violence, incitement of hatred and racism are other triggers. The banning of actors is then usually explained as them breaking the community guidelines (or a new interpretation of those guidelines). These practices also work on the level of an individual activist, movement or influencers, but get a different meaning when this is deployed in waves. Think for instance of the banning of all the identitarian movements in Europa, including Schild & Vrienden in Flanders by Twitter. This happened on the same day in the whole of Europe (EDM, 2020), which facilitates a ‘victimization discourse’ by the identitarians. Dries Van Langenhove could then suggest a McCarthey-like censorship: ‘Today it’s Schild en Vrienden, tomorrow it’s up to the next one, until everyone with a migration-critical opinion has been silenced’ (Van Langenhove Tweet 10 July 2020), he wrote on his personal Twitter account. Community guidelines address the individual user but are deployed collectively, which feeds the myth of left-wing political correctness of the church. Alt-right frames this expulsion from the digital economy as part of the struggle, as proof of liberal and left-wing power and of the oppression of the white man.

The global new right between visibility and invisibility

Deplatforming and deplatformization, just like less invasive instruments of social media platform governance, are now ubiquitous. Far-right actors have to adjust their strategies if they want to keep using mainstream media for metapolitical goals. Alternative platforms like Bitchute, Telegram, GAB and Odysee cannot mitigate the loss of reach by being deplatformed (Fielitz, Schwarz & Hitziger, 2022; Rogers, 2020; Rauchfleisch & Kaiser, 2021), but they can be complementary to mainstream platforms. They have different functions than mainstream channels. Whereas mainstream channels are crucial for metapolitical goals, alternative channels help them in community building. They also allow users to post videos that were not allowed on the mainstream platforms and even get massive numbers of viewers there. Even though it is quite exceptional that a far-right actor has the same reach there 270as on the mainstream platforms, they can become successful main platforms after a metapolitical actor has been deplatformed from all mainstream platforms. Nick Fuentes did succeed in using DLive and having a substantial reach before he also got banned there.

Community rules, metapolitics and mitigating potential deplatforming

This central role of mainstream digital platforms for metapolitical action means that platforms are having more power over far-right actors, which in practice also results in them co-constructing metapolitical discourse. The community rules of platforms are thus not just rules, they are directing metapolitical discourse in specific directions. Certain topics and words shall be avoided in the hope of maintaining one’s reach to a broad, more mainstream audience. When the alt-right subreddit was shut down, Red Ice posted a quick blog in which it emphasized that it was always extremely careful about what it allowed on its subreddit and that it scrupulously moderated hate speech. ‘As one of the moderators at the subreddit, I would say we are pretty vigilant about trying to abide by Reddit’s terms of service by removing “hate” speech such as slurs or taking down material that is proliferating personal information of people, i.e. “doxing”’ (Red Ice TV, 2017)’. Note here that Red Ice, in their own shows and on their own website, are clearly not removing or taking town material that is considered hate. Even more, the use of brackets shows that they do not agree with Reddit’s qualification of their discourse as being ‘hate’, but they clearly saw the need to adopt their ways in order to stay integrated on mainstream platforms. ‘In fact, we were purposely hyper-vigilant by having absurd warnings like NSFW tags on posts and an age restriction warning on the subreddit just to inform readers that they were entering a “dangerous” part of the internet’ (Red Ice TV, 2017). So even though Red Ice didn’t agree on the definition of hate speech (indexed by the brackets around ‘hate’), they do follow the guidelines. The affordances of the platform and the community guidelines shape – orthopraxically – the metapolitics of Red Ice TV. Paradoxically, this could further boost the metapolitical impact of Red Ice TV because it allows users who first get acquainted with Red Ice to be smoothed in.

Considering the centrality of digital mainstream platforms in the practice of metapoliticians, it is not a surprise that far-right metapoliticians spend quite some time discussing the topic of social media governance. The Golden One for instance dedicates 6 out of 45 videos in 2021 explicitly discussing the role of social media. The first video is called ‘Why they hate me’ (The Golden One, 2021a). In this video, he discusses the removal of the Legio Gloria Instagram page: ‘Got no warning, no reason given and we absolutely did not break any community guidelines’. The reason the account was banned, according to him, is because ‘it is politically motivated. I’m a public dissident and I’m in opposition of the current regime. Therefore they harass me in this way and no it doesn’t have anything to do with mass reportings, because then 271you could appeal, but this couldn’t be appealed’. In this discourse, we see two elements: (1) the Golden One is very explicit about his knowledge of the community guidelines. The guidelines define the borders of his metapolitical activity, and he is clearly careful not to transgress those. He is clearly also knowledgeable about the procedures that are in place. In the same video, he even dares YouTube to find anything harmful or hateful he has ever said on this platform. (2) The banning is understood as political repression. Instagram is thus not just a commercial firm, it is part of the current regime.
