This discourse does not only say something about his understanding of the guidelines and how he applies them, but it is also a discourse that is directed at uptake, at mobilizing his followers against mainstream social media by framing those media as biased, unfair and thus as part of the liberal elites trying to control the right. The message of The Golden One immediately gets uptake. The video is seen more than 20,000 times, and 491 people commented on it. The most popular posts are the ones that framed The Golden One’s intervention as ‘speaking truth to power’. The fact that Legio Gloria is banned is indeed read through the discourse of The Golden One: it is an act of political repression against someone who is not scared to tell ‘the truth’.

This discourse on social media as the enemy, and thus part of the established order to use ‘hate speech’ to suppress the right and the voice of the people, can be seen all over the global new right. Brittany Sellner for instance argues that content moderation and deplatforming strategies are slippery slopes. ‘We went from Milo to Trump in the span of four years. It’s absolutely insane how fast it is happening’ (Chen, 2021). One of the important drivers of these deplatformizing waves, according to Sellner, is the ‘left’:

The left is very good at this, to their credit, they are so good at destroying, both through guilt by association, so they say you spoke to this person once, and therefore you are completely in league with everything they are believe. And they are able to convince other people of this as well, for instance Patreon.

(Chen, 2021)

This narrative is also visible with The Golden One when he argues that they frame him as some kind of terrorist, a radical (Golden One, 2021). Maybe more interesting is that this narrative is also visible in the many comments below The Golden One’s videos. If we look at the comments, we see that two out of the three most popular comments articulate the stereotype of the ‘feminist left’ that pushes for the deplatforming of the right. This surveillance and ‘guilt by association by the left’ is framed as a massive undertaking, succeeding not only in deplatforming President Trump but also in generally installing a repressive climate where far-right activists don’t dare to be seen with other far-right activists out of fear of being framed as more radical and thus get deplatformed. ‘This is how they get you! It is really risky’, says Sellner, ‘to be talking to people openly (…) it is very hard to do, but very effective as they can then atomize and isolate everyone’ (Chen, 2021). In the case of Brittany Sellner, this fear of being seen in the company of others is to be taken literally. Her husband, Martin Sellner, is not only deplatformed by Instagram (and Facebook and Twitter) but according to Brittany Pettibone, all pictures of Martin Sellner are also algorithmically banned from the platform. That is why she regularly posts pictures of herself with her husband while he is looking away from the camera or with his face hidden from view.

273The uploading of such pictures usually quite rapidly triggers a whole series of reactions on the ‘stupid fascists’ algorithmically banning Martin Sellner’s face. In the reaction, a clear us-them categorization is visible where mainstream digital media are portrayed as irrational fascists censoring the right. The Sellners, through such pictures, are framed as the victims of an oppressive totalitarian regime of the ‘lefty tech companies’. Such photos are thus metapolitically speaking very productive without breaking the community guidelines of the platform that they post them on. They implicitly and sometimes explicitly construct an all-powerful enemy that controls all major platforms. At the same time, the practice itself illustrates the constructive role of such moderation policies in the actual form of contemporary metapolitics. Brittany Sellner complies with those guidelines and thus doesn’t show her husband’s face in the hope of still being integrated herself. The fear is thus not only a fear towards the left’s ‘guilt by association’ politics, but especially of being deplatformed.

Such metapolitical discourse creates a perception of a massive repressive culture driven by the left and eventually institutionalized in mainstream media platforms. It also distracts attention from the actual hate and racism they produce and reframes it through a victim discourse. Dries Van Langenhove also regularly posts about censorship on social media and from Facebook in particular. Every social media warning, temporary ban or full ban is framed in a narrative where social media functions as all-powerful censorship machines in service of the left, the politically correct elites. In one post we see Van Langenhove complaining on Twitter that he, yesterday,

Denounced the anti-white racism that is growing day by day. The result? Facebook deletes the message and blocks my account for 30 days. They want to prevent at all costs that you will get to know the truth about the growing hatred of immigrants for Flemish people.

The narrative is again clear: social media governance has nothing to do with legitimate demands, but everything with a non-defined ‘they’ trying to control the narrative. Digital media platforms are seen as the ones destroying the right to freedom of speech.

Freedom of speech, attention and the hypermedia strategy

This narrative on ‘freedom of speech’ as a legitimation to produce racist and sexist talk being freely reproduced is not new. Already in the nineties of the last century, we witnessed the far-right politicization of freedom of speech (Zemni, 2007). Freedom of speech was the banner par excellence that legitimized radical talk in the mainstream public sphere. The idea that far-right voices were ‘cancelled’ was already a thing decades ago. And its function was 274quite similar then as it is today: it pushed journalists (and today’s platforms) to not intervene. Even more, in the nineties, this ‘freedom of speech’ discourse generated massive amounts of mass media attention. This is also the case today. Van Langenhove’s post above generated 387 likes, 247 retweets and 87 reactions. It is not only one of his more popular posts on Twitter, but it also shows the dominance of the right to the idea of freedom of speech. Freedom of speech is dissociated from democracy as a grand narrative and is now used for legitimate anti-democratic talk.

An interesting fact about this last Tweet is of course the use of Twitter to complain about Facebook’s governance. In other words, it is an index of the hypermediality of the far-right. Metapolitical activists, movements, intellectuals and influencers try to be integrated into as many mainstream media platforms as possible. They all try to be on Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, Instagram and TikTok. It is only in the second instance that they also make accounts on more niched platforms like Telegram, GAB, Odysee and Bitchut. Many of them use their presence on mainstream digital platforms to recruit their followers and invite them to follow them on their alternative platforms. When Schild & Vrienden got banned from Instagram, Van Langenhove let the image circulate of a laser-eyed Zuckerberg with the caption ‘Stop Censorship, follow us on Telegram’. These kinds of posts have become very common among far-right actors who prepare for potential deplatforming. They use their precarious integration in the digital mainstream and the network effects in order to recruit new followers on new channels.

The Golden One too uses his presence on YouTube to recruit new members and turn them into custumers, financial donators and followers on other social media platforms. Contrary to Pettibone, he clearly favours building audiences on more niched platforms like GAB and Mind. As a result of this platform precarity, new right actors are commonly early adopters of new platforms. Certainly, at first, those new platforms function as duplicates of the mainstream platforms. The same videos appear on YouTube and BitChute, but the more pressure there is to abide by the community rules, the more we see them differentiating between the platforms. The Golden One will post similar things on GAB as on Twitter, but will also show himself shooting his Victoria (an FN-Mag 58 assault rifle) and his Elisabeth (an AK5 assault gun) on GAB. GAB functions more as a close community, where influencers have the feeling to be more ‘among friends’. Their behaviour seems less constructed in relation to imagined surveillance (Duffy & Chan NK, 2019). Rauchfleisch & Kaiser (2021) found similar results, and they concluded that mainstream media are more for ‘agitational activities’ aimed at the mainstream audience, ‘while alternative platforms are necessary for forming and keeping a collective identity’ (Rauchfleisch & Kaiser, 2021: 7). This community building is certainly present on The Golden One’s GAB page. On that page, The Golden One actively engages in interaction with his fans.

275This complex relation between new right actors, mainstream digital media and alternative far-right media shows the complexity of the network. Community guidelines are not only read by new right actors but also by many who try not to cross the lines of the platform. This is a precondition for successful metapolitical action. Alternative platforms, and especially far-right platforms like GAB, are primarily used as a back-up. The less an actor is known by the public at large as a far-right activist, the less the chance that they will explicitly praise media like GAB. Digital platforms clearly do direct user behaviour through community guidelines, temporary bans and of course permanent bans. New right actors adjust their discourse, but this orientation towards the cultural power of those platforms is not to be read as an orthodox orientation: it is orthopraxy at its best. The new right influencers play lip service. Within the boundaries set by the platform, they try to mobilize and ‘educate’ the broad audience and direct them to more radical niches. Of course, this is only possible for those still integrated into the mainstream. As a result of several waves of deplatforming, more and more actors are only visible on some platforms and not on others. In the worst case, they are pushed to the margins of the internet and even into the so-called dark web.

Deplatformization: the case of The Daily Stormer

The ‘ironic’ neo-nazi website The Daily Stormer is one of the sites that was not just deplatformed, but became the object of deplatformization after the Unite the Right Rally in Charlottesville. Up until the Unite the Right rally, The Daily Stormer was an überradical ‘ironic’ neo-Nazi clickbait site and an influential node in the alt-right network (that doesn’t shy away from making an ‘ironic’ tribute to Mein Kampf and Nazism). With its ‘ironic’, controversial, or ‘edgy’ posts, it was a hub legitimating antisemitism, racism and white nationalism through layers upon layers of irony. The Daily Stormer functioned as a far-right meme factory, producer of far-right discourse and an educational hotspot for many far-right activists around the globe. According to Andrew Anglin, the founder of the site, The Daily Stormer page visits were on par with Breitbart before the site got deplatformed.

The Daily Stormer’s journey to the dark side started on 11 August 2017, the night of the Charlottesville tiki torch march. On that night, the site was first hit by a DDOS attack which was so massive that it went offline. Cloudfare, the company that The Daily Stormer hired to protect the site from such attacks, was unable to contain the storm. The well-known grey hat hacker The Jester informed The Daily Stormer’s administrator, Weev, via Twitter that ‘it would be a shame if something happened to his beautiful site’. Not much later, a new article appeared on The Daily Stormer, apparently posted by Anonymous: ‘End of Hate: Anonymous now in control of Daily Stormer #tangodown’. #tangodown is the signature The Jester leaves when he takes 276down a site. Anonymous denied having hacked the site, something The Jester happily retweeted several times. Not only was the site hacked and attacked, but also The Daily Stormer’s Discord server and The Daily Stormer’s webmaster, the far-right troll Weev, and its own Discord server went offline, as did Weev’s LinkedIn account. It was the beginning of The Daily Stormer’s digital disintegration.

On August 14, 2017, domain provider GoDaddy announced that it was giving The Daily Stormer 24 hours to find another provider. The first step Weev and Anglin tried to take was to register a domain with Google. Three hours later, Google withdrew that registration. The Daily Stormer then moved to Moscow, where the site appeared on the domain www.dailystormer.ru. At the same time, the site also moved to the dark web address http://dstormer6em3i4km.onion/. Moving to the dark web of course means being part of the internet that is not indexed and can therefore not be found on Google or Yahoo. That migration was a necessary move because the Russian domain and the subsequent lol domain were to be cancelled. The Daily Stormer was wandering from one domain to another for the next years. The Daily Stormer’s PayPal account was already blocked since 2014, and the site no longer had access to the crowdfunding site Patreon.

In 2017, the site was successfully pushed to the edges of the ecosystem. The Daily Stormer wasn’t just deplatformed, but it was also the object of deplatformization. The site was pushed to the fringes of the digital ecosystem. Without a mainstream domain name indexed in Google and other search engines, without a platform to collect crowdfunding and without a presence on any of the mainstream social media, The Daily Stormer lost access to all the infrastructural services needed to function in the regular internet. Deplatformization is not a content moderation strategy of a single platform but affects the whole ecosystem of platforms. It isn’t just about blocking specific actors on specific platforms, but it is also the denial of infrastructural services throughout the stack. It was not only deplatformed by social media but also, for example, by browsers, cloud services, pay systems, app stores, advertising services, domain name systems, and so on (Van Dijck, de Winkel and Schäfer, 2021: 5). Deplatformization can thus be seen as the guarding of the ideological boundaries, not of one platform, but of the whole mainstream digital ecosystem. Private companies individually and collectively decide who has a voice in the digital mainstream. The power of those private companies isn’t limited to the known social media platforms. To become the subject of deplatformization means not only being pushed outside of the mainstream, into the fringes, it also means that you will have to endure financial, metapolitical and even juridical blows.

The Daily Stormer is a good case to study the impact of such deplatformization strategies. Since 2017, the Stormer has been trying to come back and be present in the mainstream ecosystem. This journey can read as a perpetual 277story of integration and disintegration in the margins of the mainstream digital ecosystem. GAB consistently functioned as the gateway through which Andrew Anglin, the founder of The Daily Stormer, could reach out to more mainstream audiences. He – or other militants of The Daily Stormer – used GAB to update his followers on the digital whereabouts of The Daily Stormer and to financially support it. The Andrew Anglin profile on GAB has 21.5K followers. In comparison with other far-right activists like Martin Sellner (3.1K followers), The Golden One (8.4K followers), Nicholas J. Fuentes (137K followers) and Paul Joseph Watson aka Prisonplanet (573.6K followers), Anglin generates substantial uptake through GAB. Even compared to Watson, who has more than 20 times the number of followers, Anglin’s posts on average get several hundreds of likes whereas Watson in many cases collects fewer likes on his posts. That is remarkable because Anglin’s profile mostly uses GAB to post about the whereabouts of The Daily Stormer.

In the about section of his GAB profile, Anglin informs his followers about the loss of another mainstream domain register, and educates his followers on where and how they can find the site on TOR. Introducing this media literacy is crucial for the survival of The Daily Stormer, and it is thus a common subject of his GAB posts. The Daily Stormer is not only dependent on its reach for metapolitical goals but also on keeping the site floating financially. And for the latter, The Daily Stormer visitors need careful directions as well. The Stormer cannot use PayPal or process credit cards. It also stopped using bitcoins as this could potentially endanger the privacy of the supporters. It now uses Monero to accept financial support. To guide the visitors of the Andrew Anglin GAB page, he lists a long code. Pasting this code in your browser directs you to a bulletin board called ‘Gamer Uprising’, where The Daily Stormer explains why they opt for Monero and why fans should use it. It is through GAB and the perpetual fight to reintegrate The Daily Stormer in the mainstream that the site still exists and still has influence.

How The Daily Stormer navigates deplatformization policies and still tries to impact the mainstream becomes clear if we zoom in on some organized trolling by this neo-nazi platform. The action starts on 5 October 2017, a couple of months after the deplatformization of The Daily Stormer. The site had, only recently, found a Catalonian domain name (dailystormer.cat) which allowed them back in the indexed part of the internet. Nevertheless, most visitors to that new domain name were probably directed there through a GAB post where Anglin announced the umpteenth resurface of the site. The main article of the day was a call for action. It focused on a tweet from a non-public figure out of Highland Park, Illinois. This person and his brother owned a deli. This man sent out a distasteful tweet after the Las Vegas massacre saying ‘Soon as I heard it was country music, I felt relief. White people shooting white people isn’t terrorism, … it’s community relief #lasvegas’. This tweet, considering Stephen Paddock murdered 58 people in Las 278Vegas, made this common man Tweeter an ideal target of trolls. The Daily Stormer launched an attack from its new Catalan domain, dailystormer. cat. They doxxed this man by posting his phone number, the address of his deli and his Twitter address. Hundreds of Twitter users bombarded the man with accusations, curses, memes and threats. The result? He had to publicly apologize and quit his deli. This trolling spree drew attention to The Daily Stormer’s core message: Whites are under threat.

This trolling spree of course also highlights the impact The Daily Stormer still has from the margins. It shows that even though the site had been the object of deplatformization, it is still at the centre of a network of activists. This network of activists still has a presence in the mainstream ecosystem and with that network, the influence of The Daily Stormer far exceeds the fringes it was pushed into. Even in the platform ecosystem dominated by the Big Five, we see that The Daily Stormer still is active. That being said, its influence has diminished considerably after deplatformization. No one will accidentally stumble on its website: The Daily Stormer is now a website for the people already in the know, for their own filter bubble. If we now look at deplatformization from a complex system’s perspective, we understand that The Daily Stormer is maybe invisible if we would scrape important far-right hubs, but it is still very much active underneath the surface. Even more, it still contributes to practices above the surface. The invisibility of The Daily Stormer creates a potential bias. What seems like organic counter comments (and perceived as chaos by the victims of this trolling) is seen from that below-surface perspective as the result of structure and order. Even at the fringes of the system, sites like The Daily Stormer can still be found and have an impact. The Buffalo shooter for instance explicitly mentions the role of The Daily Stormer – now on a Chinese domain name – in his ‘awakening’. In other words, we need this hub to explain how the global new right has evolved, and how it is structured even today: it organizes interaction in the digital ecosystem, without being visible in it. In other words, it is still part of the structure of the global new right, now operating on a different, lower scale than before. The deplatformizaton has seriously affected the visibility of The Daily Stormer, its impact and the scale it operates on, but it has not fully erased its impact.

Deplatformed and prosecuted: the transformation of Generation Identitaire

Next to platforms, states and legacy media also have a substantial impact on how the global new right is shaped and changed. The power of the so-called fourth estate operates largely indirectly: mass media reporting on far-right actors can initiate government and platform interventions. The Atlantic reporting on Richard Spencer speaking in front of alt-right activists giving 279them the Roman salutes had a substantial impact on the metapolitical project of the alt-right, and the Pano reportage not only destroyed the image of Schild & Vrienden as a positive movement, but it was also the start of a court case against the movement. States exert quite some impact on the shape and form of the global new right. They do this by defining and enforcing specific legal boundaries and shaping a political context in which specific practices, actors and discourses come to exist. For instance, the widely accepted definition of freedom of speech as (rather) absolute in the United States has had a formative impact on the political context there, and on the metapolitical discourse of the alt-right. This is especially clear in the alt-right’s explicit embrace of race as a main diacritic.

Such local conditions can have global impacts. Section 230 of the US Telecommunication law for instance not only created a safe haven for the Silicon Valley platforms (Gillespie, 2014: 26–28), but also indexes the power of neoliberal digital utopianist ideology (Turner, 2008) of those platforms and the moderation policies they rolled out. It was this ideology and the government policies that enabled the alt-right to build a complex network of sites, blogs, vlogs and social media accounts that were explicit about race, circulated ironic ‘Hitler’ memes and were able to finance itself, and become an influential node in the global new right. In Germany, this would have been always much harder to accomplish. As a result of the country’s history, Germany has much stricter legislation on hate speech, racism and of course the celebration of Nazism. Sharing symbols reminiscent of the Third Reich and Holocaust denial are considered a crime there. This history embedded in the national practice of law has resulted in a specific approach to combatting online hate crimes: ‘The German Network Enforcement Act (NetzDG) has assumed an internationally pioneering role in obliging platform operators to enforce national laws and regulations within a given timeframe. This strict approach stems from the realization that social networks have played a major role in the emergence of violent right-wing actors in recent years’ (Fielitz, Schwarz & Hitziger, 2020: 28). The NetzDG bill forces social media companies to remove illegal content within 24 hours or face large fines. This of course formats what far-right actors can still post, and what not. It has for instance caused a diminished visibility of explicit neo-Nazis and of the identitarians in Germany (Fielitz, Schwarz & Hitziger, 2020: 31).

The power of the state is clearly not completely distinct from platform power, as states can demand platforms to delete users, posts or even certain networks. Even though the power of states over platforms is substantial, the scale of this impact is usually active on a lower scale than the globally operating digital platforms. States and their institutions also tend to work slower. Whereas digital platforms can decide to ban all identitarian accounts overnight and execute that decision immediately on a global scale, states 280only have jurisdiction on their own territory and this juridical route normally takes time. To understand the impact of the state on the form and reach of the global new right, we zoom in on Generation Identitaire. I zoom in on the morphing of Generation Identitaire after the movement was banned from several mainstream platforms, and actually dissolved in France after a judgement from the court.

The dissolution of Generation Identitaire

Generation Identity was one of the most successful European hubs in the global new right. The French movement eventually had global uptake. At its height, the original French invention became a truly transnational movement with chapters in the UK & Ireland, the Netherlands, Flanders, Italy, Spain, Germany, Austria, Australia and America. The movement became highly visible not only on mainstream digital media platforms but also in the whole hybrid media system, and this is present on a global scale. National and international broadcasting companies, newspapers and magazines dedicated space and time to describe this new right-wing movement and thus introduce them into their national mainstream. At the start, the movement was known for its controversial actions, and especially its style – not uncommonly where they were described as hipsters. As a result of these actions, and the uptake of their discourse by many far-right terrorists, they increasingly were framed as extreme. On a global and European scale, the Christchurch attack, and especially the news that the Tarrant had email contact with Martin Sellner of the Austrian chapter and had supported the movement financially, eventually led to the fall of the movement.

In France, Generation Identitaire was finally dissolved in March 2021 after the Minister of the Interior, Gérald Darmanin, had requested the dissolution of GI in January 2021. The direct cause of his question was the ‘Defend Europe: Alps mission’ of Generation Identity. The mission, argued Sellner in front of the live stream of Lauren Southern (2018b), who was at the scene, was set up by some French and Italian members of their national chapters. They invited all the European chapters and the mission became a transnational action. During that mission, the members of Generation Identity mimicked a border police patrol, including white jeeps with blue Defend Europe logos, helicopters with the same logo and police-like uniforms. The whole point of the action was metapolitical. It was set up to capture eyeballs in an attention economy, and especially draw attention to the issue of migrants coming into France. The hope was that they could illustrate that the national French police doesn’t mobilize against those migrants, but does arrest those who try to stop these nationalists from defending their country. In other words, it was set up to install the idea that ‘the elites’ don’t want to protect their own country and thus facilitate the replacement of the natives.

281The activists took it too far with this mission. Their biggest mistake was impersonating a police force which de facto made them a militia under French law. This was enough for the mayors of Occitania and the minister to press charges. As a result of the court decision, Generation Identitaire needed to be dissolved. Before the court ruled, 1,500 activists and sympathizers from France, the Netherlands and Belgium (including Dries Van Langenhove and several other members of Schild & Vrienden) marched the streets in Paris in support of the French identitarian movement. As habitual, the protest march was prepared meticulously for uptake. Militants carried French flags and blue and white protest signs with emblematic figures like a French soldier in a World War I outfit saying: would you dissolve them too? The metaphor is clear: just like the French soldiers in World War I, Generation Identitaire is fighting for the future of France, but now, the government tries to dissolve this army.

This march was the last visible manifestation of the movement. The website (generationidentitaire.org) was put offline. The last newsletter was sent on 18 February 2021. This dissolution of the movement is a serious blow to the mobilization and the metapolitical project of the movement. Not only did the activists lose the Generation Identity brand, its structure and its website, but they also lost the community that was carefully built around the movement and its digital presence. That being said, the dissolution of the movement is of course not the end of its discourse, its ideology, its actors and their tradition of practices.

Thaïs D'Escufon: from spokeswoman to metapolitical influencer

Thaïs d’Escufon, spokeswoman of the movement, could already make her case on the Canal 8 show Touche pas à mon poste the day after the dissolution, which was then remediatized by the Daily Motion (Daily Motion, 2021). A couple of months later, in May 2021, d’Escufon also started her own YouTube channel. She capitalizes on her fame as a spokesperson for the movement and her integration into the global new right. In less than a year, she managed to collect 51.3k followers on YouTube. This strong rise on YouTube was also a side effect of her collabs with other influencers like Brittany Pettibone (2021) who interviewed d’Escufon in a vlog called ‘Fighting for France’ and in which she urged her followers to subscribe to d’Escufon’s channel, adding that her videos are subtitled in English. This vlog was seen over 36k times.

Just like all influencers, d’Escufon deploys a hypermedia strategy, setting up accounts on Instagram (already banned), Telegram (24k subscribers) and Gettr (24,5k). This intermedial approach is set up to prepare for potential deplatforming. D’Escufon cleverly uses mainstream digital platforms to invite people to follow her on more obscure, but less moderated platforms. In her 282YouTube video “3 Arguments à NE PLUS UTILISER en débat!” (D’Escufon, 2022b), she for instance cleverly announces that she will also give a fourth argument that right-wing people shouldn’t use in debates, but that this will be posted exclusively on her Gettr account. This of course leads people to her Gettr account. The uptake of her initial YouTube video is quite substantial: 27,000 people watched it in the first 20 hours. The views of the Gettr exclusive video are not made public, but this post on her Gettr wall got 354 likes and 66 shares. She also succeeded in building a substantial following on Gettr: 24,6k followers is half of the followers on her YouTube account. Considering that Gettr is a really niched platform compared to YouTube and that she only made an account in October 2021, it is safe to say that her hypermedia strategy seemed to work. She is also not shy to address the topic of deplatforming and to explicitly ask her followers to migrate with her to Gettr (D’Escufon, 2022c).

D’Escufon’s (2021a) first YouTube video ‘Thaïs d’Escufon – JE PARS EN CROISADE SUR YOUTUBE!’ was uploaded in June 2021. The video cleverly mentions her name in the title, capturing all search traffic on her name. Considering the fact that Generation Identity was dissolved just a couple of months before, this would allow fans, militants and sympathizes to find her on this new platform. Her first video introduces her goals with the platform. The viewers see d’Escufon walking through the city, saying that she ‘doesn’t fit in this society’. The reason for her feeling like an outsider is not surprising: She doesn’t want to be on Tinder or be a climate activist. She doesn’t want to be taught about gender theory at university. She sketches a world in decline, a world where the woke left is in control and where – to succeed and not feel like an alien – one needs to conform to this left-wing ideology. In order words, just like the video’s thumbnail says, ‘the battle continues’. She is continuing her fight, but now with other means. Interesting to see is how multilingualism is mobilized in the different modes of communication afforded by YouTube. The title is French, the thumbnail pic is in English. The video is French-spoken, but subtitled in English. Thais d’Escufon now has become a metapolitical influencer, and she targets not only a French audience but all identitarians. The global new right is imagined as part of the audience that can help her find new clicks, likes and subscribers and thus generate visibility in France and abroad. She publishes on average one video every month on topics like why white privilege is normal, patriotism and Europe, and the role of women on the right.

Next to international metapolitical influencers like Brittany Sellner, Lauren Southern and Laura Loomer, we now have a French girl that echoes Guillaume Faye’s and La Nouvelle Droite’s discourse. This is illustrated very well in her video on patriotism and Europe. She starts this video by arguing that ‘we cannot defend the French identity, without defending European identity’. She is aware of the radicalness of this discourse on the right, even today, as she incorporates potential criticism in her discourse:

283You may answer that between France and Europe you have to choose. That I’m a Europeanist or even a fake patriot and yet I am firmly that we have to move beyond French patriotism to be fully effective in the relentless battle for our identity.

(D’Escufon, 2022a)

d’Escufon explicitly positions herself as an activist that fights for a European empire in which Frenchness gets its place. This European dimension in which to understand her French nationalism is reminiscent of La Nouvelle Droite’s innovation of the far-right. The identitarianism of Faye and Generation Identity is now mediated by a young French girl.

Important here to note is how she mobilizes not just this identitarian new right discourse, she also brings in style and adopts influencer tactics. She is always dressed in a feminine style with a French flavour: skirts with pastel-coloured tops, and in this case also stiletto boots. Her appearance is carefully staged. She usually has this nostalgic blue background accompanied by hip white seventies space-age furniture. On the television, we see a purple-coloured vaporwave graphic with the words ‘Defend Europe’. These words not only refer to the topic of the video but of course also to the former ‘Defend Europe’ missions of Generation Identitaire. The logo in the background pictures a hand with a flare that turns into Thai. The flares are again echoing her activism with Generation Identity. Even though we see her in this professional décor, she also uses clever influencer tactics like addressing her audience directly, sharing more personal experiences and creating a para-social bond with her followers.

Le natifs Paris

Thais d’Escufon is not the only way in which Generation Identitaires lives. Generation Identitaire also reappears in a series of new movements operating on a lower scale. One of the most prominent of those movements is Les Natifs Paris (The Parisian Natives). Les Natifs presents themselves as a group of ‘young, proud and rooted Parisians’ engaged in ‘action, community building and sports’. The logo of the movement is a hipster-like figure, including an (ironic) so-called French moustache and vintage hat, a playful take on the far-right hipster image of Generation Identitaire. The blue and white colours of the logo echo the logo of Defend Europe and the Generation Identity billboards during the march in Paris a couple of months before, and of course also those of Thais d’Escufon’s YouTube décor.

The movement officially started on 11 November 2021 with a post on Instagram and Telegram. This hypermedia strategy, from the very start, shows how this new movement is very aware of potential deplatforming, and immediately prepares for it. The post is a series of three photos of drawings of a 284French World War I soldier glued on walls and pillars in the French Capital. The intertextual connection with the panels during the last Generation Identitaire March is explicit. The French soldier is again used as an emblem of the battle for the survival of the nation. Les Natifs claim to have redecorated Paris with these posters to honour those ‘men who have sacrificed themselves so that we could stay French’. This first post immediately has uptake: more than 600 people like it, among which are Dries Van Langenhove, the president of Schild & Vrienden, and activist accounts like deus_vult and Patria, and movement accounts like Nemesis Besançon (the identitarian feminist movement) and La Relève (Free and conservative youth movement). In the first 15 days, the page managed to have 1,000 followers, and they doubled that in May 2022. This is not a page that starts from scratch; Le Natifs are clearly heavily networked and that network is not limited to the Parisian borders.

In the press release of 12th of November 2021, the new movement claimed to be forced into the resistance as a result of the growing insecurity, cosmopolitanism and third-world-ism, and the fact that ‘the natives’ are forgotten by media and politicians. The former members of Generation Identitaire now appropriate a discourse of ‘the natives’ against their colonizers. This type of discourse of course echoes the work of Guillaume Faye on the colonization of Europe. It is thus also not a coincidence that Guillaume Faye’s ‘Why we fight’ is the first book they recommend their followers to read. In that same Instagram post, they also recommend Dominque Venner. In another Instagram Post dedicated to their ‘Cercle de lecture #1’, we see again books of Venner, but also the Clash of Civilizations by Samuel Huntington and a book from Eric Zemmour, the far-right presidential candidate in 2022. The ideology and the discourse of Les Natifs echo Generation Identity and the ideological work of Faye and La Nouvelle Droite. Generation Identitaire may be dissolved, but we see a whole series of new pages, movements and influencers popping up.

The practices of this ‘new movement’ are also clearly informed by the ‘repertoires of collective action’ (Tilly, 1974: 143–171) developed in Generation Identitaire. The spectacular but albeit small, local, offline but afterwards heavily mediated activism on social media has been introduced on the right by Generation Identitaire. The French identitarians followed de Benoist’s call to learn from the methodologies of the left, to renew the right and enlarge its metapolitical impact. This repertoire of collective action was first appropriated by the original French movement Generation Identitaire from organizations like Green Peace to serve their nationalist cause. Les Natifs reuse this model when they mobilize around Notre Dame, the famous medieval cathedral in Paris that burned in 2019. They published the first Instagram post dedicated to the perseverance of La Notre Dame on 29 March, and four more posts followed. The posts frame La Notre Dame as part of the French patrimony that has to be rebuilt in its original form. In this discourse, Notre Dame is mythicized as an exceptional and fascinating Parisian heritage ‘that 285brought Paris closer to heaven’ (Les Natifs, Instagram post, 29 March 2022). The metapolitical potential of Notre Dame is not to be underestimated. Roland Barthes already captured the mythological power of gothic cathedrals as they are ‘the supreme creation of an era, conceived with the passion of unknown artists, and consumed in image if not in usage by a whole population which appropriates them as a purely magical object’ (Barthes, 1957: 88). In their online communication about the Notre Dame, this cultural capital is appropriated in the metapolitical battle. The cathedral is discursively framed not just as a cathedral, but as part of the identity of the French and even more, as an object from another universe.

The Notre Dame is also symbolic among identitarians for another reason. It is the place where Dominique Venner – one of the prominent intellectuals of La Nouvelle Droite – committed suicide in 2013. He saw his suicide, according to his suicide note, as a sacrifice ‘to break the lethargy that overwhelms us’. This sacrifice was done in order to protest and lay the foundation of protest by others. His ‘voluntary death’ was meant to awaken ‘the slumbering conscience’. In order to do this he said that he has chosen this ‘highly symbolic place, The Notre Dame Cathedral in Paris, that I respect and admire, because it was built by the genius of my ancestors on even older places of worship, recalling our immemorial origins.’ (Venner, 2013 my translation). He understands his suicide as a potential rebirth, as a negation of the inevitability of the civilizational decline caused by individualism, consumer culture and the replacement of our people. The Notre Dame, In Venner’s mind, stands for the complete opposite: the eternal, the spirit of tradition and the ancestors.

The Notre Dame is thus in many ways a central symbol of this identitarian struggle. Les Natifs dedicate 4 out of 20 posts to the topic of Notre Dame. It is also around the Cathedral that they mobilize and organize offline action. On 9 December 2021, they distributed flyers with the cathedral on it and the slogan ‘Stop Au Saccage’ (Stop the Rampage). They target the idea to turn the cathedral into a tourist museum and demand that it is rebuilt the way it was. This taps into that magical feeling that a cathedral evokes, and this re-enchantment of the cathedral contributes to the overall metapolitical goal to create an irrational, affective bond between people and this superlative object of history. On 16 April 2022, they again put an Instagram post online, now with a movie of the burning Notre Dame and the slogan to never forget the fire and ask people to fight for it. The movement uses hashtags to have a broader uptake: #notredame, #france, #honneur, #patrimonie, #paris and #incendienotredame. The hashtags allow them to tap into a broader audience, not necessarily in tune with the identitarian ideology. These hashtags serve as an indexing system in a clerical sense (Rosa & Bonilla, 2015: 5): they allow people looking for these topics to stumble upon these posts and maybe become convinced about the battle of Les Natifs. Hashtags of course 286also function as semiotic indexes as they frame the post as a fight for the patrimony of Paris and France. The metapolitical function is the result of these two index systems combined. The post, with its hashtags, presents Le Natifs’ activism as a committed but not necessarily radical fight for France to new audiences, and it uses the object that is commonly read as an object of brilliance, of an absence of origin (Barthes, 1957: 88) to fight against its desacrification by turning it into an all too human tourist museum.

The protest in front of Notre Dame follows the recipe of Generation Identitaire: small-scale protest with a limited number of activists, but remediatized on social media to have a large impact. This upscaling of activism – from the local to the national scale – is done by using social media: Twitter, Instagram and Telegram are used to generate uptake. The action is also mediatized by the Instagram account Occidentis.fr. This social media page has over 41,000 followers and the reel post they made receives 3,323 likes. Occidentis is a far-right news site dedicated to the same topics as the identitarian movement: the fight against wokeness, antiracism and LGBTQ+ movement and for homogenous cultures and nations. Les Natifs Paris uses the repertoires of resistance of Generation Identitaire and uses heritage to mobilize militants and French citizens for their cause. At the same time, the visibility is also realized by trying to generate uptake in a large French and international network of sympathizers.

Metapolitical networks

Les Natif Paris and Thais d’Escufon form, together with many different identitarian nodes that have been created in the last years, a new metapolitical French network. Thais d’Escufon explicitly referred to this network in her May 2022 video. She sees La Furia (22,3K followers on Instagram), La Cocarde Etudiante (16,7K followers on Instagram), SOS Calvaires (24,3K followers on Instagram) and Generation Z (42,7K followers on the main account on Instagram) as different nodes in a larger network of influencers, movements, and think tanks that fight metapolitically and politically. Generation Z is the most obvious reemergence of Generation Identitaire in France. Interestingly, this reemergence came in the form of a new political movement in support of the presidential candidacy of Eric Zemmour. Zemmour was, after the dissolution of Generation Identity, one of the more prominent talking heads to support Generation Identity. Generation Identity, said Zemmour, is a victim of the ‘at the same time’ policy of Macron. With this, he referred to a policy that he accuses President Macron to deploy. Namely, he suggests that Macron wants to balance out the banning of some Islamist groups by banning a victim on the right to compensate (Figaro, 2021).

Considering this explicit support for Generation Identity, it is quite unsurprising that Damien Rieu, co-founder and former spokesman of Generation 287Identity, announced that he would join Eric Zemmour in his fight for the French presidential elections.

While I originally could be counted among the skeptics, I gradually acquired the conviction that it is around Reconquest! and Generation Z that the recomposition - and therefore the future - of the rooted right will take place (…). I made the decision to join in my turn the campaign of Eric Zemmour.

(Bourgeois, 2022)

Note here the stress on the word ‘rooted right’ (la droite enracinée in French), which is also very visible in the framing of Les Natifs Paris as ‘Les jeunes Parisiens fiers & enracinés’.

The presence of the former spokesman is very clear, not only in the name of Generation Z, its ‘rootedness’ or the overall topic of the party, namely the reconquering of France but also in the digital presence of this political youth movement. Each large French city gets its own chapter of this political movement and its own digital presence on Instagram and Facebook. As such, the movement builds a layered, polycentric movement and a digital environment in which they can produce information that steers the minds of the followers. The same digital structure of local chapters of identitarian activists is also visible in the already mentioned network of identitarian ‘feminist’ movements called Nemesis (Collectif.nemesis on Instagram). This French collective has dozens of local chapters on the city level (Nemesis_lille59, Nemesis_lyon69, Nemesis_caen14, Nemesis_morbihan56, Nemesis_reims51, …) active on Instagram, but also chapters in Switzerland (Nemesis_suisse) and Belgium (Nemesis_ Bruxelles). All these pages have between a couple of hundreds and a couple of thousands of followers, and the pages are also following each other. The result is the construction of an identitarian ecosystem now targeting especially women. Note how these identitarians appropriate the label ‘feminism’ in their metapolitical battle. The appropriation echoes the metapolitics of de Benoist and Champetiers claiming to be ‘feminists differentielle’. In the manifesto of these ‘non-comformist feminists’, we read that they fight for ‘Western women’ and that they have three objectives:

(1) Denounce all violence against women both in their daily life, at their place of work or even in the street. (2) Denounce the dangerous impact of mass immigration on Western women so that this subject becomes a public debate. (3) Promote European civilization, not as having reduced women to the role of objects, but as the cradle of their fulfilment.

This ‘feminism’ is a good example of what Farris (2012) calls femonationalism, or the contemporary mobilization of (specific) feminist ideas by nationalists, or in this case identitarians for metapolitical goals. The fight for 288women’s rights is here subordinate to the fight for ‘European civilization’ and against mass immigration. In other words, feminism is here metapolitical discourse for the embrace of ‘white women’ and the expulsion and demonization of the migrant other.

Generation Z, Les Natif Paris and Nemesis are all metapolitical digital networks that propagate the same discourse: an identitarian discourse targeting specific niches (based on age, location, gender and nation). Together they upscale this network and bring together many different niches in one national polycentric movement. Generation Identity may be dissolved, but it has come back in many different forms, through many different digital accounts, addressing many different audiences and topics. From ‘identitarian feminists’, to ‘heritage fighters’, to political movements and metapolitical influencers: Generation Identity morphs in many different constellations. And this change, as a result of bans and deplatforming, will probably be perpetual. It is also not limited to France. In Belgium, we see that Schild & Vrienden has lost traction and that Feniks was the first spin-off that tried to take off where Schild & Vrienden left off but is now tailored to generate uptake in times of Covid-19. Dries Van Langenhove is now functioning as a metapolitical influencer on YouTube, but also as a politician that uses his speaking rights in parliament for metapolitical goals.

The global new right as a complex system

The global new right today, when I’m writing this conclusion of the last chapter of the book, looks nothing like the global new right when I started this project seven years ago. And it will probably look entirely different when the readers read these sentences. Understanding the global new right as a layered, polycentric and transnational network benefits from a perspective informed by the notion of complex systems. All the practices and publications of new right intellectuals, influencers and movements are historical documents; they are testimonies of the histories of those actors in ever-changing compositions. The case studies in this book shouldn’t be read as attempts of fixing for once and for all what the global new right is; they are chronicles of complexity, indexes of this complex system that is perpetually changing and evolving.

In such a complex system, we encounter different historicities and different speeds in interaction. In the period 2008–2015, not that much was visible of that network, at least for ‘normies’. But the building blocks of that global new right network were already decades in the making. This happened slowly, at least seen from the outside. The rise of Web 2.0 allowed new right actors to increasingly connect, upscale, play above their game and reach a broader audience. Even more, it changed the whole movement. The alt-right label for instance was not owned by Richard Spencer anymore when it enjoyed global uptake: it was the digital culture of Web 2.0 and its prosumer-oriented 289technologies and practices that turned ‘the alt-right’ into an important node in this global new right network. The alt-right that became globally famous was a networked movement. The prominent actors of that network were not in first instance the think tanks and the long essays, but the #alt-right hashtag, the trolling and meming by anonymous and less anonymous actors. The intellectual foundation was years in the making, but the actual success was the result of digital culture and the affordances and algorithms of the digital ecosystem. ‘The alt-right’, said Spencer, ‘is what it is today not because of me; it is what it is today because I let it go. I didn’t possess it, and it was taken up by all these people’ (Spencer quoted in Hawley, 2017: 68). This sudden success is a classic network effect and it cannot be understood as the result of the internal strength of the movement; it is the result of a complex series of socio-technical assemblages. The controversies that accompanied the #altright movement were ticking all the algorithmic boxes of the mainstream digital platforms at the time. The uptake was not just an uptake of ideas, it was very much an algorithmic uptake biased towards sensation, controversies and in general, attention-grabbing content. Activists succeeded in gaming the algorithms in order to acquire spreadability.

This in turn introduced very fast changes in the network: the alt-right became an important node in a truly global phenomenon. A phenomenon that, especially after the election of Trump, drew global mainstream media attention. The alt-right became the talk of the town. This visibility, in the end, triggered all kinds of external forces: platforms, governments and civil society actors were all of a sudden very conscious about the emergence of this new right movement. Counter-movements were born, and a leftist activist punched Spencer, governments were increasingly alarmed and platforms were pressured by government and economic interests to take action. New right and extreme-right movements, activists and intellectuals took notice of this new edgy and seemingly polar movement. The alt-right functioned as an important order of indexicality on a global scale.

The story of Generation Identity is quite similar, albeit different. It came into existence when the right adopted left-wing methodologies and used them to launch a new identitarian discourse. The use of digital media platforms allowed the movement to grow rapidly: it became a pan-European networked movement first and in the slipstream of the alt-right it became a global phenomenon. The larger the movement became, and the more attention it grabbed through the mediatization of their metapolitical activism, the more it became the object of intense scrutiny and counteractions from platforms and governments. This crackdown was not the end of this movement, but it did have to reinvent itself and morph in many different and unpredictable ways. New nodes operating on different scale levels with different tools are emerging, and as a result not only does the French metapolitical landscape change but also the global new right takes new shapes, acquires new faces, 290new discourses and new practices. This perpetual change as a result of internal (infighting, ideological differences, …) and external causes (prosecution, deplatforming, deplatformization) is the essence of this metapolitical network.

The global new right is a perpetually changing system of systems united in a metapolitical battle for a different world order. The backbone of this network is the different media platforms they use to fight and undermine hegemony. As long as the digital mainstream platforms were committed as much as possible to a non-intervention governance strategy, this global new right could easily upscale through networking and expand its reach and thus gain more power. The libertarian and digital utopianist ideology embedded in much of the Silicon Valley-based platforms wasn’t much of a strong supporter of the neoliberal hegemony. This changed after 2016. First, we saw the ban of Milo after relentless trolling and then the case of the first deplatformization wave in 2017 after the Charlottesville attack. This dialectic between metapolitics and violence has caused increased platform governance, and thus – from the perspective of the far-right – guardians of hegemony. The Web 2.0 set-up of these digital platforms is of course in its core vulnerable to the perpetual reemergence of new accounts, new platforms and new groups who use those platforms for new metapolitical projects and to lure the mainstream audiences to more niched platforms with less moderation.

As a result of these dynamics, we see an increasingly complex multitude of crisscrossing and overlapping multiscalar metapolitical projects. The different scales can display different kinds of order, some can be stable for a very long time, but then all of a sudden as a result of external or internal causes, morph rapidly into new projects and new networks. The new right is thus not a homogenous group, fighting for power. What all these groups do seem to share is an acute understanding that for this new world to be born, metapolitical action in the digital realm is necessary. This metapolitical action is deeply embedded in several digital cultures operating more towards the mainstream and at the same time also extremely niched in the case of metapolitical terrorist culture. A second essential characteristic of the global new right is that this system is perpetually in motion. The global new right is a highly unstable system, but it is still a system and thus a structure. A structure where some features are stable for a long time (metapolitical, La Nouvelle Droite, ….) and others have a higher pace of change and development.
