8 Metapolitics, algorithms and violence

DOI: 10.4324/9781003283379-9

This chapter has been made available under a CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 license.

On 17 May 2021, Jürgen Cönings, a Belgian soldier suspected of extreme-right leanings, stole heavy weaponry among which were four rocket launchers, a personal defence weapon and a semi-automatic weapon from the military depots in the Belgian army station in Leopoldsburg. The day after, he left three farewell letters and took his military decoration with him to put it on the family grave. Cönings was listed as a potentially violent extremist and was known to be in contact with Thomas Boutens, a convicted far-right terrorist. In the years before, he had already threatened Marc Van Ranst, the Belgian virologist who became known during the Covid-19 pandemic. Police confirmed that Cönings had two targets for his intended terrorism, Marc Van Ranst and the Tevhid-moskee in Eisden (Maasmechelen, Belgium). In his farewell letters, he focused on the political elites and virologists controlling our lives:

‘I can’t live with the lies of people who decide how we should live’ (…) The so-called political elite, and now also virologists, decide how you and I should live. They incite hatred and frustration (…) and nobody resist. And if you say something, you get punished. I go in the resistance’. (Cönings, my translation)

That Cönings was serious about his plans about going ‘into the resistance’ is beyond any doubt. On the 18th, Cönings drove to Van Ranst’s house with an SUV full of guns. When he found that the virologist was not at home, he fled into a nearby forest. Those letters, his presence at Van Ranst’s house and the theft of the guns were the start of a manhunt which lasted until 21 June 2021 when a passer by found Coning’s dead body.

296

Jürgen Cönings and the dialectics of metapolitics

The heavily mediatized manhunt also led to the Facebook page ‘Als 1 achter Jurgen’(As one behind Jürgen). The about section of the page stated: ‘Save our hero. This is abuse of power’. In three days’ time, the group had managed to have over 8,100 members. In the end, more than 45,000 people joined the group. Even though not all members of the group fully supported JC’s intentions and narrative, the dominant narratives depicted Jürgen Cönings at the very least as a victim of the system and its imperial wars, the majority even saw him as more, as a ‘hero of the resistance’. To them, Cönings was a ‘freedom fighter’ and the mass media, politicians and even the police were seen as liars. This shared mindset is the product of their previous socialization in different niches and their interactions in this group. Some people had a longer history within the far-right, others were more recently socialized within anti-vax groups or groups that were highly critical of Covid-19 policies of the government, and several had a long history in more conspiracy-oriented groups. What people in this new social niche shared was a distrust of mass media and the ‘elites’ in society. In the interaction in this group, a dominant meta-narrative that constructed an oppressive and especially untrustworthy and hypocritical elite that doesn’t care about its people emerged. The exact definition of those elites could vary substantially. One user would see the so-called Vivaldi government of Belgium as the elites in control, another would frame the national mass media as the elites lying to the people. The elites were also described as ‘rats’ and ‘filthy whores’. In other posts, ‘the elites’ would suddenly refer to actors operating on a different scale: Facebook & Zuckerberg and of course, Soros and his Avaaz became targets of their anger. No matter who exactly was depicted as the elite, they were imagined to be all-powerful: in control, being able to set up conspiracies on a global scale, organizing not only what is acceptable in public debate, but also controlling the people in the public sphere. Some of these populist depictions have long local histories in the discourses of the Flemish far-right party Flemish Interest, other discourses have more recent and international origins. They all got synchronized together in one layered narrative that framed Jürgen Cönings as the ‘resistance’ fighting for the people – our children in particular – against those lying elites.

The post from one of the admins of the Facebook group is emblematic of this populist narrative. Jürgen Cönings, according to him, can count on ‘a lot of support of the people’ which gives the ‘Vivaldi government an uncanny feeling’. Cönings makes them uneasy because he is seen as too knowledgeable about things that the government wants to hide. Cönings is described in a QAnon kind of narrative: as somebody in the know, who knows the system from within and is now fighting for us. And this is of course life threatening for those elites, and subsequently also life threatening for Cönings, as those elites will not hold back to save their power. As a result of his inside 297knowledge, the elites try to discredit him. That is why they frame him and his supporters as ‘extreme right’. The admin of the page openly dreams of a mutiny within the army that will force the government to resign and ‘throw the virologists under the bus’. This post is emblematic of the pre-revolutionary narrative in the group. The uptake of it was substantial; within the first four hours, more than 50 people shared it on their own profiles. This engagement indexes a culture of commitment, and a shared view on the political constellation and the need for resistance.

This discourse and its niched popular uptake align well with the conceptualization of the government, media and ‘the elites’ in the discourses of the many niches that made up the Capitol Riots. That narrative also framed the state and the media as bad for the people. Covid-19 discourses only reinforced this distrust of the government and the elites. Conspiracy thinkers constructed all kinds of wild claims about Covid-19 as part of a scheme of world domination. The Covid-19 measures were a new fault line in society and far-right and radical right movements, parties and influencers were using this new world to produce new discourses, find support and of course also metapolitically exploit this health crisis. They fed the myth that Covid-19 was nothing more than a tool to issue a society of full control (Fuchs, 2021). Whereas in the United States Fauci was seen as the demon by Trump supporters, in Flanders the radical and extreme-right were targeting Marc Van Ranst as an emblem of a government destroying its people.

In such a constellation, a culture of violence can grow. When one member of the ‘Als 1 achter Jurgen’ group wrote, ‘I want to ask a very honest question to the thousands of members of this group: Would you reconsider your support if Jürgen kills somebody? And would it depend on the victim?’, the answers were telling. A majority of the 92 comments explicitly stated that they would keep supporting him. In the latter group some invoke the notion of self-defence, or argue that the government is mafia and thus legitimates any defence: ‘it is about the future of our children’, says one user. Several argue that they wouldn’t mind if Marc Van Ranst would disappear and some even argue that he should ‘receive another medal if he would kill MvR (Marc Van Ranst)’. Another one goes even further, claiming that he would have even more respect for Cönings if he kills some ‘snobs in BXL’ (referring to a politician in government) and that ‘he wouldn’t mind him killing some coloured people’. Such interactions normalize violence as a way to save ‘the people’ from ‘the elites’.

Just like in the United States, the manhunt on Jürgen Cönings brought together people from different niches and fused them into one temporal group. The online support of Jürgen Cönings in this Facebook functions as a learning environment. It facilitates the rapid merger of extreme-right populist discourses and anti-Corona protest spiced up with racist discourses and anti-government discourses. This new synchronized discourse is moulded on 298existing international far-right voices: we hear echoes of Trump, Groypers, QAnon discourses and conspiracy theories on Covid-19. Those discursive ingredients were made to work in the local context. This group can also not be detached from discourses that got quite some airplay in the whole Flemish hybrid media system. The focus on Van Ranst as a doctor of doom, and thus a puppet of the elites, was not limited to this marginal niche of society. Theo Francken, a popular politician of the radical right anti-Enlightenment party N-VA (Maly, 2016), called Marc Van Ranst doctor Hate. Feniks, anti-Covid protestors and Flemish Interest constructed the government as bad for the people, as stealing our freedom.

The party that capitalized the most on the Covid-19 protests in Flanders was the extreme-right party Flemish Interest. This party, of which Cönings used to be a member, was targeting the Corona policies quite hard. 18 days before Cönings’ plan started to unfold in the real world, Tom Van Grieken, the President of Flemish Interest, held his traditional 1 May speech under the banner ‘Time for Freedom!’. That speech was fully dedicated to the ‘attack on freedom’ by the Belgian government. The government was accused of unconstitutional behaviour, absurd measures and stealing the freedom of the people. The speech was remediatized on YouTube where it was seen over 5,000 times. In the opening statement of this YouTube video, we see Tom Van Grieken on his way to Mechelen saying that ‘In the last year our freedom has been taken away by this Purple-Green government’ (Vlaams Belang, 2021). And he added that ‘what bothers me the most, is that the ministers who have taken away our freedom, don’t follow those rules themselves’. The discourse of lying, untrustworthy politicians stealing the freedom of the people was produced here, long before the support group of Cönings came to life. And Van Grieken was not the inventor of this discourse either; Trump and many other radical and extreme-right voices and conspiracy theorists around the world beat him to it. This is classic politics of recognition: Van Grieken addresses different audiences – including anti-vaxxers, conspiracy theorists and of course his traditional voters – without fully and explicitly articulating the known conspiracy theories. He walks a thin line between what is ‘acceptable discourse’ and full-blown conspiracy theories.

This type of criticism targeting the Corona measures of the government seamlessly ties into more traditional extreme-right discourses linking multiculturality and crime (Maly, 2020a). The measures, argued Van Grieken, ‘have to be enforced by police and security staff. But these people are increasingly confronted with a lack of respect and even physical violence’. These utterances of the president of Flemish Interest are edited on cell phone videos showing ‘allochthone youths’ fighting with security staff of the railways. The intro of the video ends with Van Grieken stressing that they are ready to fight, to fight hard for the freedom of the people. In the next shot, we see Van Grieken arriving just in time in Mechelen to see the speech of his Flemish 299Interest colleague Wim Verheyden. In the fragment, Verheyden focused on ‘Sihame-gate’ and connected it to the multicultural policies in Flanders. Sihame El Kaouakibi was famous as the driving force behind several dance projects helping allochthone youths integrate. Because of her fame and qualities as a ‘role model’ she was invited by the liberal party to get into politics. Soon she was accused of massive fraud. Her trajectory from civil society to top politics was used by Verheyden to stress that multicultural policies are devasting for the Flemish people. This same blend of narratives was also very common on the ‘As 1 behind Jurgen’ Facebook page: the popularity of Sihame and the fact that she wasn’t jailed yet, was contrasted with Cönings’ history, his service for the country and the massive manhunt. It was all read as proof that something fishy was going on.

In a Facebook page like ‘As 1 behind Jürgen’, we see the impact of a multi-layered and polycentric far-right metapolitical battle. This battle has been waged over the last four decades and has accounted for the normalization of certain radical ideas about ‘the elites’ and the replacement of the people. This metapolitics can very quickly be adapted to new topics. Conspiracy theories play an important role here. They tap into a by now widespread and shared feeling of distrust towards governments and elites among many niches ranging from the classic extreme-right militants to the QAnon moms or yoga communities. Within those niches, this shared feeling can best be described with what Raymond Williams has called structures of feelings (Williams, 1961: 69–90). The oxymoron in structures of feeling forces us to focus on the relation between agency and structure, on the poiesis-infrastructure nexus I discussed earlier: on the becoming of, the emergence of a culture of a period. In the context of the global new right, structures of feeling do not necessarily work on the level of a period or a nation, but within the different niches of the global new right, they create a sharedness. It is that sharedness that allows members of those niches to see themselves as kindred spirits, as victims of the system, of the elites.

Structures of feeling, said Williams, are ‘the actual living sense, the deep community that makes the communication possible, is naturally drawn upon’ (Williams, 1961: 69). He used the concept to define a social experience that is still in process, in motion and in becoming. Conspiracy theories, as the Sorelian myths we have defined them, provide alternative views and new hypotheses to understand reality and form the largely ungrabbable building blocks that facilitate communication among members of such newly and rapidly emerging groups. They tie together the most extreme conspiracy theories, with the extreme-right populist discourse. They shape a general populist cultural coherence in which ‘the elites’, including scientists, politicians and journalists, are creating a fake world. Even though Van Grieken does not explicitly talk about a conspiracy, and he doesn’t mention Bill Gates, Soros or a secret group planning world domination, his discourse addresses those who 300believe in such conspiracy theories. His discourse has the quality of blending believers in such theories with older anti-migration groups. The notion of ‘the elites’ allows for that shared feeling of being lied to, being betrayed, the general feeling that ‘something is seriously wrong’, no matter in which of the different anti-elite niches people were socialized in. This shared feeling creates openness to alternative views and to the narratives of others who seem to share that same distrust.

This structure of feeling is metapolitically created and exploited by all kinds of activist movements (think of Feniks), influencers (Dries Van Langenhove, Nick Fuentes, …), far-right intellectuals (Alexander Dugin) and politicians (Tom Van Grieken of Flemish Interest, Thierry Baudet of Forum for Democracy). This general distrust in the context of the Covid-19 pandemic is then connected to other topics where that same structure of feeling is exploited. Covid-19 measures are in that respect connected to the politicians’ mishandling of migration. Not only can all topics be mobilized to undermine the legitimacy of those ‘in power’, the topics can be connected. In moments of crises, the connection of these topics, and the niched groups that gather around those topics can be mobilized and form mobs or breed resistance and even violence. All those local and translocal narratives are synchronized in a niched shared experience in which a potential far-right terrorist like Jürgen Cönings can suddenly become a hero. We cannot understand the support for Coning’s intended violence if we isolate it from the metapolitics of the right. The sharp distinction between violence and metapolitics, as Ravndal (2021) advocates, underestimates the power of ideas. Or more concretely, this hard distinction makes blind the relation between symbolic and physical violence inherently tied into the new right metapolitical project. As we have seen throughout this book, it is not metapolitics or violence. There is a far more complex dialectical relation between metapolitics and far-right terrorism. Tarrant, Roof, but also the shooters in Halle, El Paso and Buffalo were all motivating their terrorist action through the mobilization of discourses of decline, celebration of diversity, saving their people and fighting against replacement. They were all targeting the elites destroying the people. Cönings is no exception, his targets – a Mosque and a left-wing virologist – are emblematic of the metapolitics of the Flemish new right and the merger of recent anti-Covid discourses and long established anti-migration discourses. Dries Van Langenhove, Flemish Interest and Theo Francken framed Van Ranst as a left-wing and polarizing icon of a government oppressive of its own people.

Every societal topic can be metapolitically exploited and merged with other topics. Together all these narratives, and the groups that mobilize and are mobilized through those narratives, can function as one metapolitical network, and – when the time is right and circumstances collide – be mobilized into an offline mass by existing or new movements, influencers and parties. That was the lesson of the Capitol Riots. Metapolitics 2.0 succeeds 301in creating a shared feeling that everything is going wrong, and that the elites, the left and immigrants are to blame. It is this sense of urgency that mobilizes.

Metapolitics 2.0 and global digital new right cultures

Understanding contemporary new right violence and terrorism demands contextualizing it in a decade-old metapolitical battle. New right metapolitics with its stress on the decline of society, its neo-racism and the construction and exclusion of ‘the other’ in terms of the destructiveness of the left, the feminist, the liberal and the ethnic other sets a frame of ‘war’. The enemy is accused of waging war on traditions, language, culture and our identity: it shapes a worldview where there is an ongoing war against the people. Metapolitics, and especially a Faye-inspired identitarian metapolitics 2.0, legitimates the necessity of urgent action. As Faye’s compagnion du route Robert Steuckers argues, Faye’s discourse ‘hyper mobilizing’ (Steuckers, 2020: 12). This hypermobilization comes from the urgency he sketches and the hope that he provides that change is still possible. Combine this with a discourse of war, and it is a matter of time that someone sees it as a duty to act. In essence, new right metapolitics is a revolutionary project designed to first change the hearts and minds of people, but with the end goal of overthrowing the established order. In a world of networked individualism and affective audiences, this resistance can take many different shapes: from revolution and even terrorism to posting stickers, bodybuilding and binge-watching YouTube videos.

Metapolitics, as envisioned by La Nouvelle Droite, was, as we have seen, in the first instance an intellectual exercise and it was produced in classic intellectual products: journals, books, congresses, think tanks, and (intellectual) websites. It focused on giving the extreme and far-right an intellectual foundation. In the first decade of the 21st century, we saw similar strategies deployed by new right activists all over the world. The renaissance of the new right in Germany in the 21st century was embedded in new institutions and organizations like the ‘Institut für Staatspolitik,’ the ‘Bibliothek des Konservatismus,’ and magazines like Sezession (see Salzborn, 2016 for an overview). In the United States too, we see that people like Greg Johnson and Richard Spencer and the alt-right in general, influenced by the metapolitics of La Nouvelle Droite, invested in setting up think tanks (National Policy Institute), publishing houses (Arktos and Counter-Currents) and websites (Taki’s Magazine, Occident Observer, Counter-Currents) that were dedicated to intellectually ground a North American new right movement (Johnson, 2012).

The global renaissance of new right movements and their metapolitical strategies soon morphed in the second decade of the 21st century. Contemporary new right activists, as a result of their integration into digital mainstream and more niched platforms and the digital cultures they bred, used very 302different means to engage in ‘metapolitics.’ In the United States we witnessed the rise of the alt-right as a digital culture. #Gamergate was a first turning point, as it showed the possibilities for right-wing activism using trolling and memetic warfare (Yiannopoulos, 2017; Maly, 2018d). These new forms of metapolitical activism use digital media to attract young(er) people and give them an ‘edgy’ and revolting character. Adopting these new digital cultures came with the claim that ‘the right’ is the edgy avant-garde of their generation. The internet, and especially the digital utopianist moderation policies of mainstream social platforms enabled the new right, and especially the so-called alt-light in the United States, to rethink their metapolitical project in terms of ‘popular culture’ and journalism. Breitbart for instance was from the start set up as a metapolitical project. ‘Culture matters’, writes Milo (Yiannopoulos, 2017: 27) while quoting Andrew Breitbart, stating that ‘politics is downstream from culture.’ The site was set up to be integrated into mainstream digital media so it could reach a broad audience or in other words normalize and popularize its ideological agenda. It functioned as an entryist vehicle for more radical nodes in the global new right network. The same logic was also visible in other projects like altright.com, The Daily Stormer or in the visibility of new right activists in their YouTube vlogs and collabs (Lewis, 2018).

These ‘local renewals’ soon transgressed borders and influenced activists from all corners of the world. This was not an accidental by-product, but the result of already existing infrastructures of a global new right. Arktos played a pivotal role, as did several important websites with a more global reach like Reddit, 4chan and 8chan. Mass media did the rest: their attention to these new practices allowed new right activists to upscale their game. This ‘edgy’ new right digital culture found solid ground to grow in Europe. No coincidence there: metapolitics, the European new right product par excellence, came back home in a whole new package and it fused with a more activist new right culture and political climate that was growing for several decades in Europe. Pegida and Generation Identity were emblematic of those new metapolitical developments in Europe (Salzborn, 2016: 50). These movements, usually embedded within mainstream digital media like Facebook, not only try to tap into feelings of alienation, poverty, and fast change in an era of digitalization, globalization, neoliberalism, and superdiversity, but also set up new forms of activism. Whereas the mass protests of Pegida were used to make a populist claim by referring to offline mobilization power, the identitarian movements used highly mediatized activism to claim the voice of their generation and to give their positions an ‘edgy’ feel. Generation Identity used the affordances of digital media to choreograph offline protest marches and organize small-scale interventions that were later remediatized to reach bigger audiences and to conceal that they are not able to mobilize larger audiences offline. Both movements exploited the core principles of the attention economy and had huge salience in the hybrid media system, again on a regional, national and transnational scale.

303
Metapolitics Metapolitics 2.0
  • Preserve an intellectual elite
  • Papers, articles, books
  • Intellectualism
  • Content
  • Niched audience
  • High Brow Culture/analogue
  • Prosumers, influencers, activists, intellectuals, politicians, …
  • Vlogs, memes, trolling, influencers, hashtags, stickers
  • Content and form
  • Message
  • Digital/algorithmic literacy
  • Layered audience
  • Digital Culture/Algorithmic logic

Especially Generation Identity was, just like the alt-right in the United States, adopting a metapolitical strategy informed by the intellectual work of Guillaume Faye. It is in the uptake of the actions and infrastructures that facilitated this new metapolitical action that the global new right took shape and that new forms of metapolitics saw the light of day. Metapolitics was influenced by the digital utopianism that drives Web 2.0 and has fundamentally changed, becoming metapolitics 2.0.

La Nouvelle Droite’s metapolitics, as conceptualized by de Benoist, was the preserve of an intellectual elite. Only the elites – in the case of the far-right intellectuals of La Nouvelle Droite – were imagined to produce and thus introduce new ideas in society. To give legitimacy to those ideas, La Nouvelle Droite appropriated the scientific form. The focus was first and foremost on content that would be recognized by others as ‘intellectual’ and thus as deep highbrow cultural ideas. The metapolitics of La Nouvelle Droite was directed towards elite audiences of politicians, academics and journalists who would then ideally reproduce those ideas and let them circulate in society. In this conceptualization of metapolitics, the public is imagined as sheeplike consumers and mindless reproducers of the ideas of the elites.

Under the influence of Web 2.0 ideology, and prosumer culture, we see that metapolitics 2.0 is not just produced by a small club of intellectuals. Metapolitics has now been ‘democratized’: influencers, activists, movements and prosumers now produce and reproduce metapolitical discourse. As a result, metapolitics has changed form. It is not limited to articles, essays or papers anymore. We can now see memes, trolling, hashtags, stickers and posters, but also comments, likes, shares, videos, clothing, conspiracy theories and vaporwave aesthetics as metapolitical action. Metapolitics now has a populist aesthetic as it is integrated into many different popular but niched digital cultures instead of highbrow culture. The style of contemporary metapolitics suggests that this is not the discourse of the elites, but of youth, the common man. As a result of this ‘democratization’ of metapolitics, metapolitical actors now direct their communication to a much broader but layered and niched network of audiences spanning the globe. In order 304to stay integrated into this economy of virality and thus generate uptake, metapolitical influencers but also more traditional far-right activists need to be media literate. They need to develop specific strategies and make full use of the affordances and algorithms of the different media (and their specific media logics), and gain algorithmic knowledge to build an audience and/or community. This communication is not just about content, it is heavily influenced by the media that they use to communicate: metapolitics 2.0 has an algorithmic logic and is influenced by Web 2.0 ideology.

This new type of metapolitics in the digital age is clearly not only about the circulation of ideas, it is also about digital literacy and digital culture. The mediatized performance of the new right identity has in itself become a metapolitical deed. It is through this careful stylization of hair, body, clothes and language that new right actors address different audiences. Such (meta)politics of addressivity and recognition is crucial to stay integrated into many different socio-technical environments at the same time. These integrational and addressive qualities are found in ‘the details’: the logos on the shirt, the Flemish flag socks and the style of the clothing. These details not only secure their uptake or integration but also preconfigure their cool, edgy and archeofuturistic society. These norms and meanings communicated through fashion do not just spontaneously erupt, they are introduced by people who have the power and reach to do that. Influencers play, just like in other cultural niches, an important role in the construction of style; in this case, a far-right style.

The ideological strength of the new right in the 21st century stems from the fact that it is a digitally embedded, international and highly eclectic movement. The far-right has not only technologically integrated itself, but it has also culturally integrated its metapolitical battle into the digital mainstream. This integration has fundamental effects not only on concrete metapolitical practices but also on the structure and the reach of the far-right. The far-right has globalized, it has become a transnational, polycentric and layered network, a perpetually changing complex system, where certain ideas and practices and styles are operating on a global scale (think of memes, trolling or the fashy haircut for men) while other practices are only visible and productive on lower scales and in more niched groups. The metapoliticization of the far-right is now a translocal phenomenon deeply intertwined with the digital infrastructures and the local context. The advance of the new right ideology in the 21st century was deeply embedded in the mainstream digital infrastructure. This digital integration ensured that metapolitical actors could scale up and that small niches could expand rapidly. The digital structure facilitated a successful and impactful metapolitical struggle. As a result of symbolic and terrorist new right violence, states and platforms started to increase moderation and juridical measures to stop new right actors. These external pressures cause the global new right to perpetually change, gain strength in some fields and contexts, and lose reach in others. Internal and external pressures force 305it to adapt, reorganize and reappear under new names, in new formats and on new platforms. The global new right is a complex system: no matter the constant change, there is order. A complex order that binds the system together. Metapolitics is the glue connecting all those actors in their fight for a new world order grounded in the anti-Enlightenment ideals of that second modernity. A world of homogeneous nations, communities and civilizations that reject democratic ideology.

Metapolitics and the anti-Enlightenment tradition

The French philosopher Claude Lefort (2016) saw democracy and politics as inextricably linked. In his thinking, democracy and politics referred to a never-ending dialogue or struggle between ideas that make up the ever-changing constitution of society. That battle, according to Lefort, is always unfinished. There is never a final solution or an end. This endless dialogue, however, takes place within the limits of democracy. The analytical notion of politics as a discursive struggle for meaning and hegemony is usually implicitly conceived within that political democratic system. It is a struggle to create the constitution of democracy. However, in the case of the new right, their metapolitical struggle questions the very foundations of democracy itself and rejects its ideology and structure. Democracy, the new right and the anti-Enlightenment intellectuals understood quite correctly, is not ideologically empty, nor was it ever politically neutral. It is inherently intertwined with the struggle of the radical Enlightenment thinkers (Israel, 2010). Democracy cannot be separated from the Enlightenment ideology of equality, freedom and universal human rights. At least not without changing the meaning of democracy itself. And that is exactly the goal of metapolitics.

In radical Enlightenment thinking, there can be no democracy without universal human rights. The idea of universal human rights is the foundation of an enlightened democracy. According to the radical Enlightenment thinkers, each individual has inalienable individual rights in democracy. The state and those in power never have the right to restrict those rights. The state is seen as an instrument to guarantee every human being his natural rights. The state is therefore an instrument in the hands of and at the service of the people. According to the Condorcet, despotism and tyranny arise when, in the absence of representative control over the laws, human rights are infringed (Condorcet, 1790). Alexis De Tocqueville pointed out that the citizen therefore has the right to unite and resist against policies that infringe on his rights. If not, people will not live in a democratic regime, but in a tyranny of the ruling majority (De Tocqueville, 1835). Power in this democratic ideology de facto rests with the people. ‘The people’ are not imagined as homogeneous people characterized by shared values, norms and language, but consist of individual people with rights who at all times have the right to protest if 306those rights are violated (Hardt, 2007). This individualism is not the antithesis of solidarity or social groups. Individuals are social animals that join and create groups, but – and this is the difference with the anti-Enlightenment tradition: individuals also have the right to leave groups if one sees fit. To realize democracy and human rights, and only then, are revolt and revolution allowed within the Enlightenment tradition. Democracy was not a mere formality, it was always meant to be more than just elections. The essence of democracy therefore lies in respecting and extending human rights. Denis Diderot, Paul Henri Thiry d’Holbach, Emmanuel Joseph Sièyes, Nicolas de Condorcet, Jacques Pierre Brissot, Gabriel Bonnot de Mably, Constantin-François de Chasseboeuf de Volney, Thomas Paine, Joseph Priestley and the Dutch democratic patriots of 1780 all understood representative democracy as embedded in a democratic ideology. Representative democracy had to guarantee that every person was equal: that every person was equally free to live up to his or her own goals, to pursue happiness and to realize his or her ambitions (Israel, 2011: 814).

The political struggle of the global new right functions formally within the limits of democracy: extreme-right and radical right parties like Front National, Zemmour’s reconquest, Trump and Flemish Interest use the democratic system to attract voters. They set up parties, and in most cases also set up party activities. They are electable and thus formally part of democracy. But their politics are not democratic; they are a metapolitical instrument. They try to legitimize and spread their ideology through ‘democratic’ means. We can also make the same conclusion for the various action groups who pretend to speak in the name of the people and exert their ‘right to freedom of speech’. A formalistic perspective on democratic space, politics and democracy blinds us for the ideological significance of their political, metapolitical and action-based struggle. Traditionally, anti-Enlightenment conservatism à la Edmund Burke has been on a collision course with democratic ideology. You only have to pick up his booklet Reflections on the Revolution (Burke, 1790) in France to realize that Burke (1790), as Zeev Sternhell convincingly demonstrates, and his followers Hippolyte Taine, Ernest Renan, Joseph de Maistre and Friedrich Meinecke 2, waged a centuries-long ideological struggle against democracy (Sternhell, 2010). That voice was widespread in pre-World War II Europe (Sternhell, 1986), and it is on the rise again today.

If de Benoist and Champetier speak out in favour of democracy in their Manifesto of the French New Right (de Benoist & Champetier, 2000), then that notion of ‘democracy’ acquires meaning in a very different tradition. Democracy is detached from the Jacobin tradition, its Enlightenment ideology and its connection with universal human rights (de Benoist & Champetier, 2000; de Benoist, 2011). La Nouvelle Droite’s organic democracy is not based on individual rights, but on ‘organic, culturally homogeneous groups’. The new right democracy stands for the realization of 307‘the common identity of the administrators and the governed’ (de Benoist & Champetier, 2000: 18). This ‘organic democracy’ consists of a people with an identity and is based on a Schmittian distinction between the citizen and the non-citizen, between friend and enemy. La Nouvelle Droite’s commitment to democracy is not just a rejection of democratic ideology, it is a full frontal attack. The metapolitical embrace of democracy infuses it with an anti-Enlightenment meaning. It becomes a synonym of the nation or the organic group and the power of an aristocratic elite speaking in the name of the people. According to de Benoist and Champetier, the democratic debate is no more than loose opinions and accusations (de Benoist & Champetier, 2000: 19). According to them, we must move towards a new synthesis, a synthesis beyond left and right. We have to build that new order, a new politics. The Schmittian Return of Politics. The metapolitics of the new right creates an anti-democracy. Anti-democracy is not necessarily a dictatorship. It is the mirror image of Jacobin democracy. It is a democracy that has been stripped of the radical Enlightenment ideology. The basis of anti-democracy is not the idea of inalienable, natural rights of the individual, but the primacy of the organic community. As with all anti-Enlightenment thinkers, that community is presented as an independent being, as a body. That body forms a whole that cannot be traced back to the individuals of which it consists. Individuals exist only as part of the whole and the interest of the whole takes precedence.

The body of the community is essentially the moral and social order, and that order must be preserved at all costs. The social order is characterized by inequality: inequality between men and women, between leaders and ordinary people. That inequality is not only defined as natural but as something good. The different organic communities, in turn, create even more inequality or difference. Biological differences add to cultural differences and that results in separate entities that must be preserved. That is the natural order and must not be questioned. Rights are embedded in that natural order and can never be universal for new right actors, let alone inalienable. Rights are acquired within the community. The good, aristocratic elites have the right to lead, the people shouldn’t think but execute and live their lives in service of the greatness of the community. The elites think and the people feel. This division of roles within the community forms the basis of the order. The political is thus not universal, but possible only in the organic group. It is that group that has the right to grant rights. It is the group that defines as a group who is a citizen and who is not, who has rights and who does not. And it is the leaders of the group who must lead the community who are the voice of the people.

Richard Spencer takes this classic French new right line of argument in an article about the 4th of July, the American national holiday (Spencer, 2017b). In that piece, he denounces the celebration of the independence of the United States because, like France’s national holiday, it is essentially the celebration of the Enlightenment. The national holiday does not celebrate a patriotic 308war, but what Spencer, echoing Burke’s criticism of the French Revolution, denounces as the victory of ‘abstract ideas’. Abstract ideas such as inalienable rights, freedom, equality, and democracy are ‘anti-ideals’ for Spencer and the global new right in general. Those ideas stand in the way of what the real national ideals should be: ‘the soul and history of the people, the source of wisdom and tradition, a vision of something greater and more dominant and powerful than the individual’. Spencer here echoes Julius Evola’s vision of ‘the true right’ (Evola, 2013). Evola also denounced the Enlightenment and the French Revolution in particular as the cause of the destruction of European culture and prestige. According to Spencer, the alt-right should go straight to the heart of the social order, namely the resistance against the philosophers and their ideals of Enlightenment, and should argue for the obvious truth that ‘all men are created unequal’.

Enlightenment, argued Guillaume Faye, corrupted democracy. ‘Democracy is now a world dogma, but it’s a sham democracy, for it neglects the people’s interests. Western democracies are actually oligarchies that conceal their betrayal of the Hellenic-Germanic tradition of democracy’ (Faye, 2011: 111). He pleads for an organic democracy that is only possible ‘among an ethnically homogenous people’. In case of the latter, populism is the solution. ‘Populism must be made positive’, he argued, as it ‘defends the people’s interests before that of the political class and advocates direct democracy’ (Faye, 2011: 221). We see the same ideas in Génération Identitaire’s declaration of war. While the movement claims to stand up for ‘democracy’, it rejects representative democracy. Her vision on democracy is based on referendums. For Génération Identitaire, direct democracy is the ‘real democracy’ (Willinger, 2013). Here too, the democratic flag is raised to wage an anti-democratic struggle: A struggle against universal rights and humanism. The radical Enlightenment thinkers, just like the German philosopher Immanuel Kant, saw in direct or simplistic democracy an invitation for unrest, chaos and destruction. For them, it was completely incompatible with the common good and would inevitably result in the undermining of human rights and the fomenting of hatred and racism. Direct democracy reduces democracy to ‘the opinion of the people’ and thus surrenders people to demagogues. This anti-democratic interpretation of Génération Identitaire’s commitment to democracy is further substantiated by their explicit struggle: against equality, against universalism and against human rights (Willinger, 2013: 31), and for national homogeneity (Willinger, 2013: 43) for the reproduction of tradition (Willinger, 2013: 71) and for the idea of rebirth, of a new golden age, a new ethnopluralist world order. In that new order, there are no fixed principles and fixed rights, but cultural and ever-changing rights. Anti-democracy is, from an Enlightenment perspective, a tyranny, a despotic regime.

309

Metapolitics as violence: warriors and the cult of violence

The metapolitical discourse that binds the global new right together undermines not only the legitimacy of the political class but also the system in general. It attacks democracy, universal human rights, liberalism and socialism, in short, materialism. The meta-narrative is one that focuses on decline, decadence and the destruction of a people, its cultures and identity. ‘The enemy’, wrote Faye (2010: 18), ‘is no longer outside but inside the City, and the ruling ideology, paralyzed, is incapable of spotting him’. The mindset that is created is one in which people need to act now, in order to prevent the complete crumbling of society, of culture and of ‘who we are’. This type of discourse, with its palingenetic creed, tries to mobilize militants to act for change, to stop the decline and work towards a re-awakening that inaugurates a new era. It prepares for a revolution, for war. Faye is blunt about this:

The situation our forces find themselves in with respect to the system is similar to that which existed in the 1930s: no point of agreement is possible (…) the only strategy is all-out war. In adopting a revolutionary stance, aimed at overthrowing a civilization, we must be ready to face total war – fight without quarter.

(Faye, 2010: 19)

In the interregnum, the phase between the collapse of system and the new order, metapoliticians prepare for the construction of that new universe. Metapolitical actors are seen as responsible for producing the need to rethink a new world order and to fight for its birth. In order to realize that rebirth, a revolution of the mind is first needed. This is the metapolitical strategy: it is set up to socialize people. It hopes to create a shared analysis of the state of affairs and infuses a feeling of urgency. A feeling that action is needed now. After he creates that need to act, The Golden One also provides ways to act: he guides followers in finding the ‘right’ path. The Golden One tries to build ‘metapolitical warriors’, that is, alpha males that combine ideological socialization with the becoming of a ‘strong man’, a disciplined warrior willing to fight for his community, his ideals. A cult of the body is combined with ideological integration and learning how to defend oneself. That action is framed as individual and collective action. The Golden One helps turn ‘weak individuals’ into alpha men by inspiring them to go to the gym, stop masturbating and become strong. This – as we have seen – can be done individually: men are urged to become ‘real men’, to turn themselves into alpha men. This fight can also be done in relation to a network of men. The Wild Hunt challenge creates networks of individuals that socialize themselves online.

310The identitarian movement adopts a similar focus. Their narrative about replacement and the need to ‘defend ourselves, our identity and Europe’ speaks with the same urgency to take action. This action is found in the different highly mediatized controversial actions of the movement, but it was also visible in their offline boxing school where they taught their members how to box and defend themselves. This practice was also adopted by Schild & Vrienden in Flanders. They too set up regular boxing, kickboxing and self-defence classes for its militants and posted about it on their socials. Implicit in this discourse on ‘defending oneself’ is the construction of the other as aggressor, colonizer and destroyer of traditions, culture and identity. The other is the migrant, the left activist, the LGBTQ+ person, the politician, the human rights activist. The metapolitical discourse about migration as colonization is a form of symbolic violence, especially when it succeeds in becoming hegemonic, and thus imposes its meaning on society. When they successfully frame ‘the other’, they construct ‘the other’ as enemy and obfuscate the real power relationships and actual policies. This adds an enormous symbolic force to the already unequal power relationships as it frames minorities as warriors in disguise, as Trojan horses. Their humanity is denied as they are never seen as humans that seek help and deserve a humanist approach. They are the only enemies that are at war with us, that are destroying our culture, traditions, society and identity with support of the elites.

The great replacement discourse and its call directed to young men to become warriors in the face of this attack are more than just words. Words are performative. They set their mind towards certain behaviours. That behaviour can be activist in the sense of liking, sharing, posting and commenting online. They can also become members of more activist movements, and start training. Once socialized in that world, all observations can be framed in this logic: from Covid-19 to the presence of different languages in their neighbourhood. It can all become evidence that urgent action is needed. The manifesto of the Buffalo shooter draws radical but logical conclusions from the white genocide/great replacement narrative that is mainstream within the global new right. When he contextualizes his terrorist killing spree, he uses a classic new right discourse:

We must inevitably correct the disaster of hedonistic, nihilistic individualism. But it will take some time, time we do not have due to the crisis of mass immigration. Due to mass immigration we lack the time scale required to enact the civilizational paradigm shift we need to undertake to return to health and prosperity. Mass immigration will disenfranchise us, subvert our nations, destroy our communities, destroy our ethnic ties, destroy our cultures, destroy our peoples. Long before low fertility levels ever could. Thus, before we deal with the fertility rates, we must deal with 311both the invaders within our lands and the invaders that seek to enter our lands. We must crush immigration and deport those invaders already living on our soil. It is not just a matter of our prosperity, but the very survival of our people.

Not only mass immigration is a threat, but also hedonistic nihilistic individualism, our own will to reproduce and sustain our people. The difference between these terrorists and the metapoliticians is the notion of time. In the mind of the terrorist, we don’t have the time to convince others metapolitically, to work on the long term. We need to act right now for ‘the very survival of our people’. Metapolitics does not suffice, as it takes too much time. This is the paradox of successful metapolitics. From the moment it generates uptake, it opens up Pandora’s box. Especially in a digitally networked world, the ideas travel, morph and radicalize. Metapolitics may have been deployed to steer the ‘true right’ away from violence; the revolutionary ideas when one dares to take them to their logical conclusion give birth to violence. First symbolic violence, later physical violence. The transgressive humour ended up, at least in certain niches, in a terrorist culture. This evolution is not surprising, considering that the praising of the warrior, the importance of fighting skills, and the calls to action are so prominent in metapolitics 2.0. As a result, a true cult of violence has re-emerged. Professional metapoliticians know that they have to steer away from any public support of political violence, but behind the scenes, in chat groups, private servers and the darker corners of the internet, a new culture of violence is growing. This cult of violence is not mainstream within the global new right, but it is the logical consequence of their metapolitical project and it gives birth to marginal niches within this global new right network that celebrates violence, gamifies it and celebrates those who had the bravery ‘to act’, to bring it offline. Metapolitical terrorism is not just an act of networked individualism, it also contributes to a niched culture where violence is celebrated, where terrorists become heroes and stars in their own videogames. It is in those niches that new violent logics of action grow. Metapolitical terrorism is, as we have seen, strongly formatted: from the live streaming to the discourse used to legitimate their actions, there is remarkable consistency. It is a cultural phenomenon directed at awakening the masses, recruiting new soldiers in the civilizational battle. This cultural dimension becomes all the more clear when the terrorist counts on metapolitical prosumers to redistribute their content in the form of memes, Spotify lists, annotated manifestos and of course the video of the live streaming itself. After the Christchurch killing, users downloaded the live stream and edited it to circumvent automatic detection and deletion by Facebook and YouTube algorithms.

312YouTube reported that in the hours after the shooting videos were being posted at a rate of about one per second, with users editing the size of the clips, adding additional footage, or otherwise trying to fool the automatic censors.

(Byman, 2022: 96)

This type of algorithmic knowledge and practices is crucial to let this culture of violence grow.

This terrorist culture, covered in layers of irony or not, is not something to disregard. It contributes not only to the formatization of far-right terrorism, but it also normalizes violence. Users active in such radical niches get avalanches of discourses that legitimize, banalize, gamify and celebrate violence for ‘the good cause’. Even more, there is a far larger global new right network that gives an intellectual foundation for this type of action. When radical far-right platforms – like the Daily Stormer and Counter-Currents – disapprove of such killing sprees (as they don’t further the cause), the discourses that they produce do support the main theories that are used to legitimize these actions by their perpetrators. And nothing says that they wouldn’t support more collective acts of violence from the moment people in power call for urgent action. The Capitol Riots have proven that this is not entirely fictitious. The metapolitical discourse is still a revolutionary discourse and metapoliticians use the algorithmically structured platforms to prepare the militants to see themselves as warriors, as heroes in a civilizational revolution. As long as those metapolitical actors succeed in using digital platforms to find massive audiences, circumvent algorithmic moderation and use the popularity principle for their cause, so long will violence, algorithms and metapolitics stay intimately connected.

Epilogue Metapolitics, digital ethnography and democracy

DOI: 10.4324/9781003283379-10

This chapter has been made available under a CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 license.

‘Life’, wrote Dell Hymes (1969: 14),

Is impossible without something for which one can hope. Recognizing ourselves as members of an emerging world community, we cannot avoid hope (or despair) for it. When we study local communities, we cannot escape assumptions, open or hidden, as to that for which they hope and to what can be hoped for them.

Hymes here addresses a key issue within anthropology and ethnography (and in fact in all sciences), namely that the researcher is not an objective fly on the wall but is part of the production of knowledge. This position, he argues, shapes our role as researchers. ‘The general problem, then’, Hymes goes on, ‘is not simply empirical – what has occurred; nor only methodological and theoretical – how to study what has occurred, how best explain it. It is also a moral problem, a problem of one’s commitments in, and to, the world’ (Hymes, 1969: 14). The production of knowledge is connected not only to our position in society but also to how we want the world to look and thus to our worldview and hopes for a better world. ‘Anthropologists have indeed commonly thought of themselves as belonging to the “party of humanity”, and the world view Gay ascribes to the Enlightenment, as passionate rationalism and a tragic humanism is not alien to anthropologists’, said Hymes; ‘It is, I would urge, the view best suited to them’. In the same vein, Blommaert (2018: 16–17) argued that ethnography had the potential to become a democratic science. Ethnography is explicitly political as it has the potential to question ‘the truth’ of the powerful in society and fight to give voice to the oppressed, the discriminated and excluded.

316After reading this book, as an anthropologist or anyone who embraces a ‘tragic humanism’, feelings of despair may get the better of you. The ‘community’ studied here is not local but operates in a global network and its assumptions are not immediately favourable for those who hope that humanism, rationalism and Enlightenment values will prevail. Metapolitics in its traditional new right meaning, and its contemporary manifestation is a full frontal attack on humanism, the idea of universal human rights, Enlightened democracy, equality and freedom for an emerging world community. Ethnography, as anthropology’s most successful export product, is maybe best suited to bring back hope and the lust to fight for a world community where universal human rights are not paper tigers used to invade countries, but to work ‘in the spirit of what Marx called scientific socialism, for a just society and an individualistic culture where the free development of each is both enriched and restrained by the free development of all….’ (Hymes, 1969: 14).

Ethnography is clearly more than a method for collecting particular types of data that can be ad hoc added to other programmes. Ethnography is not empty but comes with a full scientific programme. For Hymes, ethnography could be ‘a democratic and anti-hegemonic science’ (Blommaert, 2018a: 16). This democratic and anti-hegemonic quality of ethnography starts with calling into question the status of truth, to find more and look deeper. It is this critical quality of ethnography that allowed me to not only describe the rise of the global new right and its metapolitical strategy, but hopefully also contribute to our understanding of that rise as a complex socio-technical assemblage that is only possible in specific social, economic, cultural and political contexts. The rise of the new right is clearly not a technological problem. The digital ethnographic approach (Varis, 2016) helped us to move beyond any technological determinism which is so popular today in explaining the role of technology in radicalization. In many accounts on online radicalization, one seems to blame ‘the recommendation algorithms’. The algorithms are seen as the main or maybe even the only actor that is responsible for the promotion of racism (Noble, 2018) or constructing a ‘rabbit hole’ and promoting ‘radicalization’ (Roose, 2019). Digital media scholar Tufekci, for instance, called the YouTube algorithm a great radicalizer and YouTube, ‘given its billion or so users’ (…), ‘one of the most powerful radicalizing instruments of the 21st century’ (Tufekci, 2018). Such claims give readers the impression that those recommendation algorithms work independently and overrule human agency. New research shows that YouTube’s recommendation mechanism does not promote inflammatory or radicalized content (Ledwich & Zaitsev, 2020). Both claims do rely on technological determinism, as they seem to understand the algorithms as completely independent actors. By adopting an ethnographic interactionist approach, the focus is not on the algorithms and the platforms alone but on what people do with interfaces and algorithms 317in particular contexts. It brings human (and non-human) agency in the picture when trying to understand radicalization processes in relation to digital media.

This digital ethnographic approach allows us to study metapolitics not in the abstract, but in the concrete and specific instances of metapolitical activity: in its social, political, economic, technological and historical context. The result is a theoretically inspired interpretation and description of contemporary metapolitics. It is in this thick description of metapolitics that we start seeing ‘radicalization’ in all its complexity. It is not just radical ideas that radicalize individuals. We see how contemporary metapolitical actors use existing niched and more mainstream (digital) cultures, hegemonic ideas and algorithmic knowledge to build a polycentric, transnational and layered cultural niche. How they make use of the digital utopianist ideologies that organize our digital media. How they use search engine and social media optimization, influencer culture, data voids, meme culture and trolling to normalize their viewpoints. How they build their own media and set up Green Peace-like activism under the banner of democracy and free speech to destroy both. How they embrace and support political candidates in which they see metapolitical potential. The result of these metapolitical endeavours is the emergence of an expanding translocal and polycentric cultural niche in which new recruits find a coherent world. A world that uses technologies and existing normalities to preconfigure a new world. A world that is grounded in the rejection of ‘globalism’ which functions as a shorthand for liberal democracy and socialist democracy, but also the welfare state, the idea of universal human rights and humankind in general. Enlightenment modernity is attacked fully frontal (see Faye, 2010, 2011; Krebs, 2012) in the name of democracy, anti-racism and feminism. The truth is that these Enlightenment concepts are filled with ethnocracy, organicism and inequality. This anti-Enlightenment thought is updated and repackaged, but the ideas have already proven to bring nothing good.

This new right world fuses traditionalism with technology. It is grounded in a new modernity, a modernity that embraces technological progress and digital cultures. This reconciliation of technology and traditional values and the fight for a different, archeofuturistic world, to use Guillaume Faye’s lingo, is grounded in a celebration of inequality and a propagation of war: war against everyone who is different, is born in a different place, loves somebody of the same sex or embraces queerness. This anti-Enlightenment tradition comes as a full-blown alternative for liberal democracy and socialist utopias. It uses key infrastructures of the neoliberalist economy and adopts libertarian digital cultures and injects them with far-right metapolitics. Several ideas have already escaped the margins decades ago and restructured our world in a less just world, a world with less hope for a world community, a just world built on humanist values.

318The mass movements of the 20th century have been replaced by a polycentric network. The cult of the leader has been replaced by micro-cults of many different leaders in many different niches. And the all-encompassing ideology has fragmented over the different niches. All those niches are formed around different micro-ideologies (anti-feminism, racism, conservativism, gamer culture, incels, metapolitical terrorism). In all those niches, we see essential ingredients, but rarely all ingredients of new right ideology at the same time. Note, however, that once these niches are fused, full-blown ideologically motived mass movements hit the streets: we have seen snippets of what that alternative looks like in the Capitol Riots, in the support of failed and successful terrorists and in the rise in far-right terrorism. This new right ideology has all ingredients in itself to build a radical, modern, authoritarian and exclusive world order. This new world order is now preconfigured within the global new right network. Nationalism is replaced by a transnational battle for organic communities on the one hand, and white civilization on the other. It is grounded in a fierce dislike of equality and the idea of Universal Human Rights and in a vision of humans as conditioned by history, culture and in the end race. It is this vision on humankind that is fundamental to the metapolitical battle. From the moment this view on men and women is accepted, the larger building blocks of the Enlightenment tradition will start to crumble as well. ‘The eruption of irrationality, the destruction of the idea of the unity of the human race and an absolute fate in the capacity of the political power to mold society’, as Zeev Sternhell (2010: 443) concluded, were responsible for the massacres of the 20th century. These ideas are not just back, they are finding traction among young and older generations around the world. They are promoted by influencers, activists, politicians and political parties. The new communicative economy is at least partially enabling this new wave of far-right metapolitics. And when it hits the streets, we see the same consequences as always: attacks on democracy, people on the left, migrants and of course equality and the Enlightenment tradition in general. If we turn our heads, if we do not engage in an in-depth study, and if we do not dare to draw the consequences from those studies and face the social evils, we will lose more than we would dare to accept today.
